Living and Work Literacy 3
Starting out on your own in a new business is very challenging. You may succeed or you may fail; 
you may make a modest living or you may become a millionaire. Often people go into business 
to sell something original that they have created. Protection for their invention or creation can be 
provided through copyrights and patents. Copyright and patent holders can sue any person or 
business who infringes their rights.
IP Australia is a federal government agency responsible for granting rights in patents, trade marks 
and designs. It is an agency within the Department of Industry, Tourism and Resources, but operates 
independently.
Scenario	1	–	Mikki	
Mikki is a rock musician who has written some new songs. 
She has performed them at concerts and they have been 
very popular with the audiences. Mikki decides she wants to 
make a CD of her songs, and makes arrangements with a 
recording studio. 
As the creator of something which is original, Mikki has 
intellectual property. She has certain exclusive rights in the 
same way as a writer or artist does. She can control how 
her original work is used or sold and is granted copyright 
over that work. She is entitled to royalties (a form of 
income) from others using her work. If a radio station 
wants to play the CD they must obtain permission from the 
copyright holder and pay royalties to that person. 
If Mikki becomes highly successful, she may appoint 
an agent to act on her behalf, to negotiate contracts, 
payments, future concerts and CDs. The agent would be 
paid a commission or a fee. 
Scenario	2	–	Crazy	Guggenheim
Everyone at school reckoned that she was a 
bit crazy. She was always inventing something 
and making all sorts of wacky gadgets, and so 
the name ‘Crazy Guggenheim’ stuck. 
When she left school, Crazy invented a 
gadget which attracted interest from some 
technological industries. She decided to take 
out a patent on her invention, which gave her 
exclusive rights to make her gadget or sell her 
invention to others. She began manufacturing 
her gadget, and registered a trade mark to 
distinguish it from future copies.

10	 Are business names and company names the same thing? Explain.
Naming	and	registering	your	business
A business name is a name under which a business operates. Registration serves as a means of 
identifying the owners of the business and is obtained under state or territory legislation.
A company name must be registered under the national Corporations Law administered by the 
Australian Securities and Investments Commission.
If a company wishes to trade using a name other than the registered company name, it has to 
register that name as a business name.
A domain name is the Internet address of a business – for example, the address of Internet store 
Amazon is www.amazon.com. Finding the right domain name can be difficult. A business should 
have a domain name that matches the registered business name or trade mark, but this name may 
have been bought by somebody else.  
Caution: When you register your business name, be careful that it does not infringe on someone 
else’s trade mark. It is always wise to search the trade mark databases first. IP Australia provides a 
professional search service called the Business Names Applicant Search Service

7	Buying	into	a	franchise
A franchise is a legal and commercial relationship between the owner of a trademark, trade name, 
or advertising symbol and an individual or group wishing to use that identification in a business. 
The franchise governs the method of conducting business between the two parties. Generally, the 
franchisor is the one who owns the trademark or symbol and the franchisee is the one who sells 
goods or services supplied according to the franchisor’s quality standards. 
Franchising is based on mutual trust between the franchisor and franchisee.
The	franchisor:
provides the business expertise in the form of marketing plans, management guidance, financing 
assistance, site location, and advertising 
assists in training the franchisee. 
The	franchisee:	
does all the work at the local level
provides the entrepreneurial spirit and 
drive necessary to make the franchise  
a success.
Examples	of	franchises:
McDonalds
Hungry Jacks
Subway
Tupperware
Century 21 Real Estate
The	sandwich	that	ate	Melbourne
‘Epicure’ The Age 18 October 2005 
Subway franchises are corporatising lunchtime. 
Does this mean choice is sunk? 
Melinda Houston reports.
You know you’ve made it when you feature in 
an episode of South Park. So when Jared, the 
slim(mish) spokesman for sandwich franchise 
Subway recently starred alongside Kenny, 
Cartman et al, we knew the stores had well and 
truly penetrated popular consciousness. 
And if it seems to you there are an awful lot of them, you’re right. In Australia, Subway outlets now 
outnumber McDonald’s franchises (824 to 733), although they’re still behind in turnover. There are 
12 Subways in the CBD alone, and 144 in the Melbourne metro area. And according to AC Nielsen, 
Subway is our second-most popular choice for takeaway, right behind Maccas and ahead of Pizza 
Hut, KFC, Hungry Jacks, and the rest.  
The Glen Waverley franchise is owned by Martin and Marusca Cantania. They were early adopters of 
the Subway system (they bought their first store in 1999) and now own three, with another three in 
the pipeline. In the mid-1990s the couple decided they wanted to go into business for themselves 
and started doing their homework. They thought about a cafe, a coffee shop, their own sandwich 
joint. They looked at Subway. ‘We liked the Subway concept but thought, ‘It’s very US, would it 
work here?’

‘The advantage over a corner store is the brand recognition,’ Martin says. ‘1t’s really very simple. 
Subway’s attitude,’ he says, ‘is to make entrepreneurs out of ordinary people. Subway sets up 
international conference calls for people who are multi-franchisees so we can talk, share experiences. 
So each franchisee develops their own infrastructure and business plan but they also have the 
opportunity to tap into other people’s experience.’
Becoming a Subway franchisee is reasonably rigorous. You have to develop your business plan 
and make an initial site selection, which Subway then approves according to its own demographic 
studies. There’s an interview process. A lease is arranged (the initial capital investment is about 
$200,000). There’s training, both in-store and in the classroom. And once you open, a ‘field 
consultant` drops by once a month to make sure you’re doing everything as you should. Brands 
such as Subway (or Maccas or Starbucks) live or die by the consistency of stores across cities, 
countries and international boundaries.

9	Developing	a	business	plan
A well prepared business plan is essential to success in business. You need to know what you are 
doing and a business plan will help you. It does not have to be complicated.
Some basic questions to ask:
What business am I in?
What am I selling?
Who will I be selling to?
Why would people want to buy this product?
Important	terms
Business plan: the overall plan showing how your 
business will operate
Mission statement: a short statement of the aims or 
goals of the business
Marketing plan: how the business is going to promote 
and sell the product
Action plan: step by step, what is to be done and 
when
Management plan: how the business is to be organised and run on a day-to-day basis
Financial plan: how the accounting and financial arrangements will be made
A	sample	business	plan
Jack and Jill have decided to go into business selling plants at a stall outside their house. They figure 
all they have to do is collect seeds and cuttings from friends and establish the plants in pots in a 
greenhouse in their back yard. When the plants are ready for sale, they will be able to carry them 
to the front of their house, where they can erect a small table with some advertising signs alerting 
passers-by to what they have for sale.

Being an effective manager of a business, whether large or small, involves certain skills and abilities. 
There are many personal qualities required, such as courtesy, ability to relate to people, ability to 
handle stress, capacity for hard work and willingness to accept responsibility.
Working hard is one thing but it is perhaps more important to work smart. There are some 
important skills and abilities which are either required or at least desirable.
Creativity – Creativity is one of the most important qualities in a successful businessperson. The 
whole essence of entrepreneurship is creating a new business. Creative ideas are limited only by 
one’s imagination and creative ability.
Leadership – What is leadership? Is it important in a business? There are different leadership styles. 
By examining the two emails below, from two different sales managers, you may get a clue as to 
which leadership style is the most effective.
10	Managing	a	business
Memo to all staff
 From: Malachi Berkin
To: All staff
Subject: Monthly sales figures
I have just examined the monthly sales 
figures and they are down on the previous 
month. I can only conclude that people are 
not working hard enough. In future I want 
everyone to cut back on their lunch hours, 
stop wasting time and get on with the work 
that has to be done. Failure to obey this 
directive will lead to severe consequences.
Organisational	skills
Two of the most important organisational skills one can have are:
Time management – when you consider there are 24 hours in a day and you allow some hours 
for sleeping and eating, the question is how to spend the hours available. This is why schedules, 
lists and timetables will help you organise your day and your week. Work hard by all means, but 
work smart. Balancing work and leisure time is also important.
Delegation – Delegation means asking other people to do specific tasks or take responsibility for 
specific areas of the business. One person cannot physically do everything, so he or she has to 
delegate. Knowing what to delegate and to whom is an art. You need to know the capacity or 
ability of the people you are delegating tasks to and the likely success that person will have of 
doing the task. Supportive supervision is also important. On the next page are examples of two 
methods of delegation and the likely response from staff. 
Evaluation - In managing your business you need to evaluate progress from time to time, to see 
if there are any problems, bottlenecks or better ways of doing things. You can learn from mistakes 
and put in place new or better procedures.
•
•
•
What	leadership	is	about:
Being supportive
Consulting with others
Organising people and resources to achieve 
goals
Setting an example to others
Suggesting strategies and actions for others 
to follow
•
•
•
•
•
What	leadership	is	not	about:
Ordering or bossing people around
Speaking loudly
Insisting on being right all the time
Forcing people to support you
•
•
•
•
Memo to all staff
From: Helena Polek, Sales manager 
To: All staff
Subject: Monthly sales figures
I have just examined the monthly sales 
figures and they are down on the previous 
month. I would like to ask staff if they have 
any ideas as to why sales are down and, more 
importantly, what suggestions they have for 
improvements. If anyone would like to see 
me about this, remember my door is always 
open.

11	Designing	your	own	office
Regardless of what business you are in, you need a space to work. For many it might be an office. 
Whether you are a café owner, an electrician or a solicitor you will need some office space to keep 
basic records ( such as appointments or bookings) and financial records (such as cash and credit 
transactions, profit statements, balance sheets, money owed by customers and money owing to 
suppliers). An office may be small or large, depending on need, and it may have various items of 
furniture and equipment (such as those listed below). Office furniture and equipment today tends 
to be ergonomic in design (to prevent back, leg or arm and wrist injuries ).
Furniture	
Equipment
Desk and chair 
• Telephone
Filing cabinet(s) 
• FAX machine
Workspace (bench) 
• Computer and/or laptop
Shelves 
• Photocopier
Comfortable chairs 
Where a business employs several people in an office, the design of the office is important. Today’s 
modern offices tend to be more open plan, ideally with the supervisor or manager in the centre 
where they have the greatest access to employees.
Office desks are now called workstations, set up with computer terminal, telephone and other 
electronic equipment. Some businesses use ‘hot desks’ for people who work part-time or who work 
in the field. These people are then able to ‘book a desk’ for a specific time.

12	Marketing	and	promoting
Marketing is simply a set of strategies to promote, advertise and sell goods and services to 
consumers. It lets them know what is available. Marketing can involve a whole range of strategies, 
such as discounts, special offers, promotions, prizes, competitions and free gifts.
Important	terms
Target market: a specific group of customers a business is trying to sell to
Market segmentation: dividing up the market into specific sections (such as teenagers, retirees, 
females aged between 18 and 25)
Niche market: a small selective market (such as organically grown vegetables), for a limited number 
of customers 
The	four	Ps	of	marketing:
Product – what are you selling?
Price – what price will you sell it for?
Promotion – how will you let people know about it? 
Place – how will you distribute it?
These four Ps can be identified in the story of Amy and Malik below.
•
•
•
•
Amy and Malik decided to go into business selling snack foods and drinks from a mobile van at a 
beach suburb. In their marketing plan they first identified the products they were going to sell. This 
included soft drinks such as Coca Cola and Fanta, tea and coffee, and food items such as donuts, 
cakes, biscuits, packets of potato chips and peanuts.
The pricing of their products was based on the cost of the goods bought from suppliers, adding 
a margin for profit and establishing a selling price. They would also have to cover costs such as 
advertising, electricity, repayments on their van and other costs. The selling price had to be calculated 
carefully. If it was too high, nobody would buy 
their food and drinks, especially if there were 
competitors selling the same or similar food 
at cheaper prices. If, on the other hand they 
priced their products too low, they would be 
in danger of running their business at a loss.
They needed to promote their products so 
they printed letter-box flyers and distributed 
them in the area near the beach. They also 
advertised in the local newspaper and had 
large signs made for their mobile van. One 
of these advertised: ‘SPECIAL OF THE DAY’, 
which might be ‘DONUT AND COFFEE – $5’. 
They thought that this might appeal to a 
particular market segment (such as coffee 
lovers). They had identified their target market 
as the people walking to or from the beach.
They realised that the place where they 
were going to sell their products was very 
important, so they set up their mobile van 
where they could intercept the greatest 
number of potential customers. This was along 
the boardwalk right beside the beach. They 
needed local council permission to do this, 
which they applied for and received.

If you have established and developed a successful business, you may wish to expand. You can 
change the ownership, from sole trader to partnership or company, or there are other ways you can 
expand.

prepared packs of frozen pasta dishes for sale. Their target market was busy people who would use 
their microwave ovens to heat a quick instant meal when they got home from work. Their business 
prospered and they made enough money to consider expanding. If success continued, they knew 
they could form a company by selling shares. This could be a private company (of friends and 
business associates) or a public company which would be listed on the Australian Stock Exchange 
and in which members of the public could buy shares. The company might be called Z Foods

15	Risk	management
Managing a business is always a risk. Some 
businesses start well and then go through 
difficult times. Others start slowly and then 
experience success. Many fail after less than 
one year, while some last longer. Some 
people actually go out of business only to 
start up again and perhaps succeed. There is 
plenty of evidence of people who have gone 
into business and the venture has not been 
successful. Success and failure are part of the 
scene.
John	Symond	and	Aussie	Home	Loans:	A	case	study
John Symond started out as a solicitor. He spent 15 years doing conveyancing (property) work and 
became very successful. In 1984 he branched into lending to property developers, but by 1991 
his business had collapsed because of falling property prices during the recession. In 1992, John 
Symond launched a new business based around buying homes.
As the founder of Aussie Home Loans, John Symond is now worth over $470 million and has 1000 
staff working for him. Aussie Home Loans has $17 billion in home loans and is the leading non-bank 
lender in Australia.
The case study of John Symond is an example of a businessperson who experienced success, then 
failure and success again. One reason for his success is that he was prepared to take risks, though 
this is no guarantee that a business will succeed. 
Business	risks
There are many reasons for a business to fail. The sample case studies described below provide 
a cross section of the types of risks that a business can face. They show theft or fraud, natural 
disasters, changes in regulations, luck, economic downturn or just plain bad management.

had been in operation with the current 
owner for 10 years or more. 
In 2004, there were 1,269,000 small 
businesses operating in Australia.

16	Doing	business	on	the	Internet
The growth of the Internet has been spectacular over the last ten years and has changed our lives 
in more ways than we imagine. It has changed the way businesses operate and the way consumers 
behave. Buying and selling online, for example, has grown remarkably in recent times. Many business-
to-business transactions are also done via the Internet.
Buying	online
The Internet has created a huge 
marketplace for goods and services. 
Buying goods online has become very 
popular, as more companies offer online 
buying services. You can even sell goods 
online through websites like eBay, via a 
bidding system which puts buyers and 
sellers in touch with each other.
Nudie	juice:	A	case	study
Naked ambition
Sydney Morning Herald, Enterprise  
17 August 2004
The founder of nudie is ready to squeeze 
all he can out of his cute and catchy 
brand name.
Tim Pethick, former accountant, 
management consultant, restaurant owner, 
advertising director and chief executive, is 
now the man behind nudie.
Nudie fruit juices have been on the shelves 
for just over 18 months and even Pethick 
is amazed by how quickly his branding 
experiment has caught on.
Citing reasons for nudie’s success, Pethick 
says: ‘It’s the name, which is different 
and not one you’d normally expect to be 
associated with a juice; it’s the colour, it’s 
the characters, it’s the cheeky tone of voice we have on the labels and in our copy. All the elements 
come together to make the whole. And I think we’re very lucky to have all the right elements.’
But having all the right elements requires much more than luck. There has been some very careful 
planning behind nudie.
‘Primarily, what nudie is about is a different approach to building a brand. I don’t think brands are 
built very well in this country,’ says Pethick, who has worked for a number of years in the United 
States and the United Kingdom.
Building a dialogue with consumers is central to the nudie brand proposition, and the Internet has 
played an instrumental role in this. ‘We put our web address on everything so people always have a 
place to go if they want to know more. Because we don’t advertise, people first discover nudie on a 
fridge shelf or someone tells them about it. When you hear about it, you want to know more and the 
web is the first place people go to learn more. So they start this process of becoming involved with 
the brand.
For the 10 years before starting nudie, Pethick was employed in corporate roles investigating how to 
use technology to change the underlying structure of a business. ‘The Internet has become incredibly 
important. For many businesses – including ours – the Internet is now like a front door to the 
business,’ says Tall Tim, as he is known on the website. ‘And more importantly, given that the nudie

17	Keeping	records
It is very important for businesses to keep accurate records of all financial transactions. A business 
needs to know the following.
Is the price right for the products they sell?
What is the business’s financial situation in relation to assets and liabilities?
Is the business making money?
How much does the business owe to others?
How much is owed to the business by others?
How much available cash does the business have to pay immediate bills?
How much tax does the business owe?
Many businesses fail as a result of poor financial planning and recording. A good accountant can 
supervise the financial transactions and make suggestions, and a business can also request an 
auditor (someone outside the business) to examine accounts on an official basis.
Financial transactions involve forms or documents, such as tax invoices, statements, cheques and 
receipts. In the past, book-keeping involved journals which recorded daily transactions, and ledgers 
which grouped transactions into specific accounts. Businesses today increasingly use computer 
technology to manage and analyse their accounts, and make particular use of spreadsheets which 
can do a great variety of calculations automatically.
Calculating	your	true	financial	situation
A business must always know its true financial situation so that it can make decisions about the 
future. Part of this involves the communication between a business and its bank, and reconciling 
the bank balances. This is done via a Bank Reconciliation Statement (see example below).

bank, ABZ Bank, believes the company has $2000. Why the difference? There is a time lag between

have not found their way to the 
bank. Perhaps some payees are slow 
in depositing their cheques (in the 
example below, ’Less unpresented

18	Profit	and	loss	statements
If you are running a business you will want to 
know if you are making a profit. This means 
that you want to know if your income is greater 
than your expenses, and by how much. A profit 
and loss statement, sometimes called a revenue 
statement, will provide this information. The 
statement is for a period of time, for example  
3 months, 6 months or 12 months.
Profit and loss statements are set out in a 
particular way. The main elements are:
sales – the income from the business will come 
mainly from sales
expenses – the costs incurred by the business in 
its operation (such as wages, electricity, rent)
gross profit – this is calculated by deducting the 
cost of the goods sold from the sales figure. It 
includes purchases as well as opening and 
closing stock (see example at right). To 
calculate the cost of goods sold, add purchases 
to opening stock and then deduct closing stock 
(unsold stock)
net profit – this is the actual amount that the 
business makes for its owner, although the 
owner will have to pay tax on this amount.

19	Balance	sheets
As a businessperson you may need to know what the state of your finances is at a particular point 
in time or on a particular date. Balance sheets are used for this purpose. They weigh up the assets, 
the liabilities and the owner’s equity in the business. The owner, or owners, have put money into 
the business and they therefore have a claim on that. After a business has been trading for a period 
of time, the amount the business owes the owner(s) will vary depending on whether profits or 
losses have been made.
Important	terms
Assets – things that a business owns, such as a truck
Liabilities – what a business owes to others, such as a debt 
for goods bought on credit
Owner’s Equity – what the business owes the owner or 
owners

20	Managing	finances
Tsang Yuan, the owner of the Tsang Toy 
Company, wanted to know how he was 
going in his business and whether he was 
achieving the goals he set for himself. 
He realised that his record keeping was 
important but he wanted to analyse what 
was happening. He had checked his profit 
and loss statements and balance sheets but 
there were other checks he could make. 
He could check on the accounts receivable 
and accounts payable and he could also 
prepare a cash flow report.
Cash	flow	reports
These will tell Yuan where cash is coming into the business and where cash is going out. Remember 
that not all business transactions are cash. Many businesses operate on credit, but these debts need 
to be recovered. Equally, other businesses would want you as a businessperson to pay your debts 
on time. Cash flow reports will reflect this movement of cash. Businesses in the past have run into 
trouble because of cash flow problems. Some adopt unfair tactics, in that they demand payment 
but don’t pay on time themselves. Juggling the cash flow and checking it are very important.
Accounts receivable – This will tell the business owner which customers still have outstanding 
debts and the amount they owe.
Accounts payable – This tells the business owner what their debts are and how much they will 
have to pay at some time in the future.

21	Taxes	and	the	GST
There are different types of taxes which affect individuals and also businesses. Individuals pay 
income tax based on the income they earn (using the PAYG or Pay As You Go system). A sole trader 
is an individual taxpayer and is subject to the same income tax rates that would apply to a wage or 
salary earner. Partnerships are treated in the same way.
Companies, on the other hand, are 
subject to company tax which is paid 
by companies based on the profits of 
the business. The rate of tax is a fixed 
proportion of the profits earned. The 
company tax rate was fixed at 30% in 
2001 and has not changed.
The	GST	
The goods and services tax, or GST, is a broad-based tax of 10% on the value of most goods and 
services consumed in Australia. Some items, such as fresh food, are exempt. The GST is therefore 
included in the price of most goods and services.
How	the	GST	works
While consumers ultimately pay the GST, businesses have the task of collecting this tax at various 
stages in the production process. Businesses are required to have an ABN (Australian Business 
Number) and must be registered for GST with the Australian Tax Office. They also need to use tax 
invoices when selling goods and services. To do this they fill out a Business Activity Statement (BAS), 
usually every three months. They can claim tax credits (input tax credits for the GST are included in 
the price you have to pay for any item for use in your business). Input tax credits are explained in 
the diagram below.

In small groups, discuss experiences people you know have had when they began a 
new job. Make a list of the most common experiences or situations.

What is a workplace?
A workplace was once seen as an office, a factory, shop, building site or outdoor location where 
work was carried out. It was also regarded as a place where workers or employees worked for an 
employer and provided their labour in return for 
an income. While this is still true, the workplaces 
of today are much more varied. For many people, 
their workplace is not necessarily a fixed location. 
For example, truck drivers or delivery-van drivers, 
and some salespeople who have use of a company 
car to make contact with customers. 
Working from home is also a choice that some 
people have today. Some may use sewing 
machines while others use laptops, mobile phones 
and various other communication devices. Giving 
work to people who work at home under contract 
is called outsourcing. 
Their first job
Matt and Ilsa were young and keen, fresh out of school and they had just been offered their first 
real job. A year later they both felt they had done well and they wanted to share their knowledge. 
Therefore they decided to write down some suggestions for others starting a new job. They pointed 
out that starting a new job can be quite stressful or overwhelming at first, so it is important to 
consider how to ease the transition from school to work. Here are some of the things they suggested.
•	 Check out the best way to get to work to make sure you arrive on time.
•	 Become familiar with the workplace environment, e.g. where are toilets, kitchen or staffrooms? You 
need to know your way around the building or work site to avoid becoming lost and embarrassed. 
•	 Learn your job responsibilities. This may take some time, so be patient.
•	 Ask questions. This has the double effect of providing information and showing how keen you are 
to succeed. Do not be afraid to admit mistakes and to seek help from your supervisor or employer.
•	 Become involved in the social life of the workplace. There are usually many opportunities to meet 
co-workers socially and you can learn a lot over lunch or drinks after work. Be careful however, of 
becoming involved in gossip or office politics and make sure your behaviour is professional at all 
times. 
•	 Be aware of issues such as sexual harassment and discrimination in the workplace. You do not have 
to tolerate this but should report such instances to your supervisor.
•	 Take the initiative. Do not always wait to be asked to do a task. Comments like ‘That’s not my job’ 
or ‘Why should I?’ indicate a poor attitude to work.
•	 Show some interest in advancement. Look for opportunities to do more difficult tasks once you 
have mastered your own, or to take on more responsibilities.
•	 Give yourself time. Do not make any hasty decisions to quit until you have given your new job a 
fair trial.
•	 You need to have balance in your social life and work life. Eating well and getting plenty of regular 
exercise will help you to remain fit and healthy and ready for work.

2 Payment for work
There are many forms of payment made to people who work. Some people work for an employer 
and receive wages or salaries, while others are self-employed.
Wages and salaries
Wages are calculated on an hourly basis. A wage earner may be offered overtime, which is more 
hours than the normal working day, and for these hours receives higher hourly rates called penalty 
rates.
Salaries are calculated on an annual basis even though the payment may be made in fortnightly or 
monthly instalments. A salaried worker has a job description and is expected to complete certain 
tasks during the day but is not entitled to overtime or penalty rates. Sometimes salaried workers 
may be expected to work extra hours to complete a particular task. The annual salary takes all this 
into account. 
Other incomes
People can also earn an income, not through any direct work but by using their money or their 
property. Their income may consist of interest, dividends or rent.
There are also people who receive an income, usually from the government, to assist them with 
their living expenses. This form of income is called an allowance.

3 Changing work patterns
In groups, discuss the statement: ‘There is no such thing as a job for life’.
T
R
Y
 
T
H
I
S
!
Case study:  Sonia Orchard
When Sonia Orchard graduated from high school, her main interests were world peace and feeding 
Africa. ’At the same time I was well aware they were kind of difficult things to study for,’ says Orchard, 
now 35. ’There was no diploma in world peace at the time.’
Instead, she enrolled in law. Then switched to arts (majoring in literature and classical studies). Then 
did a short course in food preparation at Melbourne hospitality TAFE, William Angliss. In the next five 
years, she travelled through Europe, Africa, the US and the Caribbean, working as everything from 
an au pair to a dive instructor. She came back to Australia and worked as an environmental scientist 
in the Northern Territory (having also completed a science degree). Then she returned to Melbourne, 
enrolled in yet another course, a TAFE professional writing and editing diploma at RMIT University 
and wrote a non fiction novel, Something More Wonderful, about the death of her best friend from 
cancer. These days, she is working on her second novel and supports herself teaching writing and 
piano. (She also managed an Associate Music Australia diploma at the Victorian College of the Arts 
along the way.)
’Theres that thing: I don’t know how I found myself here,’ she laughs. ’But I think you’re constantly 
making small choices, based on what you believe in and what’s important at the time, that lead you 
in a certain direction.’
Extract from article:  
The Itch to Switch By Melinda Houston. Sunday Life Magazine, Sun Herald 16 April 2006
Many changes have taken place in the workplace and in workplace arrangements in the past twenty 
years. The most common of these changes include:
a greater variety of jobs available
greater use of technology, especially computers and telecommunications equipment
gradual reduction in unskilled work
changing gender roles as more women become involved in professional occupations such as 
doctors, lawyers, company directors
more flexible work arrangements such as flexi-time, rostered days off, and people choosing to 
work at home or to work part-time
an increase in casual and contract work
a greater number of job changes in a person’s working life
In the past, people tended to have a job for life. In today’s workplace this is less common and 
people can be expected to have quite a number of job changes throughout their working life. One 
case in point is Sonia Orchard.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
Of course, not everyone will have the same dramatic changes as Sonia Orchard. However, in today’s 
workplace employees change jobs, companies and careers sometimes every few years. Now there 
is rarely such a thing as a job for life. Our parents and grandparents were often happy to stay put 
in one job until retirement. It was seen as secure and a way to pay off a mortgage. Employees 
today do not want a job for life and employers rarely offer it. Sometimes employers will put workers 
off and then re-employ them on a casual basis or on contract. Some companies encourage their 
workers to move from job to job within the company structure or even to leave the company, work 
for someone else and then return. 
Workers may decide to take time off and travel extensively overseas. Some take parental leave to 
help raise children. Whatever the reason or the motivation, the important thing is to return to the 
workplace refreshed and with a broader range of experiences.

4 Permanent or casual/full or part-time
There are many different working arrangements and entitlements for employees in the work force. 
However, all workers whether they are permanent or casual, work full-time or part-time, have 
certain rights. These include the right to be paid at least a minimum wage, the right to work in a 
safe and healthy workplace and the right to compensation if they are injured at work. 
What is the difference?
Permanent employees can expect regular, 
continuing employment, while casual work 
is more irregular and uncertain. Employers 
have no obligation to offer continuing 
work to a casual employee.
Full-time work is regarded as working 35 
hours per week or more on average, while 
part-time work is less than 35 hours per 
week, according to the Australian Bureau 
of Statistics.
Note that not all part-time workers are 
casual and not all full-time workers are 
permanent. There are many employees 
who have permanent part-time working 
arrangements. Equally, many casual 
employees work 35 hours or more in a 
working week.
Why do some people work 
part-time?
They may be caring for young children at 
home.
They may have other jobs, hobbies or 
interests.
They may have a personal preference to work 
part-time.
They may be financially secure and do not 
need the money.
They may have a job-sharing arrangement 
with another worker.
There may be no full-time work available 
for them.
•
•
•
•
•
•
Why do some people prefer 
casual work?
They may prefer the flexibility of working on a 
casual basis.
They may not wish to commit to a permanent 
position.
They may have other commitments.
•
•
•
Some employers may prefer to hire casual rather than permanent workers, as it may reduce their 
costs. For example, casual workers do not get all the entitlements (such as paid sick leave and 
annual leave) that permanent workers do. There is also an increasing trend for employers to prefer 
to hire workers under a contract rather than as permanent employees. There are many cases of 
employees who retire from their permanent positions only to be re-employed in the same or a 
similar role under contract. In these cases, the contract generally specifies a set of tasks to be 
completed for a set fee.

Living and Work Literacy 4
5 Working conditions
Working conditions today:
1. Hours of work
A 35-hour working week is regarded as full-time work.
There has been a steady growth in casual and part-time work.
There has been a marked increase in the number of hours being worked by full-time workers.
2. Benefits and entitlements
Leave generally consists of: annual (or holiday) leave, sick leave, family leave (maternity and 
paternity leave), long service leave, special leave (for example, to attend funerals), leave without 
pay.
In August 2005, 76% of employees were provided with one or more types of paid leave.
Full-time employees were more likely than part-time employees to have leave entitlements (87% 
compared with 41%).
Entitlements include fringe benefits (rewards for employees, income in kind), holiday leave 
loading, termination payouts and rights relating to unfair dismissal.
Fringe benefits typically include a company car, children’s education expenses, entertainment 
allowances and assistance with paying housing loans. These are often associated with a ‘salary 
package’.
Employers are required to provide superannuation benefits of 9% of wages for their employees’ 
retirement. Employees can also contribute money from their pay towards their own retirement.

worked 60 hours a week. In 1947 the trade unions

Working conditions today are very varied but there have certainly been great improvements 
since the 1850s. Some of the rules which may have applied to the clerical staff of a typical major 
warehouse company at that time are listed below.
Hours of work: 7 am to 6 pm
Daily prayers held each morning, which 
the staff were expected to attend
Staff expected to dress in ‘sober colours’
Permission to be obtained for visits to the 
toilet
Talking not allowed during business hours
Staff permitted to eat food between  
11.30 am and 12 noon, but not permitted 
to cease work.
Members of staff expected to provide their 
own pens
Junior staff required to clean the office 
after hours

5 Working conditions
Activities
1 
Why do you think many full-time workers are now working more than the 35-hour week? 
2 
Make a list of all the types of paid leave available to workers and describe the nature of each type.
3 
Read the list of workplace rules which typically applied in the 1850s.
 
a How did the hours of work compare with those operating today? Give specific examples.
 
b Why do you think daily prayers were said each day? Why wouldn’t this happen today?
 
c How have dress rules in the workplace changed over the years?
 
d Do you think there should be dress standards in the workplace? Explain how these may vary 
according to the occupations of the workers.
 
e List some of the other rules operating in the 1850s which do not apply today. Explain why they are 
no longer acceptable rules.
 
f Why are cleaners now employed to clean offices instead of expecting the clerical staff to do this?
 
g Are there still cases where employees must do cleaning? Explain.
4 
Why might a worker be granted leave without pay?
5 
What is superannuation? Is it a benefit or an entitlement, or both? Who pays it?
6 
What is meant by the following terms?
 
a paternity leave
 
b fringe benefits
 
c salary package
7 
What statistical evidence is there to show that full-time workers are more likely to have access to paid 
leave than part-time workers?
8 
Jody is a university student who works in a juice bar in the city. Her friend Nina, a university law 
graduate, works in a solicitors’ office, also in the city.
	
What differences are there likely to be in their working conditions? Mention things like hours of work, 
leave entitlements and any other entitlements or benefits.
In small groups, discuss the topic of working conditions that exist in most workplaces 
today. Construct a mind map based on these discussions.
Find out about other important industrial relations reforms over the past 100 
years in Australia. 
Choose three different countries, and draw up a chart comparing standard working 
conditions and entitlements in each country with the current working conditions 
and entitlements in Australia.
Look through the employment section of a newspaper. Find at least three 
advertisements that refer to different types of working conditions. Write a list of 
advantages and disadvantages for each one, then state which one you would 
prefer and why.

Living and Work Literacy 4
6 Sexual harassment
Sexual harassment in the workplace is any behaviour of a sexual nature which is unwelcome to 
the person concerned. Although sexual harassment is unlawful under the Sex discrimination Act of 
1984, it is still a common occurrence in Australian workplaces.
Some facts:
28% of women and 7% of men in Australia have experienced sexual harassment in some form in 
the workplace. 
Sexual harassment does not have to be physical in nature. It can include suggestive comments or 
jokes, intrusive questions about a person’s private life or repeated, unwanted invitations to go out 
on dates.
Physical sexual harassment occurred in 62% of cases while non-physical sexual harassment 
accounted for 38%.
•
•
•
Scott worked as a receptionist for a law firm. 
Morag, one of the lawyers, would often send SMS 
text messages and pictures of a sexual nature to his 
mobile phone. She would also tell him dirty jokes. 
Scott was unsure how to react to these jokes as he 
did not want to appear too narrow-minded, but he 
sometimes felt uncomfortable about them. Morag 
also showed Scott some pictures of pin-up men 
hanging on her office wall. At no time did Morag 
touch Scott inappropriately, nor did she ever ask 
him out on a date. 
Georgia worked on the cosmetics counter of a large 
department store. Her boss, Alex was constantly 
staring at her and making comments about her body. 
He also asked her to put on some perfume so he 
could check it out by kissing her neck. Georgia did 
not like this sort of behaviour and she told him so. 
He ignored her objections and then began touching 
her inappropriately and brushing up against her. 
When she objected again he called her into his office 
and told her she was being transferred to the dispatch 
office at the back of the store.
Emily and Ming started work 
together in a large insurance office. 
Ming found Emily to be an attractive 
and interesting person and he 
told her so. He would often make 
complimentary remarks about her 
appearance. Emily did not mind 
this and in fact, felt rather flattered. 
After a while Ming asked Emily out 
to dinner. She accepted and so began 
an office romance.

15
6 Sexual harassment
Activities
1 
Why do you think sexual harassment is unlawful?
2 
How is sexual harassment different from flirting among work colleagues?
3 
Can sexual harassment be non-physical? Explain.
4 
Review the stories of Emily and Ming, Georgia and Scott.
 
a Was there any sexual harassment in Ming’s behaviour? Explain.
 
b What would have to happen for it to be sexual harassment?
 
c Let us assume that the romantic relationship between Ming and Emily ends. They have a big 
argument. Emily then goes to her supervisor to report sexual harassment against Ming. If you were 
the supervisor, what would your attitude be, and what would you do about it?
 
d What should Georgia do about her situation?
 
e If Georgia’s employer tells her she is over-reacting and dismisses her case, what can she do?
 
f Do you believe that Scott was sexually harassed? Give reasons.
 
g Let us assume that Scott does report Morag to his employer. Morag is called in and when confronted 
with her actions, proceeds to sincerely apologise to Scott. What do you think should happen then?
 
h If you were Scott’s supervisor what action would you take?
 
i What would you do if Morag continued with her former behaviour?
 
j Let us assume that Scott decides to resign. As his supervisor, what is your attitude? What action 
could be taken against Morag?
5 
What is the percentage of Australian women and men who have experienced some form of sexual 
harassment in the workplace? Do you think these are high percentages? Explain.
6 
Make a list of the different types of behaviour which can be classed as sexual harassment.
In groups, take each of the three case studies and write a brief sequel to their stories. 
Each member of the group could propose a different ending for each story. 
Find out more about the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission and the 
statistical data related to sexual harassment in the workplace. Make a brief summary 
of this statistical information.

What can be done?
Any worker, whether male or female, can and should report cases of sexual harassment in the first 
instance to their manager, supervisor or employer. If there is no satisfactory outcome from this, a 
worker may report the matter to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission (HREOC).

Living and Work Literacy 4
7 Equal opportunity
Discrimination is defined as: Unfair treatment of a person or group on the basis of prejudice.
Society has come to realise that some groups of workers in the past have been treated unfairly. 
Equal opportunity is an important principle which operates in workplaces today and is now 
supported by legislation. In workplaces throughout Australia, it is against the law for any employee 
to be discriminated against by being refused employment or promotion, given less favourable 
conditions of employment or being dismissed because of their:
sex
pregnancy
race (colour, nationality, ethnic background)
marital status
sexual orientation
disability (physical or intellectual)
age
religion.
This law applies to all employees, including those on probation, apprentices, trainees, whether they 
are casual, permanent, part-time or full-time. 
The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission is a national independent statutory 
organisation established to promote and protect human rights in Australia. One of its main 
functions is to investigate and conciliate complaints of discrimination lodged under these laws: 
The Racial Discrimination Act 
The Sex Discrimination Act 
The Disability Discrimination Act 
The Age Discrimination Act.
The Commission also investigates and conciliates complaints of discrimination lodged under the 
Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission Act. Under this law you can make a complaint 
if you think you have been discriminated against in your employment on any grounds. The 
complaints process is private, confidential and free. 
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
Sex discrimination means 
being treated less favourably 
than someone else because 
of your sex or marital status 
or because you are pregnant.
Sexual harassment is a 
type of sex discrimination.
It is unlawful to dismiss 
a person from employment 
on the ground of family 
responsibilities such as 
care of children.
It is against the law for 
an employer to discriminate 
against any employees on 
the basis of race, colour, 
national or ethnic origin.
The Human Rights 
and Equal Opportunity 
Commission inquires into 
complaints of racial hatred. 
Racial hatred is defined as a 
public act which is likely to 
offend, insult, humiliate or 
intimidate a person or group 
and is based on race, colour, 
national or ethnic origin.
Employers are obliged 
to make reasonable 
arrangements to assist a 
person with a disability to 
carry out the required tasks 
of his or her job.
Age discrimination 
is not unlawful if a 
person is unable to 
carry out the required 
tasks because of his or 
her age. 
The law provides for positive age discrimination. 
This means helping people who experience a 
disadvantage because of their particular age.

7 Equal opportunity
Activities
1 
Complete the following sentences. It is unlawful for any employer to discriminate against an employee 
on the basis of their ___________________, their ___________________, their ___________________ or their 
___________________. The four Acts of Parliament which relate to this are the ___________________ Act, 
the ___________________ Act, the ___________________ Act and the ___________________ Act. These 
Acts apply to all employees, whether they have ___________________ or ___________________ status and 
whether they work ___________________ or ___________________.
2 
What do the letters HREOC stand for? What does this organisation do?
3 
What is sex discrimination? Give an example of how it might happen in the workplace.
4 
Why do you think the law prevents employers from discriminating against people with disabilities?
5 
You employ Jane, who has a disability. She has great difficulty in concentrating on a task for too long. 
You give her a task to do but you find that she can’t manage it because of her disability. What do you 
do?
6 
Maria works as a legal secretary and is regarded as being very efficient at her job. One day she informs 
her boss that she is pregnant. A week later her boss terminates her employment.
 
a Has Maria’s boss acted lawfully? Explain.
 
b What should Maria do in the first instance?
 
c What action can Maria take if her initial approaches are unsuccessful?
 
d What options might be available to Maria’s employer in this situation?
7 
Tran is employed as a carpenter on a building site. His supervisor regularly makes nasty comments 
about Tran’s ethnic origin. Tran is a good worker but he finds he is given all the unpleasant work to do 
while other workers seem to get preferential treatment.
 
a Is Tran being discriminated against at work? Explain.
 
b Could Tran’s supervisor be charged, and if so under which Act of Parliament?
 
c What action should Tran take if this situation continues?
 
d You have been asked by Tran to write a letter formally complaining about his treatment. Write 
the letter for Tran, describing the treatment he is receiving. Give details of specific behaviour, and 
comments made to Tran at his workplace.
8 
Sean is 65 years old and works as a sports commentator for a television network. He has had a 
successful career lasting over 30 years. One day he receives a phone call telling him his services are no 
longer required. He is told that the network is looking for a new image.
 
a Is Sean being discriminated against? Explain.
 
b Does the television network have any legal rights in this case? Explain.
 
c What might the network offer Sean?
9 
Fabio is a very good accountant for a major company. One day Tyrone, his employer, discovers that 
Fabio is gay. Tyrone instantly dismisses Fabio and tells him bluntly that having gay employees is not 
good for the company’s image. 
 
a Was Fabio dismissed unfairly? Explain.	
	
b  What options does Fabio have?
 
c Under which Act of Parliament could Fabio’s case be pursued?
Discuss the theme of equal opportunity as a class group. Provide specific examples of 
discrimination in the workplace from your own knowledge or personal experiences.  Make 
a list of the most common forms of discrimination.

Living and Work Literacy 4
8 Workplace agreements
Workers are generally employed on the basis 
of an employment contract. This sets out the 
pay and working conditions agreed to between 
employers and employees. Employment contracts 
may be either awards or workplace agreements.
What is an award?
An award is the minimum rate of pay and 
working conditions for a particular job. It is set 
by an industrial court such as the Australian 
Industrial Relations Commission. Awards are 
generally negotiated by trade unions for 
relatively large numbers of workers on an 
industry basis, e.g. the mining industry or the 
hospitality industry. 
What is a workplace agreement?
A workplace agreement is an agreement between an individual employee and an employer in 
their specific workplace situation. It aims to provide more consultation and greater flexibility in the 
workplace.
History of employment contracts
Employment contracts are governed by Australian Government legislation which sets out how 
agreements can be made. To understand the current situation with regard to workplace relations, 
it is important to consider the most significant developments in recent history. Some of these 
developments were:
The Conciliation & Arbitration Act of 1904 established the Award System. It had extensive powers to 
prevent and settle industrial disputes by conciliation and arbitration. In 1907 the concept of a basic 
wage was adopted. Some workers were covered by state awards and some by federal awards. 
The Industrial Relations Act of 1988 established the Australian Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC). 
Its aim was to conciliate (resolving disputes by consultations and compulsory conferences), and 
to compulsorily arbitrate (settle disputes) where necessary. Each state also had its own industrial 
commission to cover workers under state awards. 
Equal Pay Case. In 1993, the AIRC was given the power to make orders to ensure equal pay for work 
of equal value for both men and women. Female workers once received little more than half the 
pay that male workers received.
Major changes often come with a change of government. The 1996 Workplace Relations Act 
introduced Australian Workplace Agreements (AWAs). The AIRC lost its authority when a new body 
called the Employment Advocate was established. Awards could still be negotiated with the trade 
unions but the intention was to simplify them and reduce them in number.
Useful definitions
Basic wage:  pay which was considered enough for a family to live in reasonable comfort. The 
principle of the basic wage was adopted for all future wage fixing cases.
Consultation: process of two parties talking together about issues.
Conciliation: a process which attempts to resolve disputes by compromise or voluntary agreement.
Arbitration: making a decision or a judgement on an industrial dispute.
Compulsory conference: an industrial court orders a meeting between two parties in dispute.

agreements

8 Workplace agreements
Activities
1 
Explain the difference between an award and a workplace agreement.
2 
Explain the difference between the words ‘conciliation’ and ‘arbitration’.
3 
What did the Conciliation and Arbitration Act of 1904 establish? 
4 
Why do you think some workers were covered by state awards and others by federal awards?
5 
The basic wage was determined to be ‘that payable to an adult male worker supporting a non-working 
wife and two children’.
 
a Why do you think the basic wage concept was introduced? 
 
b Is the basic wage concept still relevant today? Explain.
 
c What could happen if there was no basic or minimum wage?
6 
What was the purpose of the AIRC?
7 
What major changes occurred with the Workplace Relations Act of 1996?
8 
In your own words, describe the changes that were made in 2006 to the Workplace Relations Act.
9 
What effects do you think this will have on: 
 
a the trade unions?
 
b young workers?
10 Do you think employers will benefit from the most recent changes? Explain.
Find out more information about ‘Work Choices’, in particular the impacts of the 2006 
legislation on different individuals or groups. 
Hold a class discussion on current industrial relations issues. Check the daily newspapers 
or the web for the latest developments.

The Work Choices Act, passed in 2006, brought major changes, amending the former Workplace 
Relations Act of 1996. The following fundamental changes were proposed.
Encouraging workplace agreements without the intervention of trade unions
Establishing the Australian Fair Pay Commission to set and review federal minimum wages
Prohibiting some working conditions from being included in workplace agreements
Removing the Australian Industrial Relations Commission’s powers to conciliate and arbitrate 
disputes or create new awards
Retaining unfair dismissal laws but confining their application to businesses with more than  
100 employees
Overriding state industrial relations laws, with a view to creating a national workplace relations 
system

Living and Work Literacy 4
9 Unemployment
Definitions   
A person is considered to be 
unemployed if they are:
not working
available for work
taking active steps to find work.
A person is considered to be employed 
if they work for one hour or more for 
pay, profit, commission or other form 
of payment.
The labour force includes all persons 
who are employed and unemployed.
The participation rate is the percentage 
of the population over 15 years who are 
in the labour force. 
Why are people unemployed?
Some may be in the process of 
changing jobs.
They may be unsuccessful in finding a 
job.
Some may have jobs which are seasonal 
with no work available in the off season.
In an economic downturn, 
unemployment levels may be high.
People with low skills or no job training find it more difficult to find a job.
Some people may need to consider retraining.
Young people may have difficulty finding a job because of their lack of experience.
Some people are fussy about the jobs they are prepared to do.
Youth unemployment
Many young people cannot find jobs because they have no experience. Yet how can they gain 
experience if no one will employ them? This is the dilemma faced by many young people and is a 
major reason why youth unemployment rates are higher than unemployment rates in the general 
community.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
Devi had a weekend job selling ice creams. When a new owner took over the business he demanded 
that Devi sign a new work contract. She refused as she realised that her pay was going to be cut. Not 
only was her hourly rate reduced, but she found she would not be paid penalty rates for working on 
Sundays. Her refusal to sign meant that she lost her job. She is now unemployed.
Leo and Russell worked as coal miners in a remote part 
of the country. Unfortunately, the mining company 
they worked for ran into financial difficulties because of 
falling coal prices. The mine was forced to close and as a 
result Leo and Russell are unemployed.
Sef was an early school leaver. He 
looked for a job but couldn’t find 
one. Wherever he went he was 
told that he had no skills and no 
experience. He is unemployed.

9 Unemployment
Activities 
1 
Is a person who is not actively looking for a job considered to be unemployed? Explain.
2 
Explain what is meant by the participation rate. What factors would cause it to change?
3 
Make a list of the reasons for unemployment in the workforce.
4 
Why is youth unemployment such a problem?
5 
What do you believe are the attitudes of employers to young workers? Give examples from your 
personal knowledge or experience.
6 
Review the story of Devi.
 
a How did Devi become unemployed?
 
b Why do you think Devi refused to sign  
the new work contract?
 
c What options did Devi then have?
 
d What is your view of Devi’s situation?
7 
Review the story of Leo and Russell.
 
a What caused them to become unemployed?
 
b What could they do about their situation?
 
c What would you do if you were in their situation?
8 
Read the story of Sef.
 
a Why was Sef unemployed?
 
b What could he do about his situation in the short term, and also in the long term?
 
c How is Sef’s story related to the problems of youth unemployment?
9 
Write your own story of a person who is unemployed. Your story should explain the circumstances and 
therefore the reasons for their unemployed status.
10 Study the table showing labour force statistics for April–May 2006.
 
a How many unemployed persons were there in May 2006? 
 
b Compared to the previous month, what was the actual difference?
 
c What was the unemployment rate in May 2006?
 
d What was the participation rate in May 2006?
 
e What has happened to the participation rate over the past year?
11 Study the graph showing unemployment in Australia since 1978. 
 
a In which year was unemployment at its highest level?
 
b Suggest a possible cause for this high level of unemployment.
 
c Why is it important to study unemployment rates in Australia?
12 Unemployment rates are higher in regional and rural areas of Australia than they are in the large cities. 
Explain some possible causes for this.
13 How does long-term unemployment affect	
a  individuals 	 	
b  their families?
14 How does the government help people who are unemployed? Check the Centrelink website to help 
you answer this question.
15 What can the government do for the long-term unemployed?
16 What effect would a growing Australian economy have on unemployment?
In small groups, discuss these statements: 
‘Take this job or be unemployed’. 
‘Employers complain that young people 
don’t want to work’. 
‘Young people complain about poor pay 
and working conditions’.

Living and Work Literacy 4
Workers’ Compensation
Workers who are injured in the course 
of their work are entitled to some 
compensation. Workers’ compensation 
generally means payments for loss of 
earnings as well as medical and hospital 
bills. All employers must take out a 
special insurance policy to cover their 
employees for workers’ compensation.
10 Workplace protection
Evelyn worked at a car parts factory which 
made gear boxes. Her job was on a metal 
press where she had to press a button to 
operate the press. One day she accidentally 
caught her hand in the press, suffering 
serious injuries. She needed immediate 
medical treatment and was off work for 
ten weeks. She reported the incident and 
submitted a Work Injury Report Form (using 
her good hand). The company paid her 
medical bills and arranged a rehabilitation 
program which involved exercising her 
hand. She was able to continue working at 
the factory but was assigned different duties 
which did not affect her injured hand. Six 
months later, her hand was fully recovered 
and she was able to resume her normal 
work.
If you suffer an injury or illness at 
work you are protected by workers’ 
compensation. 
Here are the steps you should follow:
1  Report the incident immediately to 
your employer, supervisor or OH & 
S representative.
2  If you visit a doctor, ask for a 
medical certificate.
3  Get a copy of a Work Injury Report 
Form from your employer or from 
WorkCover.
4  Fill in the details in the worker 
section on the form.
5  Give the form to your employer.
Your employer then completes the 
employer section and submits the 
form to WorkCover. When the claim 
has been processed you will receive 
the necessary medical treatment and 
rehabilitation to get you back to work 
as quickly and as safely as possible. 
Source: Starting a New Job. WorkCover Corporation 
of South Australia
Under Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) laws, both employees and employers have 
responsibility for health and safety in the workplace. Employers have a duty of care to protect the 
health and the safety of their workers.
New and inexperienced workers are more  
at risk of a workplace injury or illness than  
other workers. They are often unaware  
of the potential dangers which might  
exist in the workplace.
WorkCover authorities in each state in  
Australia provide information for employees  
who are injured at work. An example is shown  
below right.

Living and Work Literacy 4
11 Employment relations
A work buddy or a mentor
Every worker needs a buddy to lean on; someone to go to for advice; a shoulder to cry on; perhaps 
a role model; someone to be a supportive friend. Sometimes a more senior colleague can act as a 
mentor, and take a new employee under their wing, encouraging, advising and maybe helping train 
a worker for future promotion. 
Employer–employee relations
A good relationship with the boss is an 
important part of maintaining a happy 
work environment. An understanding of the 
different roles and duties of people in the 
workplace is essential for a good working 
environment. Adopting an ‘us and them’ 
mentality to employers or supervisors is 
unproductive and fruitless.
Office gossip
It can be easy to get caught up in office 
gossip or politics. Criticising work colleagues 
behind their backs is in poor taste and 
regarded as unprofessional. Relaxing after 
work, having a drink with workmates and 
having fun is OK but you need to be careful 
that you do not lose the respect of your 
work colleagues through irresponsible or 
inappropriate behaviour.
 
From: 
Sabina Bartoli, Branch Supervisor 
 
To: 
Adam Roberts
 
Sent: 
Monday 7th August 2006 2.40 pm
 
Subject: 
Professional behaviour  
I have noticed that you have been rather rude to your work colleagues 
lately. Swearing at them, abusing them and blaming them for your errors is 
unprofessional conduct. I would like you to think about this and then we can 
arrange to have a talk about it. I would like to help but I cannot allow this sort of 
behaviour to continue as it affects the harmony in the office.
Office emails
	
Anna:	
Hi, my name is Anna and I am going to be helping you in your new job.
	 Karina:	
Thanks Anna, are you going to be like my buddy?
	
Anna:	
Yes, you could put it that way. I want you to feel happy at work. I want you to understand 
that you will be relating to your work colleagues as well as your supervisor. Your own 
personality and personal skills will be visible to others and you will be judged on them. 
	 Karina:	
I hope I don’t disappoint everyone.
 
Anna:	
Don’t worry about it. You are bound to make some mistakes but that is a normal part of 
learning your job. If you approach your job with a positive attitude you will be fine. It is 
only when people whinge and complain or criticise others that problems can arise.

Living and Work Literacy 4
12 Industrial disputes
Industrial disputes occur when differences between employees and the employer arise. Some 
industrial disputes can be quickly and easily solved. A complaint about the state of the staff toilets 
or lunchroom can be brought to the attention of the employers. They examine the situation 
and agree to fix the problem. Most of the minor disputes can be solved in this way, by mutual 
agreement and a ‘give and take’ attitude by both parties. Reductions in pay rates, especially penalty 
rates, or cuts in leave entitlements however, are generally more controversial.
A typical dispute might take the following course:
Phase 1  The RU E-Tin Restaurant employs 20 people, most of whom work on weekends. The 
restaurant owners have decided to refuse to pay penalty rates for weekend work. All 
employees will be forced to take a cut in pay.
Phase 2  The employees call a stopwork meeting to discuss the situation. For this meeting they 
decide to call in a trade union organiser to discuss their options.
Phase 3  The trade union organiser addresses the meeting of employees and suggests they take 
their complaints, as a group, to their employer. If this proves unsuccessful they could 
decide to go on strike. She explains the types of strikes they have at their disposal, 
such as a lightning strike which is called quickly, often without trade union approval, 
a wildcat strike which is not organised by a trade union, a sit-down strike where 
employees go to work but do nothing, or a rolling strike where there is a succession of 
strikes at short intervals.
Phase 4  Negotiations with the employer fail and so a strike is called. Most employees withdraw 
their labour. Some however, are not trade union members and do not agree with the 
strike, and so they decide to return to work. Union members who are on strike then 
form a picket line at the entrance to the restaurant.
Phase 5  Meanwhile, the restaurant owners hear of this proposed strike and decide to lock out 
the workers and employ members of their own family to run the restaurant.
Phase 6  The restaurant owners and the employees meet again to try to resolve the dispute. No 
agreement is reached.
Phase 7  Since this is an industrial dispute, both parties are summoned to appear before an 
industrial court. The court calls for a compulsory conference between the two parties to 
try to resolve the dispute. This fails and so the matter is subjected to arbitration. 
Phase 8  The industrial court orders the employees back to work. Some of them go back to work 
and accept the reduced pay, while others resign on principle.

Living and Work Literacy 4
13 Trade unions
What is a trade union?
It is an organisation which represents a group of workers who unite to maintain and improve pay 
rates and working conditions.
Falling membership
At the beginning of the 20th century, Australia had the most unionised workforce in the world. 
Although membership rose and fell at different times, over 50% of employees belonged to a union. 
Today, union membership is less than 25%. There are many reasons for the change, one being the 
increase in self-employed Australians.
The trade unions have embarked on membership drives aimed at signing up new members as well 
as retaining existing membership. Over the years, workers have become more critical of unions 
and want to see some benefit in being a member. The trade unions in turn have begun offering 
incentives such as discount housing loans, free legal services, travel services, credit cards and health 
benefits. The main focus of the trade union movement however, is to protect workers’ rights.
The trade union movement is also trying to address the falling membership by arranging 
amalgamations, so that small trade unions join together to form a large super union with more 
power. 
Changes to the Workplace Relations Act in 2006 resulted in increased interest by employees in 
joining a trade union. This was indicated by a 4% increase in membership from August 2004 to 
August 2005 from 1 838 365 to 1 911 900. 
The main union body is the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU). It plays a key role in wage 
fixing in Australia through submissions in National Wage Cases which set minimum rates of pay for 
award-covered employees.
Do I have to join a union?
You do not have to join a union. Federal laws 
make it illegal to either compel anyone to join a 
union or to prevent them from doing so. It is also 
illegal to discriminate against a person for either 
joining or choosing not to join a union.
What benefits are there in joining 
a union?
Unions can represent their members in the 
following areas:
Negotiate the terms and conditions of awards 
and enterprise agreements or Australian 
Workplace Agreements (AWAs) with employers. 
Investigate suspected breaches of award or 
underpayment of wages. 
Resolve industrial disputes.
Advise on health and safety and workers’ 
compensation issues. 
Investigate unfair dismissals and redundancies. 
Investigate sexual harassment and 
discrimination claims. 
Discuss superannuation issues.

13 Trade unions
Which union to join?
Each trade union has rules which allow it to cover certain types of work or certain trades. Advice on 
which union to join may come from your employer or the ACTU, which has offices (called Trades and 
Labour Councils) in all capital cities and regional areas throughout Australia. Most major unions are 
affiliated with the ACTU. 
Once you become a member of a union you 
are bound by its rules and are obliged to pay 
membership fees. You must give notice if you 
intend to resign from the union for any reason, e.g. 
if you are no longer going to work in the industry. 
Some of the larger unions in Australia are:
Australian Services Union
Community and Public Sector Union 
Australian Manufacturing Workers Union
Shop, Distributive & Allied Employees Union 
Liquor, Hospitality & Miscellaneous Workers Union 
Association of Professional Engineers, Scientists & 
Managers, Australia

Living and Work Literacy 4
14 Paying income tax
Income tax is a percentage of each individual’s income that is paid to the government. The money 
raised is used to pay for government services and other expenditures. There are several types of 
taxes, such as income tax, company tax and the Goods and Services Tax (GST).
As an employee you are required to pay personal income tax. Under the Pay As You Go (PAYG) 
system, employers are required to withhold tax from the payments they make to you and send it 
to the Tax Office regularly. When you lodge your income tax return at the end of the financial year, 
you are entitled to a credit for the amount of tax which has been withheld from your pay. From the 
information you provide on your tax return, the Tax Office works out how much tax is payable on 
your income and whether you have paid more or less tax than required. If you have paid too much 
tax, you are entitled to a refund, but if you have not paid enough tax, you will have to pay the 
difference.
The financial year is from 1 July to 30 June the next year. You have from 1 July to 31 October to 
lodge your tax return unless it is prepared by a registered tax agent. Using a tax agent is becoming 
increasingly popular with taxpayers because of the complexity of the tax system and the tax return. 
When you lodge your tax return you need to quote your tax file number (TFN). This is a unique 
number issued by the Tax Office. Only one TFN is issued to you for your lifetime. Information on 
tax returns is available on the Australian Tax Office’s website (www.ato.gov.au). 
Lodging your tax return
A tax return is a document in which you declare your annual income so it can be assessed for tax. 
The Tax Office provides the form for you to complete your tax return.
You can lodge a tax return in paper form using TaxPack, or to do it more quickly, you can lodge 
online using e-tax. It is done over the Internet using a special software package which can be 
downloaded from the ATO website. It helps you prepare your tax return by doing many of the 
calculations for you, based on figures you provide. It also gives you an estimate of your tax liability 
for the year and whether you will have a refund or tax debt.
Calculating your tax refund or tax payable
You do not have to pay tax on your total income. The Tax Office will allow you certain deductions 
for work-related expenses, e.g. the purchase of tools is an allowable deduction for a carpenter, 
electrician or plumber. You can claim work-related travel expenses but not the cost of travelling 
from home to work.  Other allowable deductions include self-education expenses if the course 
is directly related to your job, and gifts and donations to registered charities. After you subtract 
these deductions from your total income, you arrive at your taxable income which is the amount 
you have to pay tax on. Under the PAYG system, you have already paid some tax so whether you 
receive a tax refund or have to pay tax depends on whether you have paid more or less tax than 
you should have.
Emma works in an office and bought a computer for $3000 in July 2006. She uses her computer for 
work 60% of the time. As a result she can claim 60% of the decline in value of the computer over a 
period, e.g. 4 years. This is a work-related expense.
Chanda also works in an office but has enrolled in a TAFE cooking course. This course has nothing to 
do with his work so he cannot claim self-education expenses. 
Emma’s tax return
Emma works as a computer operator and received a total income for the year of $45 000. She had 
work-related deductions of $5000. Her taxable income was therefore $40 000.
Emma had paid $8200 in tax instalments under the PAYG system. The tax payable on her taxable 
income (under the tax scales) was $7800. Therefore Emma received a tax refund of $400.
