© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2006
32  
Living and Work Literacy 4
15 Superannuation
 
C The Bank of NSW, now Westpac, 
began Australia’s first superannuation 
fund in 1862 for its long-serving 
employees. In 2006, superannuation 
was worth $700 billion and is expected 
to reach $2.3 trillion in ten years.
S
T
R
A
N
G
E 
B
U
T
 
T
R
U
E
!
What is superannuation all about?
Superannuation is really a way 
of saving for your retirement. 
As employers, we must pay 
superannuation contributions on behalf 
of all our employees. This compulsory 
contribution is called the superannuation 
guarantee. For all employees between the 
ages of 18 and 70 who are paid $450 or more 
in a calendar month, their employer makes 
superannuation guarantee contributions to a 
super fund which complies with government 
guidelines. It does not matter if you are a full-
time, part-time or casual employee. 
How much do they contribute?
 
Employers must contribute a minimum 
of 9% (the charge percentage) 
of employees’ earnings base to a 
complying superannuation fund or 
a retirement savings account. This 
is normally done every three months. It is 
important to know that the superannuation 
guarantee is the responsibility of employers. 
Employees are not obliged to pay or do 
anything. However, as employees you can 
contribute your own money towards your 
retirement, as a sort of investment in the future.
What is a superannuation fund?
Superannuation funds are financial 
organisations which are run by 
trustees. Their responsibility is to 
ensure your money is invested with 
care. Each has its own rules but must 
also follow government rules that are designed 
to ensure all superannuation is properly 
managed.
I suppose superannuation will give 
you more money to live on when 
you retire than the age pension 
would provide.
The aim of the superannuation 
guarantee is to ensure as many 
Australians as possible enjoy the 
benefits of an income in their 
retirement. Superannuation does 
not replace the age pension. It remains 
for those who need it but for most people 
superannuation savings will replace or 
supplement the age pension to provide a 
greater level of retirement income.
What happens if you change jobs?
No problem. Your benefits 
accumulate no matter how many 
employers you have over your 
working life.
OK, when I retire, how do I get the 
money that is owed to me? 
Ella and Louis had just left school and 
were successful in gaining employment 
in an insurance office. They knew a 
fair bit about their rates of pay and 
general working conditions such as leave 
entitlements, but they confessed they 
knew nothing about superannuation. 
After all, it would be a long time before 
they retired. They felt however, that they 
should at least find out a bit about it so 
they asked their supervisor at work. Here is 
a record of their interview.

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2006
Living and Work Literacy 4	
33
15 Superannuation
Activities
1 
What is superannuation? 
2 
What obligation does the employer have in relation to superannuation?
3 
What must the employee do?
4 
What is meant by the following terms?
 
a the superannuation guarantee	 	
b  a superannuation fund	
c  a complying fund	
 
d roll-over 	
	
	
	
e  ETP
5 
Do you lose anything if you change jobs? Explain.
6 
Does superannuation replace the age pension? Explain.
7 
Can you get your superannuation benefits before retirement age? Explain.
8 
What do you think is meant by the term ‘preserved benefit‘? How is it used?
9 
What payment options do you have when you retire?
10 a Why do you think Ella and Louis decided to ask about superannuation?
 
b Do you think it is relevant when you are young? Why?
When you leave us, you will receive 
a range of final payments. Many of 
these payments are known as eligible 
termination payments (ETPs). You 
may be terminating employment 
because you are changing jobs, you could be 
made redundant, you could be unable to work 
due to permanent disability, you could be 
dismissed or you could be retiring. Whatever 
the reason, these final payments may consist of 
unpaid wages, unpaid annual leave, unpaid long 
service leave, pay in lieu of notice, and bona 
fide redundancy and approved early retirement 
scheme payments. 
Yes, but how do we actually get the 
money?
You have three payment choices. First, 
you can roll-over all of the payment 
to a fund for your retirement savings. 
Second, you can take a cash payment 
and third, you can take part of the 
payment in cash and roll-over part of the 
payment to a fund for your retirement savings. 
You can roll-over your ETP to a superannuation 
fund, an approved deposit fund or a life 
insurance company fund.
What if I find I am broke. Can I get my 
superannuation money early?
Not really. Superannuation is money 
invested for your retirement. Early 
access to preserved superannuation 
benefits can only occur in very 
limited and restricted circumstances, 
including severe financial hardship or on 
compassionate grounds.
	
Is there anything else to know about 
superannuation?
Yes. Superannuation can be quite 
complex. There are issues such as 
tax, preserved benefits and non-
preserved benefits, and all sorts of 
government regulations which do 
change over time. Even though you may be a 
long way off retirement, you need to keep up 
to date with what is happening.
Thanks for your advice.
Yeah, thanks.

Daniel Lyons and Lucy Tan have just completed Year 12 at Orangeville High School. This is a record 
of their conversation. 
	 Daniel:	 Since we’re leaving school next week I 
think I’ll apply for a job.
	
Lucy:	 Yes, me too. What are you going to do?
	 Daniel:	 I thought I’d just front up to a few places 
and see what they’ve got.
	
Lucy:	 I don’t think it’s that easy Daniel. We 
need to do some preparation. Are you 
after a part-time job or holiday job? Or 
do you want this to be the start of your 
chosen career?
	 Daniel:	 I hadn’t really thought about it.
	
Lucy:	 Do you have an up-to-date résumé?
	 Daniel:	 Not really. I have a few bits of paper 
and certificates in a folder somewhere at 
home.
	
Lucy:	 I’ve organised a job file. It contains my 
birth certificate, school reports, including 
the most recent ones, personal references 
from family friends and a school 
reference. I also have work experience 
reports as well as certificates and awards 
from my cricket and basketball teams. I 
used all that to prepare my résumé.
	 Daniel:	 That’s a good idea. I should do that too.
	
Lucy:	 Make copies of your original documents 
to send to employers so that you keep the 
originals.
	 Daniel:	 All right. Now, how are you going to go 
about getting a job?
	
Lucy:	 I'm going to write a letter applying for that 
job at the Ace Sports Store advertised in 
last Saturday’s Bigtown Gazette. But there 
are lots of other ways of looking for a 
job. Apart from the newspapers, we can 
check on the Internet, we can make direct 
approaches to employers – they call that 
‘cold calling’ – or we could contact an 
employment agency.
	 Daniel:	 What about going to Centrelink? Will they 
help?
	
Lucy:	 Yes, we can register our names there as 
looking for work. 
	 Daniel:	 I might try the Internet first as they have 
some good jobsearch sites.
	
Lucy:	 I think we need to be pretty active. We could write letters, knock on doors, fill out 
application forms, leave our telephone number, show we’re interested and keen. All that 
is supposed to help.
	 Daniel:	 OK. Thanks for your advice Lucy. Good luck! I’d better get cracking.

I have already had some work experience

I have enclosed a copy of my résumé and

Lucy Tan

18 Work experience
Work experience
Allows students to explore and 
experience the world of work
Aims to broaden students’ experience of 
career opportunities
Allows students to observe different 
aspects of work within an industry and 
in certain cases, allows them to complete 
tasks allocated by their supervisor
Gives students an assessment by the 
school according to school-based criteria 
Asks employers to give feedback on 
the performance of the students in the 
workplace. In general, employers are 
happy to take work experience students. 
Work experience can be of mutual 
benefit to all concerned.
Some states and territories make Occupational Health and Safety lessons compulsory before work 
experience can take place. There may be regulations in place, for instance where school students 
might be handling animals or dangerous equipment in a factory situation.
Vocational Education and Training (VET): is a nationally recognised training available to senior 
secondary school students as part of their normal school curriculum. Students have the opportunity 
to complete their secondary education with a senior secondary certificate qualification, a university 
entrance score or equivalent, and practical work skills and a VET qualification.

•

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/L.subject: Economics and Business
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/L.searchText:
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2006
38  
Living and Work Literacy 4
Types of interviews
Simple one-on-one interview
Simple interview before a panel
Complex series of interview sessions (which may involve psychometric testing) 
Types of questions
Open questions, e.g. ‘Tell us a little about …‘
Hypothetical questions, e.g. ‘What would you do if …‘
Double-barrelled questions – two or more questions linked to the same topic
Behavioural questions, e.g. ‘What is your view of …‘
Multiple choice questions – used in aptitude tests
What is psychometric testing?
Psychometric tests aim to measure attributes such as intelligence, aptitude and personality. This 
provides an employer with an insight into how you might cope with stress, how well you work with 
other people, and how ambitious or motivated you are. 
Types of tests
Aptitude tests: these are used to assess your numerical and verbal abilities, your spatial reasoning 
skills and comprehension. They tend to use multiple-choice type questions. 
Example: Which of the following is the odd one out?
	
A car
	
B train
	
C bus
	
D bank
Obviously answer D is correct as the others are all forms of transport. Of course, there are more 
difficult questions than this. Some tests may also involve computer skills which test knowledge and 
application of computer programs.
Personality tests: these are not a mystery. You can find examples in magazines, books and on 
the Internet. Many are of dubious quality, but a good test is one which is proven to be reliable 
by extensive research and developed over time. Often there are no right or wrong answers, but 
responses can indicate how people think, how they view particular issues and what their interests 
and motivations are. From personality tests, psychologists develop a profile indicating which type of 
person you are.
	
Example: Which of the following statements best sums you up as a person? 
	
A I enjoy organising other people.
	
B I have a wide circle of friends.
	
C I look for variety in tasks.
	
D I always feel calm and relaxed.
Group tests: for some jobs, group tests may 
be used. You may be put with a group of other 
people and asked to build something with 
blocks, or with string, glue and newspaper. 
In these situations, employers are looking for 
people who are innovative and have lots of 
ideas, as well as people who can work co-operatively in a group situation.
Psychometric testing does not provide all the answers. However, it does provide an indicator of a 
person‘s character, aptitudes and preferences, to assist both employers and employees to find the 
best match of individual to occupation and working environment. It is not supposed to replace 
interviews or reference checking. Some companies may rely too heavily on these tests and as a 
result fail to employ some excellent people. Other experts believe they are very accurate in that 
they assess personal traits that may affect job performance and work behaviour.

uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/L.subject: Economics and Business
uploads/humanities-and-social-sciences/L.searchText:
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2006
40  
Living and Work Literacy 4
20 Career planning
The most logical way to approach a career choice is to analyse yourself in relation to your interests 
and your abilities. In today’s job market, it is important to look at your interests in a broad and 
open way. For example, ‘I like helping people’, ‘I like working with mechanical things’, ‘I like being 
outside and working with animals’, rather than ‘I want to be a vet, or a car mechanic’ as this 
narrows the job opportunities. 
Look at your skills in a broad sense, at what are called ‘transferable skills’, such as being good with 
numbers, computer keyboard skills, knowledge of mechanics of cars. In this way, these skills can be 
used for a wide range of jobs.
If you have special skills your school record (reports, references and other documents) should 
provide you with a useful guide.
Vocational pathways
In the past, young people were 
advised that after they left 
school they should train for 
a life-long career. Today, you 
can expect to spend some of 
your working life as a casual or 
part-time worker, you may be 
unemployed for some periods 
of time and you are likely 
to be involved in retraining 
or professional development 
programs. It is highly likely that 
your career path will change 
several times during your 
working life. 
There is much more flexibility 
today in the vocational 
pathways available to young 
people. Universities, for 
example, are now taking more 
mature-age students than ever 
before.
Workplace Training 
Unskilled people find it more 
difficult to find a job than 
those who are skilled in some 
way. This may involve formal 
education, e.g. at a university 
or TAFE, but it is also important 
to get ‘on-the-job’ training. 
Training, and therefore skills 
acquisitions, should be seen as 
a lifelong process. All workers 
can improve their skills, no

Technological change is occurring at such a rapid rate 
that it is very difficult to predict what sorts of jobs 
will be in demand in the future. You may even find 
yourself working in occupations which at present do not 
exist. Workers who lose their jobs may need to retrain, 
perhaps in an entirely new field. This can be an exciting 
and satisfying experience.
Government support
Governments and education authorities in Australia are conscious of the need to assist young people 
to develop career pathways by: 
encouraging and supporting all young people to engage in post-compulsory learning
recognising a wider variety of patterns of participation in learning and employment (flexible 
pathways)
facilitating easier transitions through and between learning and employment
providing effective individual pathway planning and transition support.

Living and Work Literacy 4
21 Promotion
Some useful tips
Work out what you want to achieve, and draw up a plan of how you will do it. Acquiring new 
skills may be necessary.
Look for opportunities. You may be able to come up with a more efficient process for something 
you are working on, or you may look for ways to gain new experiences.
Do some networking. Remember, ‘It is not what you know but who you know’. The more you 
know about the organisation you work for, the better. Usually the best way to learn about an 
organisation is to talk to people who already work there.
•
•
•
Your 
qualifications:
 This includes your formal 
education as well as informal 
qualifications like courses 
and workshops.
Your knowledge:
This may include 
content-specific knowledge 
about an area of work or 
a specific issue you have 
been working on, as well as 
knowledge about people, 
networks, and procedures 
and processes.
 
Your skills: 
This may include writing, 
negotiating, organisational 
and problem-solving 
skills.
 
Your experience: 
Experience gained at work, 
such as positions held and 
duties associated with 
them
Your values: 
Consider what you value and look 
for in a job and company, such as a good 
work ethic, self-management as well as the 
geographic location of a job.
 
Your personal 
attributes:
This would include 
reliability, a sense of 
humour, honesty, integrity 
and adaptability.
Self-assessment
Case study
Nathan said that he was not aware of all the options available to him after finishing Year 12. ‘I 
planned to go on to do a law degree after Year 12 although I wasn’t really looking forward to all the 
study involved. I thought twice about it, however, when I was offered training in the hospitality 
industry’. During Year 12, Nathan was employed as a part-time dishwasher at a local hotel. On 
completion of his final year, Nathan’s employer encouraged him to commence a traineeship. With 
further information about the hospitality traineeship and the enthusiasm of his employer, Nathan 
decided that this just might turn out to be his preferred vocation. He always enjoyed working with 
people and he felt that the industry offered good career prospects.
Nathan learned a broad range of skills during his traineeship and was soon involved in organising 
functions, weddings and other important events. He said, ‘I am ready for more responsibility and have 
my sights set on a management or supervisory position’.
Nathan says he learnt quickly during his traineeship due mainly to being able to put his newly 
acquired skills into practice.
Nathan was one of a class of 10 hospitality trainees. He said, ‘I made some very good friends during 
my training. We compared our different work environments and learnt from each other. We still see 
each other regularly, and who knows, given the nature of the hospitality industry, some of us might 
become very successful indeed’.
Although Nathan did well, promotion is not always an automatic process. If you want to progress in 
your career you should take active steps rather than waiting to be tapped on the shoulder. 

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2006
Living and Work Literacy 4	
43
Keep abreast of issues and new trends in your line of work by reading journals, surfing the 
Internet and attending relevant conferences.
Take stock of your achievements. Compile a record of all work-related achievements, samples of 
great work, letters of recognition and other materials that demonstrate good job performance.
Consider a horizontal move. It may be better to make a sideways move to a job at your current 
level in the short term so you can learn new skills that will help you move upwards in the future.
Be pro-active. Let your supervisor know that you are interested in progressing and learning more. 
Approach someone to act as your mentor. This is usually a more experienced person who can 
take you ‘under their wing’ and help develop your skills. 
Improve your skills. This is particularly important if you 
see a skills gap between the job you have now and the 
one you want.
Dangers
Seeking and gaining rapid promotion may be great, but 
you need to consider other factors, such as your health and 
your personal relationships. Is promotion worth it if you 
have a breakdown, or if you lose valuable friends? Working 
extremely long hours with not enough time for rest and 
leisure activities can cause problems. Taking annual leave is also an important part of this. Many 
Australians now are not taking their annual leave because they fear that their job may not be there 
when they return, or the employer may discover that they can get along well without them. Some 
are just too absorbed in their job to take leave. Taking holidays is an important part of the balance 
between work and leisure.

Living and Work Literacy 6 
45
Selected answers 
1 EMPLOYMENT IN AUSTRALIA
1 Australian Bureau of Statistics; provides statistics to the 
Federal government.
2 a 4.2%, increased.   b 10 706 100   c The proportion of the 
working age population actually in the workforce, 65.4%, 
increased from 65.3%.   d Seasonally adjusted figures were 
slightly higher in April 08.   e It takes account of seasonal 
fluctuations, such as Christmas, Easter, harvest times, 
summer, winter.   f Strongly upwards, indicating growth.    
g Downwards trend.   h Summertime, or fruit-picking times 
when labour is required.
3 a 5.6%   b Decreased, from 5.6% to 4.2%.   c Increased, 
from 63.9% to 65.4%.   d More jobs available, economy 
stronger, businesses expanding.   e Sharper rises and falls in 
2008 than in 2004.   f 1 052 000 [10 706 100 – 9 653 700]
4 To provide detailed and ongoing information about the 
Australian workforce. Businesses, the government and many 
other organisations as well as individual citizens use them.
2 TRADE UNIONS TODAY
1 A group of workers united to improve their wages and 
working conditions.
2 Australian Council of Trade Unions. Formed in 1927. It 
speaks on behalf of the union movement.
3 Protection against unfair treatment, workplace health and 
safety, better wages and conditions, membership benefits 
such as loans and discounts, support for better workplace 
laws. 
4 Trades and Labour Councils. They speak on behalf of state-
based trade unions.
5 a 20% or 1 in 5.   b Fell by 6.6%.   c Casualisation of 
workforce, less support for trade unions generally.   d Men,  
public sector employees.   e Machinery operators and 
drivers, electricity and gas, water and waste services, 
education and training.
6 Policy relating to the rights of workers and the role of trade 
unions, set by the government of the day. Controversial 
because it can affect workers in one way and businesses in 
another.
7 People have strong political views about trade unions, from 
those strongly against to those very passionately in favour.
9 Kerry believes trade unions have brought benefits in wages 
and working conditions to ordinary workers through 
collective action.
10 Chris believes trade unions are disruptive by going on strike 
all the time and inconveniencing the public. 
3 DEALING WITH DIFFICULT 
WORKMATES
1 It is part of human behaviour, which is often unpredictable.
2 Leadership style refers to the way a leader behaves towards 
his or her staff and can vary from autocratic styles to those 
which rely on consensus and mutual cooperation.
3 b Own view, but generally accepted that relationships such 
as this are acceptable as long as they do not interfere in 
any way with the work situation.   c Autocratic boss who 
relied on intimidation. Probably did not respect his workers. 
Respect should be mutual and work both ways.   d Own 
opinion, but may be sympathetic if it was the first time. If it 
happened regularly, perhaps say, ‘We are here to work and 
I would prefer not to discuss personal matters.’   e Perhaps 
jealousy or envy that Mandy had been promoted instead of 
them. Mandy could talk to them and reassure them of her 
continuing friendship, but explain that she had a different 
job to do now.   f Ron could be reminded that the world 
changes very quickly and that new ideas should be given 
due consideration. Likewise, Ron is entitled to have his views 
respected.
5 Mutual respect means respecting others, and having others 
respect you too – regardless of who is the supervisor and 
who is being supervised. 
4 CASUAL EMPLOYMENT PITFALLS
1 Casual employment involves irregular work. Part-time 
employment is regular work that is less than 35 hours per 
week.
2 Often on a weekly basis but sometimes fortnightly, based on 
the number of hours worked.
3 Casual workers do not have security of employment, nor do 
they receive benefits like paid sick leave, annual holidays or 
other special forms of leave. 
4 False. Despite not having the same working conditions as 
permanent employees, they do have workplace protection 
under Occupational Health and Safety laws.
5 An understanding of the importance and value of work. 
It is important to employers as it demonstrates a positive 
attitude.
6 A contractor works for herself or himself and bids for a 
specific job for a specific payment, like a contract. A casual 
employee is employed on an hourly basis.
7 Employers who do not follow minimum standards in record 
keeping or taxation arrangements, shifts being cut without 
notice or explanation, shifts which are unfair, compulsion to 
buy expensive uniforms, first employees to be dismissed.
8 No. They are paid hourly and are not permanent employees.
9 Casual employees may be entitled to some proportion of 
long service leave or unpaid parental or carer’s leave in some 
circumstances.
10 The right to be treated fairly and the right to safety in the 
workplace.
5 KEEPING THE CV UP TO DATE
1 Even if you currently have a job, you may want to apply for 
a promotion or change jobs at any time.
2 Computers have special software programs which sort CVs. 
3 They can look for key words and phrases which identify 
an applicant’s skills. This is so that the CVs with the right 
content can be identified quickly and then read more 
closely.
4 It would be confusing and would not reflect what the 
computer program is looking for.
5 It is a statement that indicates that a person is capable of 
doing a particular task or skill; for example, word processing.
6 It is easier to read and more likely to impress the reader.
7 Good communication skills between employees increase 
levels of productivity, as the employees work better as 
a team. Communication skills between employees and 
customers can result in income via sales or contracts, which 
is what businesses require to succeed. 
8 Initiative, energy and enthusiasm are qualities which reflect 
a person’s personality and therefore their ability to learn 
on the job and be more productive. Jobs which deal with 
members of the public are a good example, like sales.
9 The specialised words and phrases used in a job or an 
industry. 
10 A job application must be specific and address the particular 
skills specified in the job ad, as these are the applications 
that the employer will consider in choosing a person for a 
role. If the employer can’t easily see how the applicant fulfils 
the requirements, they may simply reject that application.
11 A generic CV is a ‘one size fits all’, listing general skills that 
may be irrelevant to a specific job vacancy. A specific CV is 
tailored to suit a particular job or type of job. 
12 Aisha has specific skills related to typing, Internet and email 
skills, handling of basic office machinery like photocopiers 
and telephone systems. She would be suited for an office 
clerical job.
6 INTERVIEW SKILLS IN THE 
WORKPLACE
1 You may wish to apply for promotion or change jobs, or you 
may have an annual review which involves an interview.
2 Annual review interview, internal review interview, 
disciplinary interview, interview for promotion. Yes, as it 
depends on the circumstances, but a positive attitude is 
important in each interview type.
3 To assess progress over the past year and to find out if any 
improvements have been made or could be made in the 
future. Normally conducted by an immediate supervisor.
4 Advise him to admit his error, offer apologies and promise 
not to do that again – not an outright denial of guilt.
ISBN 978 1 76020 204 0

46  
Living and Work Literacy 6
© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2009
5 How you communicate with others without speaking, what 
signals your body sends, such as facial expressions, hand 
gestures and posture. Good body language involves smiling, 
facing people and making eye contact. Bad body language 
includes looking away or down, folding arms and scratching 
or picking at body parts.
6 Appearance gives a good first impression which is important 
in an interview. While people may wear casual clothes in 
some interview situations, they should be clean and neat, to 
give the impression that the interview is important to them 
and that they have taken care with their appearance.
7 No. It is always essential to be well prepared as you can 
anticipate questions and answer them more effectively. 
You can still anticipate the types of questions. You can also 
practise positive body language signals.
8 a For her annual performance review.   b Emily was Sarah’s 
supervisor and her task was to conduct a performance 
review.   c Yes, as she was spoken to politely and praised, 
and was given some positive advice and help.   d Advised to 
enrol in a TAFE course to further develop selling skills.    
e Extremely important, as it impresses others and suggests 
high productivity.
10 No. There are other methods such as examining an 
employee’s output such as sales figures, amount of work 
done and quality of work.
7 WORK IN THE FUTURE
1 Greater use of modern communication technologies, 
widespread use of the Internet, emails, modern telephone 
systems, fully automated machinery in factories, e.g. car 
manufacturing assembly lines.
2 Machinery can now do the work previously done by 
unskilled workers.
3 De-skilling is when machinery is so sophisticated that it can 
do what a skilled worker can do and so that skill is in less 
demand, such as spray painting in car manufacture. 
4 Allowing for different working hours, flexi-time, rostered 
days off, working from home, working from a mobile office. 
Providing bank loans or financial advice using a car and 
laptop and visiting a client’s home.
5 Decreasing the workforce by eliminating middle 
management jobs. It is sometimes necessary to save money 
or to rationalise the tasks being done.
6 On-the-job training is very important as skills should be 
further refined and developed to make a worker more 
productive.
7 Less job security today than in the past, and more mobility 
in the workforce. It is easier to transfer to other jobs and to 
be retrained.
8 Profit-sharing offers, offers of shares in the company, pay 
incentives, annual bonuses.
9 Megan could apply for a job in a different IT company to 
gain more experience, or apply for promotion in her current 
situation.
8 WORKPLACE BEHAVIOUR: BULLYING
1 Yes. Many Australian workers are bullied in various ways in 
the workplace.
3 Personality clashes can mean people disagree with each 
other or can’t relate to one another. Bullying suggests a one-
sided conflict, usually with someone in a more senior role.
4 a False   b True   c False   d True   e False
5 a Yes, not a personality clash but an unreasonable demand 
and delivered in an abusive manner.   b No, the time frame 
appeared unrealistic.   c No, as he was polite and apologetic 
and requested help.   d Perhaps Shelley’s lack of time 
management and people management skills. If Shelley had 
given the job to Adam the day before, or listened when he 
asked for help, the list might have been completed on time.    
e Unrealistic demand with no help or sufficient time to 
complete the job and the abusive, aggressive attitude of the 
supervisor.   f The boss would probably reassure Adam that 
the matter would be investigated. The boss would interview 
Shelley and advise her of her obligation to set reasonable 
tasks and to treat employees with respect.
6 a The bullying was a type of initiation behaviour with 
intimidation and inappropriate and dangerous practical 
jokes.   b That this type of behaviour was common and 
acceptable practice.   d Apprentice was paid compensation.
7 Report the matter immediately to a supervisor or other 
person in the organisation. If your complaint is not acted on, 
report the matter to the Anti-discrimination Board.
9 SKILLS REQUIRED FOR SPECIFIC JOBS
1 Yes. They may be basic, such as interpersonal skills and 
communication skills, but are still important and should be 
valued.
2 Self analysis is always useful. You should record them in your 
CV or in a computer document so they can be used later 
when applying for a job.
3 Skills involving meeting and relating to people, being a 
good listener, getting along with people and working 
cooperatively with them.
4 Skills required for a particular job. Typing skills would be a 
skill required for office jobs.
7 Student opinions, but as an example, a chef has to make 
decisions and delegate tasks.
8 a Labouring skills, graphic design or drawing skills including 
computer graphics, music and debating skills.   b For 
example, graphic design or architecture.   d Advise him to 
consider what he likes doing and what he is good at, and 
finding a match. He could get help from his careers advisor 
or relatives and friends, or people in the industries he is 
considering.
10 WORK ENVIRONMENTS: ETIQUETTE
1 Interested is your attitude to the job, interesting is how you 
impress others by your personality.
2 D
3 It is unprofessional and it may cause conflict with others. 
4 Seek an interview with your supervisor and mention it 
politely. This is how the grievance is most likely to be 
resolved.
5 At first yes, unless the senior person invites you to use their 
first name.
6 a Being over familiar for a first contact. Sam should be more 
polite and careful in his use of language to create a better 
impression.   b Jane is trying to be pleasant and polite 
and not abusive while still pointing out what is acceptable 
behaviour in the workplace.   c As above, highlighting 
areas of behaviour which need improvement.   d Personal 
behaviour not acceptable, being over-familiar, poorly 
dressed, not cleaning up after himself.   e No. Even if his 
work is up to standard, his behaviour is not and should be 
fixed.   f Point out that you are part of a team and you 
should pull your weight and not rely on others to clean up 
after you, also to show respect to other workers.
7 Christmas parties can be a trap for young employees, 
where behaviour standards may slip because of the party 
atmosphere. If the behaviour becomes too extreme there 
may be consequences later, such as drinking too much 
alcohol and forgetting to think before you say anything. 
8 That it is not appropriate to use the office time and 
equipment for personal use unless there is an emergency.
9 When there is a family emergency such as the death or 
serious injury of a family member or close friend.
11 WORK ENVIRONMENTS: CULTURAL 
ISSUES
1 A workforce from many different countries, with different 
cultural backgrounds.
3 Because it is morally and legally wrong.
5 Women were historically treated differently from men, but 
this attitude has changed and most people now expect 
equal treatment for women and men in the workplace. 
Some people still act in a sexist manner. 
7 Disabled workers are now being integrated into the 
workforce where possible. Sheltered workshops are not a 
form of integration and can discriminate unfairly against 
disabled workers.
8 Governments and private companies now have policies to 
actively encourage the employment of disabled workers.
9 Jonah felt he was too slow. Miriam’s attitude was that he

2 Trade unions today 
What are they and how did they begin?
A trade union is a group of workers who unite to promote and defend wage rates and working 
conditions through common ideals and actions. The principle of unionism is that a group acting 
collectively can exert more power than an individual can in negotiating for better wages and working 
conditions. 
Trade unions have always generated considerable debate within the community, with many people 
fiercely opposed to them and many people strongly supportive of them. Australia’s history is littered 
with struggles between employers and trade unions, such as the Great Shearers’ Strike of 1891 – one of 
the first big industrial disputes in Australia. A more recent example is the 1998 Maritime Unions dispute.
The Australian Council of Trade Unions or ACTU was formed in 1927. It is the national organisation 
authorised to speak on behalf of the unions. At the state level there are Trades and Labour Councils 
(TLCs) which represent unions in issues affecting individual states. The ACTU and the TLCs have 
common aims. The most important ones are:
wages
s�hours of work
s�working conditions (including health and safety)
s�welfare issues.
s�The ACTU lists on its website five reasons to join a trade 
union, which are summarised below. 
 
1  Protection against unfair treatment at work
 
2  Workplace health and safety
 
3  Better wages and conditions
 
4   Membership benefits (such as cheap loans, 
discounts on goods)
 
5   Support for better workplace laws (such as  
unfair dismissal, setting minimum wages)
The ACTU states that all Australian workers have the right to join a union: ‘Whether you work in a small 
or large business, in an office or on a construction site – there is a union to represent you.’
Trade union issues today
Trade union activity today is highly dependent on the current state of industrial relations in the country 
and on the legislation that reflects it. Industrial relations laws are very complex and often the subject of 
much argument. They are constantly changing, especially when there is a change of government.
One of the most significant issues relating to trade unions today is the fall in membership. There are 
several reasons for this, but the most important one relates to the casualisation of the workforce.

in 1834 when six farm labourers 
in the village of Tolpuddle in 
Dorset formed a group to discuss 
their working conditions. They 
were charged with forming an

They have since become famous 
as the ‘Tolpuddle Martyrs’.

3 Dealing with difficult workmates 
Difficult and awkward situations always arise in the workplace. Some common ones are described below. 
The important thing is that you are aware when difficult situations crop up and know how to deal 
effectively with them. 
The boss from hell 
People in leadership positions often display vastly differing 
leadership styles. Some bosses lead by consensus and mutual 
cooperation and respect, while others have an autocratic 
leadership style, consulting nobody else, which can be 
intimidating. Yet others may be indecisive and muddled in 
their thinking, so that no real leadership takes place. You need 
to be aware of the many leadership styles and try to work 
harmoniously as part of the team. Leaders often project their 
own personality into the workplace and you may have no choice 
but to accept the type of boss you have. The term ‘mutual 
respect’ applies, no matter what style of leadership your  
boss uses.
It is important not to be too emotional 
or argumentative, but to try to manage 
situations sensibly. This could involve 
thinking before speaking, being 
diplomatic, or just trying to understand 
the situation. Of course, if the situation 
becomes intolerable and the boss begins 
personal abuse against you, then you 
may need to take the matter further.
The blocker
No matter what suggestions or innovations are made, the 
blocker is someone who will always find fault with an idea. They 
will say things like ‘that’s not how we do things here’ or ‘we 
have been doing it this way for the last 20 years’.
The best response to a blocker is to point out examples of 
technological progress which have occurred in recent years and 
how they have made a difference to efficiency and productivity 
in the workplace. It might also help to point out to a blocker 
what the price of bread was 20 years ago – in other words, we 
have moved on.
The office relationship
It is inevitable that personal relationships will 
develop in workplaces. It is human nature for 
people to be physically and emotionally attracted 
to each other when working side by side.
Dealing with an ‘office romance’ can be tricky. 
You should treat your ‘partner’ in the same way 
you would if you were not romantically involved 
– in other words, just like other work colleagues. 
Giving special favours is never a good idea as it 
will be seen by others to be unfair.
Raphael and Jessica were working together on an 
important project for a large IT company. Before 
long they had fallen in love. Their supervisor, 
Joe Brash, was horriﬁed and demanded that they 
immediately cease their relationship. Raphael 
and Jessica pleaded for leniency, saying that they 
tried not to let their feelings for each other affect 
their work output or their working relationship. 
Joe admitted that their work was ﬁne but insisted 
that they should not be romantically linked.
What do you think?
Tony had a reputation for being a 
tough boss. He constantly abused 
his staff for their work output and 
their attitude. He would boast to 
his friends that the only way to 
get work out of people was to ‘get 
stuck into them all the time’ and 
to ‘show that he was boss’.
What do you think?
Ron had been with the company 
for 25 years. He was loyal and hard 
working, but always critical of new 
ideas. He would always say things 
were better before and there was 
no need for all this new-fangled 
technology stuff. Despite his 
loyalty he was becoming a problem 
for the company’s future prospects.
What do you think?

The drama queen
Sometimes people – both females and males – bring all their 
personal problems to work and this can have a negative effect on 
the whole workplace, as listening to personal problems can distract 
people from their work tasks.
While it is probably all right to sympathise at first, it is probably 
best to stay out of the person’s personal dramas, especially if they 
become stressful and affect the whole working environment. A 
better approach is to communicate with the drama queen only on 
work-related matters. 
The workmate who gets promoted
Sometimes the transition from work colleague to 
supervisor can be difficult. The person who once mixed 
with office mates now finds that he or she has been 
promoted and the relationship changes. However, 
this need not be a problem if both sides understand 
the situation. Again, mutual respect for each worker’s 
position should be mixed with mutual respect and 
friendship.

4 Casual employment pitfalls 
Permanent or casual?
Permanent work usually involves regular, continuing employment. Casual work is more irregular and 
uncertain. Casual work is usually, though not always, part-time rather than full-time. Employers have 
no obligation to offer continuing work to a casual employee. However, this does not mean that casual 
workers are not protected in the workplace.
Sometimes an employer will hire contract workers to do a particular job. Contractors are different from 
casual employees in that they submit a quote for a job detailing the specifications and complete the job 
for a specific fee which is paid when the job is finished. For example, a builder may hire an electrician or 
a plumber to do specific tasks for an agreed price.
Typical casual work
Casual work is common among many groups of people, including those juggling work with study or 
childcare, those who can’t find suitable full-time jobs and work two or even three casual jobs to make 
ends meet, and those who choose to avoid the strict routine of full-time work as a lifestyle choice. There 
has been an increase in the ‘casualisation of the workforce’ as casual work opportunities expand.
Advantages
Some of the benefits of casual work are listed below.
It provides you with valuable work experience and helps you 
s�to develop transferable skills valued by employers.
Part-time jobs provide you with some income and 
s�independence.
It is a way to make new friends and develop networks.
s�It offers flexibility and the possibility to work as much or as 
s�little as you want, when you want. 
For students from overseas countries it is a way to make 
s�new friends, become familiar with Australian work culture 
and improve English language skills.
The pitfalls
Maintaining a balance between work, study and leisure is very important. 
Working too many hours may have a negative effect on your education 
and neglecting leisure time can even affect your health. For most 
young people, priority needs to be given to education as it equips you 
for the future. Another issue is the income you earn. Casual work can 
be unreliable and it may not provide you with a regular income. This 
can become a problem if it is your only source of income, especially if 
you are supporting others financially. Casual and part-time workers are 
sometimes mistreated regarding the allocation of shifts, payment and 
basic conditions. Some things to watch out for are listed below. 
Employers who do not stick to required minimum standards in 
s�relation to record keeping, taxation, superannuation and OHS 
(Occupational Health & Safety), which all workers are entitled to.
Shifts being cut without consultation or warning so you work less than you want to and need to. 
s�Your pay will be withheld for shifts that are cancelled, even if you did not want to cancel them.
Shifts may be organised unfairly so that some people do all the unpopular times.
s�You only get paid for the hours you work.

Casual workers:  
rights and entitlements
Just because you are a casual worker does not mean 
you are not protected under government legislation. 
You should be aware of your rights and also your 
entitlements. For example, a casual employee is not 
entitled to annual leave, sick leave or paid for public 
holidays. However, in some cases casual employees are 
entitled to a proportionate amount of long service leave, 
unpaid parental leave and carer’s leave. There may be 
additional leave entitlements if your position is covered 
by an award or agreement.
As a casual worker, you should not have to put up with inadequate conditions at work and you should 
not risk your own wellbeing. It is important to understand your rights and the terms and conditions you 
can expect in the workplace.
What is required?
Many casual jobs require only basic skills. However, a positive attitude and a good work ethic are 
important. If an employer is concerned about a casual employee’s attitude to their work, they can quite 
easily stop giving them further work or limit their work roster by reducing their hours.

5 Keeping the CV up to date 
It is important to keep your CV up to date, even if you currently hold a job. You may need it to apply 
for a promotion or a job opportunity that can further your career may suddenly come along. You may 
not realise it, but you do develop skills in the course of your work. You need to identify these skills and 
include them in your CV.
Who will read your CV?
You might assume that your CV is read by a person such as an employer 
or someone in the human resources department of an organisation. 
Increasingly, computers with special software are used to ‘read’ CVs to 
help sort through the huge numbers of applications that are submitted. 
These programs look for key words and phrases commonly used by the 
type of person that the employer wants. Once the computer does an initial 
sorting, the best CVs are read by people and analysed more closely.
What is a competency statement?
A competency statement can address an applicant’s knowledge, skills, abilities and  
even attitudes. In a few short sentences, the applicant identifies a specific situation,  
explains what action was taken and the results of that action. Competency statements 
are extremely important in a CV as they tend to impress the reader. 
Matching your skills to the job ad
When reading a job ad, you need to analyse what skills the employer is  
likely to want. If the job is in finance and accounting, the skills required will  
obviously be a high degree of numerical reasoning ability, as well as attention to detail and diligence. 
These particular skills may not be so important if you applied for a job as an actor or circus performer – 
other skills would then come into play.
Once you have identified the skills required for the job you are applying for, then  
you need to organise your own particular skills in your CV to match. It has been  
found that applicants who can do this successfully have a 30% better chance 
of being shortlisted for a job.
What are employers really looking for?
Recent research has highlighted the eight most common qualities 
employers ask for in job ads:
communication skills

6 Interview skills in the workplace 
You have completed an interview for a job and been successful in gaining that job.  
Do you think there will be no more interviews? Then think again! 
Interviews are now an integral part of the continuous  
assessment of a worker’s progress in an organisation.  
In other words, there are many other types of  
interviews apart from the initial job interview.  
They include:
annual reviews
s�internal reviews
s�disciplinary interviews
s�internal promotion interviews.
s�Annual reviews are often used by companies or organisations to assess the performance of their 
employees each year. Employees are expected to participate openly and honestly in the process, and in 
return receive feedback from their manager or supervisor. This process is sometimes referred to as an 
Annual Performance Review. It is sometimes assessed against agreed goals or performance indicators. For 
example, a salesperson could need to demonstrate a specific sales target for the year. 
Internal reviews are similar to annual reviews, except that they may occur more or less often and may 
be held for a specific purpose. For example: 
a new owner may wish to hold an internal review soon after taking over a business
s�there may be a problem in the company or organisation, such as falling profits or evidence of 
s�fraud, which requires an internal review of performance.
Disciplinary interviews are held when an employee has done something which is either impolite, illegal 
or against the company or organisation’s policies. They may involve a penalty, a demotion or a warning 
that future indiscretions will lead to instant dismissal.
Internal promotion interviews are a typical way of promoting employees to a higher position within 
the organisation. They may be one-on-one informal interviews or more formal, where the interview 
panel consists of three or more people.
Sarah’s annual review interview
Sarah had worked at the XL Furniture Company for a year.  
She was called in for an annual review by her supervisor, Emily.
Emily:  Well Sarah, you have been with us for a year now.  
How do you feel about working for this company?
Sarah:  To be honest, I really enjoy my work here. I’ve made some  
good friends and had lots of help along the way, especially  
when I ﬁrst started.
Emily:  That’s good. I’ve noticed that your attitude to work is very  
positive and that you have a good work ethic. Your personal  
dealings with customers have been excellent and your sales  
ﬁgures have reﬂected that.
Sarah:  That’s good to hear.
Emily:  One thing I would suggest you consider is enrolling in an advanced sales course at TAFE to 
further develop your selling techniques. We can give you some time off to do the course.
Sarah:  Yes, I would like to do that. I really want to succeed in this business.
Emily:  Well, you have the ability and the right attitude. With more experience and an upgrade  
of your qualiﬁcations, who knows where it might lead?
Sarah:  Thank you Emily for your advice and feedback.

7 Work in the future 
Have you ever wondered what work will be like in the future?  
There will probably be many jobs available which haven’t been  
invented yet, and many jobs once popular are likely to  
disappear. This makes it hard to predict what will happen,  
but it is wise to be aware of the rate of change in  
our society in general – much of this change is  
driven by new technology. You only have to  
look at car manufacturing in today’s world  
to see how automated some industries  
have become. Modern communication  
technologies, especially the Internet, have  
also revolutionised the nature of work.
Workplaces are likely to be different too. Working from 9 am  
to 5 pm in an office or factory may not be the norm any more.  
For example, to borrow money from a bank you once went into the bank  
branch near you and made an appointment with the manager. Today it is common for bank employees 
to come to your house with a laptop computer loaded with financial software and talk about your loan 
application, which you could have submitted online. 
Some of the many changes that have occurred in the workplace in recent years are listed below.
Workplace changes 
R  Greater use of technology, such as computers and telecommunications equipment
R  Gradual elimination of unskilled work, which is increasingly done by machines
R  Increase in the importance of on-the-job training and higher qualifications
R  Skilled tradespeople in danger of losing their jobs due to complex computerised machinery 
replacing them, leading to de-skilling
R  A greater variety of jobs available, especially in the service sector
R  Greater job mobility with increased chances of working overseas
R  The concept of a ‘job for life’ which was once the norm,  
is becoming less common
R  An increase in the percentage of part-time workers compared  
to full-time workers
R  An increase in the hours worked by full-time workers
R  An increase in casual work and contract work
R  Changing gender roles, with more women taking up professional 
occupations and those traditionally done only by men
R  Greater flexibility of working hours and conditions, such as  
flexi-time and rostered days off
R  An increase in the number of people who work from home
R  More profit sharing between company owners and workers or pay 
incentives to achieve work targets
R  A decrease in the number of workers in ‘middle management’ – 
the result of firms downsizing
R  Increasing consideration for disadvantaged groups in the 
workforce, including people with disabilities.

well into the future.

8 Workplace behaviour: bullying 
Bullying is often seen as something that happens in the 
schoolyard rather than the workplace. Yet it has been 
found that over one million Australians are bullied at work 
every year. A significant number of people are subjected to 
long-term bullying.
What is bullying behaviour?
There are several aspects of behaviour that can be 
regarded as bullying. This is not a complete list, but 
bullying can include the following behaviours.
It is important to understand the difference between bullying and a personality clash. With a personality 
clash, both people involved may develop a dislike for each other and engage in some form of mutual 
verbal abuse. A personality clash may only flare up once and then the people may agree to disagree or 
simply try to avoid each other. 
On the other hand, bullying tends to be one-sided, in a situation where there is a power or status 
difference between the bully and the victim. Bullying behaviour is usually repeated, sometimes over a 
long period of time. It may be a series of incidents, each of which seems minor at the time, but when 
considered altogether they constitute unacceptable bullying.
Workplace bullies can be:
The following two case studies illustrate aspects of workplace bullying.  
The second case study is a true story.

deadlines

Shelley was a supervisor at Zipfast, a large interstate transport company. She was 
responsible for organising the drivers’ rosters. One Friday morning she asked Adam, a 
new employee at the company, to provide her with a list of all the pick-up locations 
from the past twelve months, including addresses and other contact details. She 
wanted that information at 5 pm that day. When Adam questioned whether he could 
get that job done in time, Shelley turned on him and shouted, ‘Are you stupid or 
something? Just get it done and that’s an order.’
Promptly at 5 pm, Adam presented Shelley with a list but it was incomplete. He said 
he was sorry but completing the task would take much longer than the time allowed. 
He also said that he needed help to do the job properly. Shelley immediately started 
screaming again, saying that it had to be done before he knocked off work for the weekend.

9 Skills required for specific jobs 
Nobody is completely unskilled. Everyone has skills of some sort or another, but perhaps they are not 
aware of them. In fact, people have skills which can be related to one or more occupations. Many skills 
are transferable, which means they can be used in a variety of occupations. Interpersonal skills such as 
being able to relate to other people and to communicate effectively are very important in almost any job. 
It is useful to complete a systematic analysis of your skills, and the skills you already have should be 
listed in your resume or CV. And you need to update them as you accumulate more skills.
Job-specific skills
There are some skills which are specific to particular jobs. For the 
position of typist, an applicant is expected to be able to type. Not 
only that, but to have reached a certain standard such as 50 words 
per minute. The skills required of a doctor are very different from 
those required of a carpenter or a computer operator.

11 Work environments: cultural issues
Multicultural issues 
When you begin a new job you’ll probably find yourself 
working with people of different racial backgrounds and 
religions. Their cultures may seem foreign to you, and your 
culture may be equally foreign to them. Recognition and 
respect for other people’s cultural beliefs is an important 
part of working harmoniously in a workplace.
Here are some comments you may well hear in a workplace. 
What do you think?
‘I don’t like working with Asians.’
s�‘Yes, but he’s a Christian.’
s�‘Ahmed is from Iraq you know. What can you expect from 
s�a fellow with that background?’
‘I don’t want to be supervised by a Serbian.’
s�Gender issues
Women and men should be treated equally in the workplace. It has now been decades since it was 
socially acceptable to treat women as being inferior to men. Women were once paid less, discriminated 
against and often passed over for promotion. Even today, women talk of the ‘glass ceiling’ when it 
comes to promotion prospects.
Despite the equal treatment you may hear these comments in the workplace.
‘That’s a woman’s job.’
s�‘You get the women to make the morning tea so the men can do the important work.’
s�‘Oh, don’t promote her. Now that she’s married she’ll only get pregnant and leave – and you’ll have to 
s�pay her maternity leave, you know.’
Disabled workers
In the past, people who suffered a disability, no matter how severe, were not welcome in the workplace. 
During the 1950s, parents of people with disabilities set up sheltered workshops to provide employment 
for their children. Some voluntary organisations also opened workshops. Today that situation is no 
longer acceptable. People with mild disabilities are accepted and encouraged to join the workforce 
and employers are obliged to provide them with opportunities and facilities to assist them as needed. 
Expectations of work output are often adjusted to allow for disabilities, but rather than have sheltered 
workshops, integration in the workforce is the goal.
All governments at every level in Australia as well as private organisations work together to ensure equal 
employment opportunities for people with disabilities. Some people with disabilities may require support 
or assistance to find an appropriate form of employment.
Assistance is available to:
help determine job interests and suitable types of employment
s�search for relevant jobs
s�prepare for job interviews
s�help with understanding employment conditions
s�provide ongoing support.
s�People with more severe disabilities may require more intensive support and some organisations 
provide this. Whatever the disability, making sure that wherever possible the workplace is accessible for 
employees with disabilities is a responsibility of all employers. Attitudes to working with people with 
disabilities are unfortunately still varied. You may hear comments like the following.
 
Jonah: 
I can’t work with him, he’s so slow.
 
Miriam:  But do you realise he has a disability? Give him a chance. How would you like to be 
discriminated against and have nobody prepared to employ you?

12 Workplace communication 
The importance of communication
Communication is basic to all aspects of modern life and 
therefore important in every job. The quality or level of 
communication required depends on the nature of the job, 
and how much interaction with the public and other work 
colleagues is required. 
There are two basic types of communication:
verbal – involves speaking skills and listening skills 
s�written – involves writing letters, reports, articles, summaries, emails and notes.
s�Verbal skills
Verbal skills include speaking skills. This means:
speaking clearly
s�speaking with confidence
s�analysing your thoughts and putting them into words
s�using correct grammar.
s�Listening skills are just as important. A person with well developed verbal 
communication skills needs to be a good listener. This means concentrating 
on what is being said by the person speaking to you and analysing what 
their message is. 
Written skills
Communicating in writing has two pitfalls which  
verbal communication doesn’t:
SPELLING��s�GRAMMAR
s�While it is now becoming commonplace to abbreviate words and use a 
special ‘mobile phone, SMS’ language in emails, there are many occasions 
when formal writing is necessary. Different types of formal writing have 
different guidelines and layout requirements.
Writing letters
A business letter should have:
Writing reports or articles 
Formal English is again necessary in these forms of written communication. Complete sentences  
should be used, with no abbreviations or colloquial (slang) language.
the address of the sender at top left or top right
s�the date, at top left or top right
s�a salutation, such as Dear Sir, Dear Madam, Dear Mr Jones
s�correct spelling 
s�correct grammar
s�formal English – written in complete sentences with no abbreviations
s�an appropriate ending, such as ‘Yours faithfully’ or ‘Yours sincerely’ if  
s�the person is known to you.
Definition: Communication is the 
interchange of ideas, facts and 
opinions. It involves receiving 
and understanding information 
from others, and providing 
information to others in a way 
that can be easily understood.

Writing notes or emails
These forms of written communication are in some circumstances just as important as reports and 
articles. However, informal language is generally acceptable in emails and notes.
Notes from a meeting can contain abbreviations to save time and to make sure everything is taken 
down, especially if you are making notes from a lecture or speech. Similarly, emails have developed a 
language of their own, without formal salutations and with the widespread use of abbreviations. Some 
people even ignore capital letters and punctuation in emails, and include emoticons. There may be an 
email policy in a particular workplace. Emails are still a written form of communication and can be used 
by others as proof that communication did take place. Some workplaces require emails to be written in 
more formal language.
Sharing your opinions
There may be situations in your work where you are required to give your opinions. This requires some 
thought because you may also have to give reasons and explanations for your opinions. There is no 
need to be nervous about giving your opinion, but it is important to be prepared. Remember that 
confidence and preparation are the keys to successful verbal communication. There is no point getting 
aggravated or aggressive if your opinions are questioned. Using logical reasons communicated clearly is 
generally the most effective way of convincing others.

13 Types of management structures
When you start work in a new organisation it is important to know a little about its management 
structure. You need to know such things as:
who does what
s�who reports to whom
s�who is responsible for whom 
s�how to communicate any complaints, concerns or requests for assistance. 
s�The organisation may be either government or private, large or small. Whatever the size and nature 
of the organisation, they have some things in common. The following diagrams will show you typical 
management structures.
Types of businesses
Businesses may be small or large, but they can also differ according to ownership:
Sole trader –
s� A business with one owner that is usually small in size. Common examples of sole 
traders are a corner store owner, an electrician, a plumber, a hairdresser and a café owner.
Partnership –
s� A business owned by two or more people. It can have up to 20 owners, but usually 
two, three or four joint owners. Typical partnerships include law firms, doctors, dentists, financial 
advisors and building contractors. Sole traders and partnerships both have unlimited liability. That 
is, they are responsible for all the business debts and also receive all the profits.
Companies –
s� A business owned by shareholders who have a limited liability; they are liable only to 
the value of the shares they purchased. Companies may be private, where shareholders are invited 
to buy shares, or public companies which are listed on the Stock Exchange where anyone can buy 
shares. Companies are controlled by a Board of Directors and the Directors are responsible to the 
shareholders. Generally, the Board of Directors will appoint a person to manage the business on a 
day-to-day basis. This person is generally referred to as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), and is 
responsible to the Board of Directors.

14 Unfair and fair dismissal 
People leave jobs for different reasons. For example, you may leave of your own free will, or you may be 
asked or told to leave. There are different terms used for each situation.
Resigned – gave notice that you wished to leave your place of work
s�Retired – decided to finish your working life
s�Dismissed – forced to leave by the employer
s�Terminated – another term for ‘dismissed’
s�Sacked – a colloquial or slang word for ‘dismissed’
s�Redundant – being dismissed because there is no work for you to do
s�Retrenched – being dismissed to save the employer money
s�Fair or unfair?
As an employee, you are entitled to notice of termination, usually four weeks. You may be made 
redundant by an employer or you may be retrenched. If an employer gives adequate notice and 
provides a dismissed worker with full entitlements, the employee is considered to be dismissed fairly, no 
matter how he or she may personally feel about it.
So what is unfair dismissal? Sometimes personality clashes arise between an employee and the boss, 
and the boss may dismiss that employee – a personality clash is not a valid reason for dismissal. Some 
workers may not be as efficient or as fast as others and be targeted for dismissal. Dismissal of women 
who get married or who are expecting a child and workers because they belong to a trade union are 
examples of unfair dismissal. 
If a worker is dismissed for discriminatory reasons, that is considered unlawful and the worker has 
the right to appeal against the dismissal. Unfair dismissal laws have been written into the Workplace 
Relations Act which was revised in 2001 and again in 2008. Workers who believe that they have been 
dismissed on discriminatory grounds can lodge an application with the Australian Industrial Relations 
Commission. They must lodge an application with the Commission within 21 days of being dismissed.  
The Commission then considers things such as:
whether there was a fair and valid reason for the dismissal
s�whether the employee was notified of that reason and given 
s�the opportunity to respond
whether the employee has been notified of any 
s�unsatisfactory performance.
Laws about unfair dismissal do not apply to workers who are 
employed by a company with less than 100 workers. This issue 
has been debated at length by politicians and employers in 
recent years. Also, the laws do not apply to workers employed  
on a seasonal basis, such as fruit pickers.
Rights and obligations
A worker who is dismissed has certain entitlements, which can include:
payment for accrued annual leave
s�accrued pro rata long service leave if the worker is eligible
s�payment in lieu of notice – if an employee is told to leave immediately, he or she is generally 
s�entitled to four weeks pay in lieu, depending on the age of the employee and for how long she  
or he has been in continuous employment
redundancy payments – in some cases, especially if the worker has been with a company for a  
s�long time.
If you believe that you have not received all your entitlements, you can contact the Australian Workplace 
Ombudsman (www.wo.gov.au).

15 Occupational health & safety 
Accidents can always occur in the workplace, just as they can in the home. Although some workplaces 
are potentially more dangerous than others, it is important that all workplaces are safe and safe practices 
are adopted. Each state in Australia has Occupational Health and Safety (OH & S) laws which set out the 
obligations of the employer in providing a safe working environment. Employees also have an obligation 
to work in a safe way so that they do not endanger themselves or others. In fact, each workplace is 
required to have an OH & S committee with representatives of employees and the employer to discuss 
current safety issues.
Positive action can save lives. Many workplaces have signs  
erected to warn workers and members of the public of  
possible dangers, as you can see from the signs on  
this page. Not all workplaces require the same degree  
of signage. For example, a chemical factory would be  
governed by strict rules with signs indicating danger  
areas and hazardous chemicals.  
Even an office can have dangers  
such as faulty power points,  
exposed extension cords, furniture  
and office equipment that is not  
properly installed and may be likely to  
fall on someone. Therefore, all workplaces  
must be aware of the OH & S requirements.
Workers compensation
If a worker is injured at work there is provision for them 
to be compensated and, if necessary, rehabilitated so 
that they can resume working when they have recovered. 
Compensation can pay for such things as medical and 
hospital costs, loss of earnings and permanent damage, 
disfigurement or loss of bodily functions such as sight 
and hearing. All employers are required to take out a 
special insurance policy to cover their employees for 
workers compensation.
Work Cover
Each state in Australia has a government authority to 
administer workers compensation claims. Two examples 
are Work Cover NSW and the Victorian WorkCover 
Authority. Their job is to assess claims and to make 
decisions on the amount and type of compensation 
required. Heavy penalties apply to people who make  
false claims. Where employers have been found to be 
grossly negligent in making the workplace safe, they  
may be prosecuted in a court of law and may have  
to pay damages.
There are work cover offices 
spread throughout each state, so 
that people have access to local 
services, where possible.

13 Using Lee’s story as a model, write a story about a workplace

Lee decided to apply for a job in a local bakery. On his third day at work, he noticed that one of the 
dough-mixing machines had ceased to work even though all the others were operating. He told the 
owner of the bakery what had happened and the baker asked Lee to see if the dough was stuck in 
the machine. When Lee put his hand in the machine, it started working again and his hand suffered 
deep lacerations. Fortunately one of the other employees noticed this and turned off the power to the 
machine. There were no signs warning employees about the safety aspects of operating the machines.
Lee’s hand needed several stitches and he was unable to resume work for four weeks while the wound 
healed. He was entitled to workers compensation in the form of all medical bills being paid, as well as 
loss of earnings for four weeks.
The owner of the bakery was obliged by law to notify Work Cover who then investigated the incident. 
As a result of the investigation, the owner was given a severe warning and told to provide warning

16 Current workplace issues 
Even if you have a job, you should still follow current issues related to the workplace. The daily 
newspapers and television news and current affairs programmes are full of workplace-related stories.  
It is worthwhile to stay aware of the relationship between employment and the state of the  
Australian economy.
The economy and work
Whether you have studied Economics at school or not, you will probably understand that the level of 
economic activity in a country will fluctuate from time to time. The economy tends to operate in cycles, 
as you can see in the graph above. When the economy is booming, there tends to be an increase in 
retail sales, a rise in business confidence and a consequent fall in unemployment. This is good news for 
job seekers as there is a feeling that there are plenty of jobs to go around. 
On the other hand, when economic activity is slowing down with a drop in retail sales, there is a 
consequent lowering of business confidence. Employers are more likely to lay off workers or not employ 
new workers. This can be very frustrating for new job seekers or people wanting to enter the workforce 
or change jobs. As you can see on the graph, terms such as ‘boom’ and ‘bust’ are used to describe mild 
swings in the cycle. Terms such as ‘inflation’ and ‘recession’ or even ‘depression’ are used to describe 
more severe swings. It is the task of the Federal government and the Reserve Bank of Australia to 
manage economic activity by trying to limit these excessive swings.
The state of the economy can be measured using economic indicators. These indicators can include 
retail sales figures, new housing approvals, wage and income levels and employment figures. They are 
readily available on the website of the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Unemployment  
The level of unemployment is the result of several factors. One is the level of economic activity and 
there are other factors, indicated by the main types of unemployment.
Structural unemployment –
s� Occurs as a result of structural changes in industry. Modern machinery 
and computer technology are putting some people out of work. There is a need for people 
displaced to retrain in different jobs.
Frictional unemployment –
s� Occurs when workers are in the process of changing jobs, or are 
having difficulty finding a new job after they’ve left the previous one. There will always be a degree 
of frictional unemployment.
Cyclical unemployment –
s� Occurs when the economy is slowing down. When economic activity is 
on the rise, unemployment is likely to fall.
Seasonal unemployment –
s� This is the result of seasonal changes, such as summer fruit picking, the 
shearing season, Christmas sales. 
One of the aims of the Federal government is to maintain full employment. However, this is a difficult 
task given the types of unemployment described above. Sometimes target rates are set so that an 
unemployment rate of 5% or 4% may be considered acceptable.
Long term unemployment
This can be a serious issue for some people, especially those coming from migrant backgrounds with 
poor language skills. A person who wants a job and can’t get one after a long period of time spent 
trying can suffer from loss of pride, loss of self confidence and self esteem. This can lead to social 
problems. People can get help from the Federal government through its Centrelink agency  
(www.centrelink.gov.au).

17 Technology and communication 
The world is changing quickly in the development and use of technology. This 
is especially so in the workplace. The main advances have been in information 
and communications technology. Technology is changing the way people 
communicate, and the way that workplaces operate.
The Internet
The Internet is a worldwide network of computers linked by global 
telecommunications. It allows computers around the world to link and share 
information and resources. Growth in Internet use since the late 1990s has been 
spectacular. In Australia today there are six million subscribers. The Internet has 
enormous potential for use in the workplace. Business has become so reliant on 
the Internet that speed of access is now an important factor. 
Office emails
The use of electronic mail or email has become a widespread means of communication for educational 
and personal purposes as well as workplaces. Email has advantages over regular postal mail in that it is 
delivered very quickly into the recipient’s mailbox for them to read and reply to at their convenience. It 
is a very quick, easy and efficient way to communicate, despite the number of spam emails that clutter 
inboxes. Spam filters and antivirus packages can prevent this from getting out of hand and infecting 
computers, slowing things down and potentially causing damage to files.
Unlike a business letter, an email is informal and often uses informal language. It also has the capacity to 
attach documents which can be opened by the recipient.
Some differences between formal language and email language are listed below. 
Informal greetings – not using ‘Dear Sir’ or ‘Dear Madam’
