18 Learning at work 
Once you have a job, it is a mistake to ‘rest on your oars’. Learning is a life-long business, and you 
should never become complacent. Job security is not the same today as it was in the past, when 
employees could expect a safe job for life. Today there are no guarantees. On-the-job training is 
therefore an increasingly important aspect of workplaces today. 
Learning at work may take many forms. It can be as simple and informal as group or branch meetings, 
one-on-one interviews with supervisors or discussions with mentors. Or it can involve additional courses 
at a TAFE college or a university to upgrade qualifications. You need to keep updating your skills and 
your qualifications, especially if you are in a job where there is strong competition.
Success in your career
Here are ten tips to help you enjoy success in your career through good workplace habits.
1 
 Create a life plan – Success can be achieved if you know where you 
are going and have made a life plan. It doesn’t have to be written 
down, although this helps to clarify goals and recognise achievements 
as they happen. A life plan involves outlining the direction you wish to 
take, what steps you have to achieve along the way and what barriers 
might delay or prevent success. A life plan can be flexible, depending 
on your personal circumstances, but even so it will provide you with a 
focus for your plans.
2 
 Act responsibly – Be professional in all your dealings with people, 
whether they be work colleagues, supervisors or customers/clients.
3 
 Work efficiently and effectively – Try to avoid time wasting. 
Focus on outcomes.
4 
 Make yourself irreplaceable – Some people’s work is so 
efficient and at such a high standard that they make themselves 
irreplaceable or indispensable. Aim to show your supervisor that 
no one can do your job better than you.
5 
 Be part of a network – It is hard to work in isolation. You need 
to have people around you, contacts you can call on for help and 
people who show a positive attitude to their work. It doesn’t have 
to be the ‘old school tie’ type of network – it can take any form 
and there is much you can learn from others.
6 
 Give credit where it is due – Always acknowledge the good work 
of colleagues. Then they are more likely to acknowledge your 
good work.
7 
 Update your skills – You may come to a job with a set of skills, 
but it is important that you not only maintain these skills but 
improve them. The world is constantly changing and so is the 
workplace. You need to stay on top of the possible effects of these 
changes. Keep on learning new things.
8 
 Upgrade your qualifications – These are more formal in nature 
and involve courses at a TAFE college or a university. There is an 
ever-growing number and variety of courses available so look for 
the one that suits you best in your career.
9 
 Strike a balance between promoting yourself and boasting 
about your accomplishments – This takes care, judgement and 
experience. It is good to talk to others, such as a mentor, about 
this.
10  Anticipate barriers – There will always be times when things 
don’t go your way, despite your best efforts. When this happens, act sensibly, not emotionally. 
Above all, do not lose your focus. Always remember that you can learn from your mistakes.
Jake was a team supervisor 
for a large company. He 
always wanted to take all 
the credit for the team’s 
work. People in his team 
often became irritated by 
the way he talked about 
the solutions the team had 
come up with. Sometimes 
he would manufacture a 
problem and then come 
up with a solution which 
he claimed was his idea. 
When Jake was on holiday, 
the team worked in a more 
relaxed way, yet still got  
the job done.

Negotiation skills 
One of the most important skills you can develop in the workplace is the skill 
of negotiation. Negotiation skills are critical, not only for doing your job well, 
but for advancing your career.
Some tips about success in negotiating are listed below.
Develop a clear understanding of why you are negotiating. Consider 
s�what you hope to achieve.
Speak calmly. Aggressive talk won’t work.
s�Be a good listener. Let the other person make their point and don’t 
s�interrupt.
Consider how the other person feels – in other words, be empathetic.
s�Avoid comments like ‘take it or leave it’, or ‘I just can’t agree with that’.
s�Choose your words carefully and also be aware of your body language.
s�Be prepared to give a little ground – it makes the other person feel they 
s�have achieved something too.

19  Resignation strategies:  
knowing when to leave 
Knowing when the time is right to leave a job can be just as 
important as choosing the right job in the first place. Many 
people find that the job they are in is not really suitable for them, 
and they don’t need to stay and suffer. Workers really should be 
happy in their jobs, and many are. 
There are some resignation strategies you should know about. 
Thinking clearly about the decision
First, you should weigh up the pros and cons of resigning.  
What benefits would you lose? Would you be happier working 
elsewhere in a similar position? Or would you prefer an entirely 
different field?
Giving notice
When you decide that you want to resign, you are expected to 
give notice. This is usually done 30 days before your last day on 
the job. Giving notice allows the employer to make arrangements 
to replace you. Some organisations have a special resignation form 
while for others a letter of resignation is enough, as long as the 
exact date of leaving is included.
Some people don’t give notice. This could be due to a bitter argument in the workplace, with the result 
that they can’t stand to remain in the job a moment longer. By leaving before giving notice, a worker 
can lose some entitlements such as sick leave and holiday leave. 
Also, some employers are not interested in being given notice. If an employee decides to leave, they 
may want that employee to leave their establishment immediately. There have been some cases of 
employees being escorted by security guards out the door. For the employer, there is the risk that a 
disgruntled employee may harbour a grudge against their employer and during the 30 days’ notice may 
cause damage or access and steal company secrets. Policies on giving notice are therefore not always 
strictly enforced. Often the date of leaving is negotiated by mutual consent.
Burning bridges
Be careful in your behaviour when leaving a job, as you may find that in the future you are working for 
that same organisation again. In any case, it does not reflect well on any person to behave with bad 
grace. Also, a future employer may want a work reference from your previous employer and sometimes 
high value is placed on previous work references.
Tying up loose ends
If you want to leave in a positive way, it is 
important to tie up loose ends. Where possible, 
finish tasks that you have started and present 
the work you have done to your boss. You 
should also brief your boss on the progress 
of projects still unfinished. It will be much 
appreciated by your work colleagues and your 
employer.
Allie was not happy in her 
job. She found she was always 
ﬁghting with work colleagues 
and always seemed to be in 
trouble with her boss over her 
work output. Allie decided to 
leave. She didn’t conﬁde in her 
supervisor or anyone else, for 
that matter. She simply didn’t 
come into work any more.

Living and Work Literacy 6 
41
Personal considerations
You may have talked to your work mates about the 
possibility of leaving. However, telling everyone that 
you will be leaving before letting your employer know 
shows a lack of courtesy. After your employer knows, 
then it is okay to tell other people.
Try to show your appreciation for the job, and for 
the help you have received in your work. While you 
may have mixed feelings about leaving, maybe some 
sadness, you should also be thinking positively. This is 
an opportunity for you to get on with your working 
life and accept new challenges.

Working in pairs, conduct a series of interviews in which one of you is 
resigning and the other is your boss or immediate supervisor. Explain 
the reasons you have for resigning. Then swap roles for another 
interview where the employee and employer attitudes are different.

20 Life-long learning and pathways
The old traditional pathway was once: leave school  ➨ go to university or TAFE college ➨ get a job.  
Today there are many pathways available to people which don’t follow the traditional sequence. For 
example, a more common sequence today might be: school  ➨ job ➨ TAFE course ➨ different job ➨ 
university ➨ different job again. Another pathway could involve overseas travel or what some people 
refer to as a gap year.
Gap year
Many people are not sure what they want to do in their working life after they leave school. Taking 
a gap year and travelling or working can be a good option. If you have gained a place at university 
or TAFE, you can defer your studies for at least a year, perhaps more. Taking a gap year gives you a 
breathing space and time to contemplate your future. You will also gain maturity, confidence and 
independence through a year off formal study. You can even work while overseas if you get a work 
visa or work at home before travelling overseas or in Australia. Most people who take gap years do not 
regret it.
Gillian
Gillian worked hard at high school 
and gained entry to university to study 
for Arts/Law. Gillian thought about 
deferring her degree and having a gap 
year. She had worked at a jewellery store 
on Thursday evenings and Saturday 
mornings for the past three years and 
had some savings and a burning desire 
to travel.
She decided to go ahead and defer her 
studies for a year and work full time 
in the jewellery store for a couple of 
months before going on a trip to the 
United Kingdom. Once she reached 
London, she gained some temp work 
in an ofﬁce and travelled around 
on weekends. Then when she had 
accumulated more savings, she left her 
temp job and went to Europe where 
she backpacked for six months with a 
few English friends she had met. When 
she returned at the beginning of the 
following year, she realised that she had 
made the right choice. She had learned 
a lot about life in her time away and she 
felt she was now ready to settle down to 
her university degree.
University options
1. Mid-year enrolments
Universities today are far more flexible than in the past. 
You don’t have to enrol or start at the beginning of the 
year, as there is the option of mid-year enrolment. You 
may have missed out on the course of your choice or 
failed to apply in time. You may even have wanted a 
short break before resuming your studies. The Universities 
Admission Centre (UAC) will have information available for 
you. However, there are usually less places available than 
at the beginning of the academic year.
2. Changing universities
If you find that the course you have started is not for you, 
or if your personal circumstances have changed, there are 
ways of completing your studies by changing universities. 
You can receive credits for courses completed at one 
university and finish a course at another, although there 
are obviously some rules which you would need to find 
out about.
3. Success doesn’t require a uni degree
Many people think, quite wrongly, that a university 
degree is essential for success in the workplace. Many 
people achieve much with no formal qualifications. This 
doesn’t mean that everyone should abandon the idea of 
a university degree, but it is not the only option. Today 
there are many TAFE college courses which today are 
designed specifically to suit particular careers – without 
the large course fees. Furthermore, university degrees are 
no guarantee of success in the world of work.
There is plenty of advice you can get from your Careers 
Advisor at school, from parents and friends, or from the 
many websites which specialise in this field. Start with 
Career Guide Australia at www.yourcareerguide.com.au.

education? How?
8

Under what circumstances might this be necessary?

an example of when a university might refuse a change to 
another university.
9 
Read Keith’s story. Why did he change universities? What 
success did Keith have dealing with different universities?
10 Read Maya’s story. Was Maya disadvantaged by not doing a 
university course? What qualiﬁcations did she have? Was this 
sufﬁcient for success? What do you think was the secret to 
her success?
11 Brad left school after year 12 and decided to work as a shop 
assistant. If you were Brad’s friend, what options would you 
suggest to him in seeking a future career?
Keith
Keith was a talented actor and writer who found that work opportunities were limited, 
so he decided to start a law degree at the University of Melbourne. He had completed 
three units of the course when his wife accepted a job as an arts director for a company 
in Darwin. He decided to approach the University of the Northern Territory to see if he 
could continue his law degree and gain credit for courses completed. This was granted 
and he did three more units of study. Three years later, his wife accepted an arts director 
job in Perth. He wanted to continue his legal studies and asked if he could complete his 
degree at the University of Western Australia. They accepted two of his three units from 
the Northern Territory, but this was acceptable to him. Keith went on to complete his law 
degree at the University of Western Australia.
Maya
Maya did not have a university degree but she was successful in the ﬁeld of real estate. 
When she left school, Maya got a job with the local branch of a large real estate 
company and began selling houses. Her personality, charm and eagerness to learn 
on the job made her an instant success. She enrolled in a TAFE college course in real 
estate and gained the necessary qualiﬁcation. After a few years she was promoted 
to manager of the local branch. Five years later, Maya decided to establish her own 
real estate ofﬁce. Working with a small number of staff she continued to build on 
her success. Selling real estate is not easy. Although Maya could have enrolled in a 
university course, she created a successful business with minimum qualiﬁcations, but 
she did require enormous energy and skill.

different pathways 
available to school 
leavers. Discuss which 
qualifications are useful, 
and which are essential 
for the different career 
opportunities available. 
Record the conclusions 
reached on a display 
board.

Selected answers 
1 WHEN CAN I LEAVE HOME?
2 When you turn 18 years old. That is when you are legally  
an adult.
3 If your parents or carers agree, or if your safety and 
wellbeing are under threat.
4 Fear of the unknown, potential problems, loneliness, money 
worries.
5 Fear you’re not ready, they will miss you, concern that you 
are not married, concern about other people living with you.
6 Answers may vary. Ben ignored the tips ‘don’t leave for the 
wrong reason’ and ‘don’t act too hastily’. 
7 Jessica may have advised Ben to wait a little longer, or try to 
resolve conflict with his parents.
8 Communication skills – both speaking and listening. Ability 
to understand other people’s point of view.
9 Alicia needs to consider whether she can handle living away 
from home, and whether she really wants the job.
10 a Did Omar want to live away from home and branch out? 
Which university did he prefer?
 
b Would he move away and pursue his degree or would he 
consider a different university course?
2 MOVING OUT, MOVING BACK
1 Kipper is an acronym for Kids In Parents’ Pockets Eroding 
Retirement Savings.
2 Boomerang refers to kids returning to their home after 
moving out.
3 It revealed that young Australians are staying at home more 
than ever before.
4 Overseas research indicated similar patterns of young people 
returning home.
5 To save money for entertainment or to invest.
6 You are introduced to other cultures and new friendships, 
ways of seeing things, being entertained, cooking etc.
7 Perks such as cable TV, faster internet, free drinks and food. 
It is possible to enjoy these perks while living independently, 
but you need to budget for them.
8 Human behaviour can be rich and interesting, and meeting 
new people is a way of exploring this.
9 Style cramping refers to the cringe that can come with 
spending too much time with your parents. Even if you get 
on with your parents you (and they) still need space to do 
your own thing.
10 The article encourages readers to consider the advantages of 
living away from home.
3 HOMELESSNESS
1 Emma’s and Luke’s stories are similar in that they both were 
forced to leave home due to unhappy or abusive circumstances. 
They differ in that with help, Luke overcame his difficulties, 
while Emma’s life continued on a negative path.
3 Causes of homelessness can include domestic violence, 
family relationship breakdowns, drug and alcohol abuse. 
4 Relative homelessness occurs where people stay in boarding 
houses or in emergency accommodation, while absolute 
homelessness means living on the streets or in improvised 
dwellings such as parks or deserted buildings.
5 Causes include family relationship breakdown, domestic 
violence, sexual, mental or emotional abuse, mental illness 
or disability, gambling, financial problems, drug and alcohol 
abuse, bereavement, overcrowding. Most common and 
reasons are a matter of student opinion.
6 Roughly 50 per cent
7 Homeless people can be male or female, old or young.
8 ‘Temporary accommodation’ could refer to sleeping on the 
streets, in parks, caravans or abandoned buildings.
9 Department of Community Services in each state, Centrelink, 
organisations such as Kids Helpline or Lifeline. 
10 Kids Helpline is an organisation designed to help kids 
in need. It will help young people who urgently need 
immediate housing and food.
4 DIFFERENT TYPES OF ACCOMMODATION
1 You need to be aware of all the options open to you before 
deciding.
2 Prices are important if you are on a tight budget. For 
example, full board or share accommodation would normally 
be cheaper than renting on your own.
3 More independent people may prefer to live alone, or with 
just one other person.
4 a boarding houses – houses offering a room and meals, run 
by a landlord.
 
b studios – small apartments with no separate bedroom but 
combined bedroom/living area.
 
c apartments – separate bedrooms, kitchen, bathroom and 
living area, often in multi-storey buildings.
 
d hostels – a type of shared accommodation with private 
bedrooms but shared cooking and washing facilities.
 
e Student residences – usually based on university or college 
premises and often furnished.
 
f Free accommodation – provided in exchange for work such 
as childcare, live-in housekeeping or other arrangements to 
work for board.
 
g Townhouses – houses that share common walls with a 
neighbour. Usually have a garden or terrace at ground level.
5 Protection is provided by the Residential Tenancies Act.
6 Generally cheaper and perhaps safer if others are there to 
help.
7 Different in terms of price, availability, type of premises 
(terrace house and apartment), type of tenants they want.
8 Jack appears very personable and confident, someone who 
likes socialising and having fun. Some might be happy to 
share with him, others not.
5 HOW DO I FIND A PLACE TO LIVE?
1 Proximity to place of work/study, and availability of public 
transport. 
2 Cost of accommodation; travel costs. 
3 Boarding house, shared accommodation, independent living 
in rented accommodation.
4 Options include visit local real estate agents, look online, 
check newspaper advertisements, check notice boards, word 
of mouth.
5 Yusuf probably decided too soon and should have checked 
other alternatives before making a decision.
6 Suggestions may include: tell Tora to find somewhere else  
to live; try to resolve the problems with her housemates.
7 ac: air conditioning; lug: lock up garage; ens: ensuite 
bathroom; dbl gar: double garage; furn: furnished; ldry: 
laundry; lng: lounge; bir: built-in robes; wi pant: walk in 
pantry; mod: modern.
6 CHOOSING YOUR ACCOMMODATION
1 The illustration is trying to show the many different factors 
to be considered in choosing a place to live.
2 People have different personalities – some like being 
alone, other are always seeking company. Advantages and 
disadvantages depend on who you are and the particular 
circumstances.
3 Cost is important if you are on a tight budget – it is 
important to ensure you can afford the cost of your chosen 
accommodation.
8 Safety and security are very important and could affect 
location choice.
7 WHAT IS A LEASE?
1 a bond; b tenant; c landlord; d lease; e rent; f premises.
2 True
3 Landlord (or their agent) and tenant 
4 Rent to be paid, date payment is due and rental conditions.
5 You are better protected in law if you have the agreement 
in writing, in case something goes wrong. 
6 Landlord and tenant need to agree on things like standards of 
cleanliness, repairs, responsibilities such as lawns, garden etc.
8 The office or Department of Fair Trading (in each state) will 
provide guidelines and advice for tenants.

8 THE BOND AND THE RENT
1 Rent money is what the tenant pays the landlord regularly 
for leasing the premises; bond money is paid in advance as 
security against possible damage to the property that needs 
to be repaired at the end of the lease.
2 At the end of the tenancy the bond money will be returned 
to the tenant, in full, unless there is damage to the property

1 When can I leave home? 
Moving out of home is a big step. Different people have different ideas about how it will work, and 
when they are ready to do it. Ben and Jessica, in the above scenario, illustrate just a couple of these 
different viewpoints. It is natural for teenagers to want their independence, and many see moving out 
as a way to achieve this. In some cases the process is negotiated mutually between the person and 
their parents or guardians, while in other cases there may be disagreement or conflict. Whatever the 
situation, there are some important legal points to consider.
What the law says
• When you turn 18 you can legally leave home. If you are under 18 you are classified as a ‘minor’. 
Turning 18 means you achieve your ‘majority’.
• If you are under 18 years of age, you can still leave home under the following circumstances:
 – if your parents or carers agree to you leaving home, despite your age
 – if your safety and well-being is under threat in your home environment
 – if you have left school and wish to attend an educational institution (such as a TAFE college) 
that is located too far from home for you to be able to attend on a daily basis
 – if you have left school and have found a job located a long way from your home.
• At age 18 you can also enter into loan contracts, sign a lease for accommodation and make major 
purchases (such as a car or motorbike).
Things to consider before moving out
Moving out of home is a big step. It is important to consider the decision carefully and not rush into 
anything. Teenagers who are considering moving out may not be fully aware of the responsibilities  
that come with living out of home. They may not be prepared to manage their finances independently,  
or they may not be ready to handle living in a shared environment with people they don’t necessarily 
know very well.
Similarly, their parents may worry about who they will be living with, or how they might cope without 
the daily support of their family. Some parents may prefer their children to live at home until they  
get married. 
Scenario – two students having a conversation in the living room at Ben’s place
Ben: 
 I’m sick of living at home. I’m always fighting with my parents – I can’t wait to get out of here.
Jessica:  I’m thinking of moving out too, but not because I fight with my folks.
Ben:   
 What do you mean? Do you get along  
well with your parents?
Jessica:   Yep, always have. They’re great –  
that’s not why I want to move out.  
I just want some more independence  
and some freedom.
Ben:  
 Yeah, I just want to be able to do  
what I like.
Jessica:  I think there’s more to it than that.  
You have responsibilities.
Ben:  
Like what?
Jessica:   Oh, it’s late! I’ll tell you later –  
I have to get home!

Tips for making the decision
Moving out can be a positive and even life-changing experience. These useful tips might help in  
the decision:
• Think it through – make sure you’ve really thought about whether you’re ready. Don’t act too 
hastily. Can you afford to move out? Is it the right time or are you rushing into it?
• Communicate effectively – discuss your decision with your parents and friends as well as  
potential flatmates. 
• Don’t be afraid to ask for help if you feel you need it – if you encounter difficulties there are other 
people willing to help you.

2 Moving out, moving back 
Not everyone wants to move out of home immediately – in fact, some people are moving back.  
Read the following newspaper article about a recent trend in society. 
JUDITH IRELAND 
January 9, 2010
Kippers, boomerang kids, rent-
free adults or freeloading lazy 
bums. 
Whatever 
the 
latest 
market 
research 
term, 
it’s 
become 
increasingly common for young 
people to live with their parents 
rather than spring off on their 
own.
Recent Australian Bureau of 
Statistics analysis indicates that 
young Australians are staying at 
home more than ever before. An 
estimated 23 per cent of 20- to 
34-year-olds are living in their 
parental home. And almost half 
of those who leave before their 
mid-30s end up rebounding back 
to their old bedrooms at least 
once over the next few years.
The Pew Research Centre 
recently found rising numbers of 
US graduates are returning to the 
family bosom, while the British 
Business and Skills Secretary, 
Lord Mandelson, has called 
on parents to be more forceful 
when ousting their little kippers 
(kids in parents’ pockets eroding 
retirement savings).
Naturally, the reasons behind 
the trend are more complex than 
just laziness or an undying love of 
mum’s lasagne. People marrying 
later, coupled with huge increases 
in tertiary study, the sky-high cost 
of housing and frosty economic 
climes are just some of the factors 
that have conspired to make it less 
necessary and more expensive to 
move out.
Yet for a significant proportion 
of young people there is also an 
element of choice in the matter. 
Those with full-time jobs in 
their 20s and even their 30s are 
staying put to save money for 
entertainment or investments 
rather than ‘’waste’’ it on rent. 
As 26-year-old labourer, Joe 
Singleton, who lives with his 
parents, recently told Britain’s 
Sun, “I could probably afford to 
live elsewhere if I didn’t go out but 
I want to buy rather than rent.’’
According to the ABS, the 
most common reasons for young 
Australians to stay at home 
are money issues along with 
convenience and enjoyment.
While the financial costs of 
moving out are widely recognised, 
the social costs of bunking down 
in the ‘burbs until the economy 
picks up or some babe pops the 
question are barely mentioned.
Share housing may still be the 
most common living arrangement 
for people in their early 20s 
but an increasing number are 
missing out on the experience. 
Unglorified by frat houses, Big 
Brother and John Birmingham’s 
horror tale, He Died with a Felafel 
in his Hand, the share house is 
also an important staging ground 
between 
childhood 
reliance 
on your family and something 
approaching adult independence, 
be it on your own or with 
someone you really love. Even 
your basic-model share house 
– with its inbuilt compromises, 
simmering disagreements, snarky 
estate agents and propensity for 
things to break - has the potential 
to teach you more about life 
than any Contiki trip through 
Thailand.
Moving out also exposes you to 
the rich tapestry that is humanity 
other than your family. Sure you 
meet some freaks but chances 
are some of your housemates will 
also drink beer with you.
In addition, up-close exposure 
to others provides an excellent 
opportunity to tinker with the 
less appealing aspects of your 
personality. When flatmates are 
not related to you by family or 
friendship, they won’t be as shy 
when pointing out that you have 
not cleaned the bathroom for 
three months.
It’s not all harsh reality. 
Flatmates inadvertently introduce 
you to new ways of seeing the 
world. From new brands of 
toothpaste to better bootleg DVDs, 
more obscure countercultures, 
a tastier way of making lasagne 
– maybe even different types of 
pasta altogether.
Life lessons lost for the 
stay-at-home generation

3 What is homelessness? 
The two stories above are fictitious, but they are based on things that happen in the community.  
These are the kinds of things that can lead to homelessness. 
Levels of homelessness
The Australian Bureau of Statistics divides the homeless into the following categories:
1 Absolute homeless (primary homeless): People without conventional accommodation (living on the 
streets, in deserted buildings, improvised dwellings, in parks, etc.) – sometimes called ‘sleeping rough’.
2 Relative homeless (secondary and tertiary homeless): People staying in boarding houses, 
people using Supported Accommodation Assistance Program (SAAP) and other similar emergency 
accommodation services, or people with no secure accommodation staying temporarily with friends 
or relatives in private dwellings.
On Census night in 2006, the homeless population in Australia was 105 000, according to the Australian 
Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Causes of homelessness
Some of the main causes of homelessness are:
• family members fighting amongst themselves can lead to one or more members leaving home 
• a family member physically assaulting other family members (this is known as domestic violence)
• mental or emotional abuse
• sexual assault
• financial problems within the household, such as unemployment or gambling problems
• physical or mental illness or intellectual disability within the family
• drug and/or alcohol abuse
• family bereavement, which can strain family relationships
• accommodation problems, such as overcrowding in the home. 
Sometimes more than one of these problems can occur within the one household.
Emma’s story
When I was 13, my father left home. My mum found a new partner who soon 
moved in. He abused my sisters and me on a regular basis. He also used to beat 
my mum but he always said he was sorry, and she forgave him.
I put up with this for about a year, then, when I turned 15, I decided I couldn’t 
take it anymore. I said to mum, ‘Either he goes or I go.’ Mum chose him, so I 
left home. I had nowhere to go, and ended up on the streets. I sometimes stayed 
with friends, but never for long. I moved closer to the city and started sleeping 
with guys I picked up on the street to get enough money to live on. I slept in 
abandoned houses and buildings with other young people who were just like me.
Luke’s story
I was 14 when I got kicked out of home. I always seemed to be fighting with my 
parents. They wanted to control me and I was a bit of a rebel at the time. At first 
I just stayed anywhere – camped, slept in cars – wherever I could find a place to 
be. I didn’t own anything except my clothes so it was easy to just keep moving.
One day a mate told me about a place that offered refuge accommodation. I 
went there to see if they could help me. The staff at the refuge organised for me 
to move into emergency accommodation. While I was there, my support worker 
helped me find a job as a labourer. I also got some information on going back to finish school. I enrolled 
in a TAFE course to become a plumber. Now I rent my own apartment, I’ve nearly finished my plumber’s 
apprenticeship and work full time for a large construction company.

Fact or fiction
*  All homeless people are older men.   FALSE 
Homeless people are all ages, and the breakdown between males and females is roughly 50/50.
*  You’re not homeless if you’re staying with friends.   FALSE 
Many homeless people stay with friends or relatives, but without a permanent home, they are still homeless.
*  Most homeless people sleep out on the streets or in an improvised shelter.   FALSE 
Very few homeless people sleep out – many stay in temporary accommodation.

Getting help
As a basic human right, all people are entitled to a safe and affordable place to live. If you find yourself 
without a home you can seek help either through government agencies or privately run services, such as: 
• State government agencies such as the Department of Community Services in NSW or the 
Department of Human Services in Victoria. There are similar agencies in all Australian states and 
territories. If you are under 18 years of age, you will be given special assistance.
• Centrelink, the federal government agency, can help with financial matters.
• Emergency organisations such as Kids Helpline (phone 1800 55 1800) or Lifeline (phone 131 114) 
can help if you are in urgent need of immediate housing and/or food.
Other sources of help can include organisations such as Alcoholics Anonymous, Alateen (for children  
who have an alcoholic in the family) and the National Children’s and Youth Law Centre (called Lawstuff), 
as well as family members, friends, school counsellors and other personal contacts.

4 Different types of accommodation  
There are many different types of accommodation available. It is important to be aware of all the 
options available to you. The main differences between the options are cost, location and level of 
independence. Do you want to share with others, or would you prefer to live alone? Will you cook your 
own meals, or would you prefer somebody did that for you? Different kinds of accommodation suit a 
range of needs. These options are explained below.
Boarding
Full board means that you will live, or ‘board’, in a family home and all or most meals are supplied. 
These arrangements can vary widely. You can generally be guaranteed your own room, but would 
normally share bathroom/toilet facilities and eat in the family dining room. 
Some properties are classified as ‘boarding houses’. These places have a landlord or caretaker who runs 
the premises, either living in the property or controlling things from another location. 
Meals may be provided (in which case you are a ‘boarder’) but if you only receive cleaning services, 
linen or other household items you are a ‘lodger’. There will be a shared kitchen and bathroom, but 
there may be no communal, or shared, living space. Tenants have no say in who shares the boarding 
house with them. The owner chooses the tenants. 
You should be aware that living in boarding houses means you don’t have the protections available to 
renters (who are protected by the Residential Tenancies Act). This means you could be asked to leave 
without notice. 
Rental accommodation
Rental accommodation means paying a set amount of money each week or month to rent a property. 
This property can either be shared (in which case, all the costs are shared among the tenants) or 
individual. Types of rented accommodation include:
Studios
Studios are very small apartments made up of one main room without a separate bedroom. The main 
room might include a bed, lounge and a small kitchen (kitchenette). The bathroom is usually separate, 
although in some cases it may be shared. A studio has the advantage of allowing you to live alone 
relatively cheaply. 
Flats, units and apartments
Places with one or more separate bedrooms are usually flats,  
units or apartments. They vary in the number of bedrooms  
(usually between 1 and 3). As well as bedrooms, they usually  
have a separate living area, kitchen, bathroom and sometimes 
laundry. Some apartment buildings have a communal laundry  
area which may be located on the ground floor or basement  
and shared with other units. 
Houses, townhouses, semi-detached houses and 
terrace houses
Houses are identified as freestanding properties. Townhouses, 
semi-detached houses and terrace houses will share one or more 
common walls with a neighbour. Most houses have 2, 3 or 4 
bedrooms, a kitchen, bathroom, living area and laundry. Many 
houses will also have a garden and/or courtyard area. 
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
11
Share accommodation 
Share accommodation is often preferred by students looking to save money. The cost of rent and bills is 
split between the occupants, and usually everyone provides some of the furniture. Rental properties can 
be shared by several tenants. Other kinds of shared accommodation include:
• hostels, which usually have secure private rooms with shared cooking and washing facilities
• student residences, which are often based on campus and usually include a furnished room with 
meals provided for an extra charge. 
• accommodation in exchange for work, which requires you to do work around the house in 
exchange for free or cheap accommodation.

5 How do I find a place to live? 
Finding a place to live can be an exhausting process. There are so many things to consider. It’s worth 
thinking it through carefully though, to ensure that you find a place that meets your needs.
Consider the type of accommodation that you want
There are many different types of accommodation, including boarding houses, share accommodation 
and independent living in a rented house or apartment. They vary in price as well as in the level of 
independence you have and the amount of cleaning or shopping you may need to do.
Note: See the previous unit for more information about different types of accommodation.
Location is another big factor 
in finding a place to live
Living close to your place of work or study 
is convenient, but suitable places can be 
hard to find because of the demand. This 
demand means that they are usually also 
relatively expensive. Places that are further 
away are often cheaper and may well be 
better quality, however travel expenses such 
as public transport fares or petrol costs 
have to be factored in. Living at home may 
be cheaper, but again transport costs and 
travel time need to be considered.
How do you find a place?
Visit real estate agents
Real estate agents have lists of rental accommodation available in their area. Visit agents in the area 
where you would like to live. Real estate agents can give you all the information you need about rental 
accommodation and can arrange inspections of any properties you might be interested in renting. 
Get online
There are also several major real estate websites online 
which list current properties available, often including 
photos. The following websites could get you started:
www.domain.com.au 
 
www.flatmates.com.au 
www.flatmatefinders.com.au 
 
www.realestate.com.au
Check newspaper advertisements
The daily newspapers have a section for real estate 
which usually includes rental properties and share 
accommodation. The main national newspapers, such 
as the Sydney Morning Herald in New South Wales, The 
Age in Victoria and the Courier Mail in Queensland have 
the largest coverage, particularly the Saturday editions of 
these papers. The classifieds section of local newspapers 
can also be useful. 
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
13
Check noticeboards
Information about accommodation, especially share 
accommodation, can be found on the noticeboards 
at universities, TAFE colleges, workplaces or on 
community noticeboards at supermarkets and  
local cafes. 
Ask around
Sometimes you can find accommodation through 
word of mouth and recommendations from friends. 
Let people know what you’re looking for, and where, 
in case somebody hears of anything that might suit 
your needs.

7 What is a lease? 
Read the definitions below to help you understand the terminology used when agreeing to rent a property.
landlord 
the person who owns a property and is prepared to let it
tenant 
the person who has permission to rent the landlord’s property to live in
lease 
 the rental contract stating the amount of rent to be paid, the method of payment, length  
of time and other conditions (see below). It is sometimes known as a tenancy agreement. 
rent 
the amount of money, per week that the tenant must pay to the landlord (or agent)
bond 
the money paid up-front as security in case of damage to the property
Tenancy agreements can be either verbal or written. It is better to have a written agreement because  
a written agreement: 
• gives you more security provided you follow the terms of the lease 
• means you cannot be asked to leave before the lease expires 
• means the amount of rent you have to pay is fixed for the term of the lease
• gives you the right to have repairs done provided they are reasonable.
There are two types of tenancy agreements – fixed-term and periodic. A fixed-term agreement is for 
a set period of time, often 6 months. A periodic agreement is an arrangement which runs from week 
to week or month to month. Written agreements must follow the wording of an official ‘Residential 
Tenancy Agreement’ form. A simplified version is illustrated below:

BETWEEN
LANDLORD    Name(s)...................................................................................................................................

AND
TENANT 
Name(s)..................................................................................................................................
PREMISES 
The landlord gives the tenant the right to occupy the premises at .....................................
 
 
................................................................................................................................................
RENT 
The rent is $......... per week, payable every ................................,  
 
 
starting on  ........./........../........ and payable in advance.
Conditions: 
1

Signed:

Conditions
In a lease agreement there will generally be a number of conditions that the landlord and the tenant 
agree upon. These may include things like:
• who is responsible for keeping the place clean, and the standards of cleanliness
• who is responsible for repairs, and how these should be done 
• who is responsible for mowing the lawn or maintaining the garden (if there is one).

Tips for tenants
Before moving in
•  Always read the lease (or Residential Tenancy Agreement) carefully before signing it. Never sign  
a blank sheet of paper.
•  If you are unsure about anything in the lease, get some professional advice.
•  The Office of Fair Trading in your state will probably have a guide for tenants that you should be 
able to access free of charge. Familiarise yourself with your rights and responsibilities as a tenant.
•  Check that the premises are clean and safe. You will probably have to pay a Bond, in which case 
you should carefully check the Condition Report (see unit 9).
•  Ensure you get receipts for any rent paid up front.
Before moving out 
•  Make sure you pay the final rent owing.
•  Arrange for the electricity, gas, water and telephone to be disconnected, and pay the final bills.
•  Check that the premises are in good order and condition.
•  Make sure that you have packed all your belongings. 
•  Organise for the landlord or agent to return any bond money paid.
•  Leave a forwarding address with the landlord or agent so you can receive any mail delivered to the 
premises after you leave.
•  Check the terms of your agreement to ensure you have met all conditions for leaving (such as  
cleaning or any repairs).

8 The bond and the rent 
After signing a lease you will need to pay both bond and rent. It is important to note that these are 
separate payments.
The bond
As the owners of property, landlords need to have some way of protecting their assets. The bond is an 
up-front payment made by the tenant before they move into the property. If they cause any damage to 
the property while they are living there, the cost of the repair is taken out of the bond and the tenant 
may only get part of their bond money back. If a tenant has not caused any damage to the property, 
he or she is entitled to have their bond money returned at the end of the tenancy. 
The bond money is held by the Rental Bond Board (NSW) or the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority 
(Victoria), or similar organisations in other states and territories. At the end of the tenancy, the tenant 
can apply to get their bond money back, but the agreement of the landlord is required before the 
money is released. 
The rent
Tenants are expected to pay rent in full and on time. The rent is usually paid in advance. The landlord 
or agent is entitled to take action if rent is not paid in full on the due date.
Paying the rent
There are several methods of payment available to tenants (see box at right) and 
the method agreed upon may be included in the residential lease. Some payment 
methods may incur extra costs, such as credit card charges or fees.
When the rent is paid the landlord (or agent) must issue a receipt. If the rent is 
paid in person the tenant must be given a receipt on the spot. For other payments 
a receipt must be sent or available for pick-up within five days. A tenant should 
always keep a record of the rent paid as proof in case there are any disputes.
A receipt should contain the following information:
•  the tenant’s name
•  the address of the property
•  the date
•  the total amount paid
•  the period that the payment covers.
Problems with paying rent
Tenants sometimes have trouble meeting their regular rental payments, for a variety of reasons.  
If you run into trouble with your rent, consumer affairs advice is available from state government 
agencies (such as the NSW Office of Fair Trading or Consumer Affairs Victoria). There are similar 
agencies in the other states. When experiencing problems with rental payments, bear in mind the 
following do’s and don’ts:
Do
• contact your landlord or agent as soon as possible to explain any problems and try to work  
out a solution
• seek assistance from state or local consumer affairs organisations.
Don’t
•  withhold payment of rent because you are not satisfied with lack of action on repairs
•  fail to pay the final weeks’ rent at the end of the lease – this can be deducted from any bond 
money owing to you.

 8 The bond and the rent 
If your rent is more than 14 days overdue the landlord can give you notice to vacate and apply to the 
courts for an order to evict you. This is not automatic, however – tenants do have rights and a landlord 
cannot simply lock a tenant out for not paying their rent. A legal procedure must be followed and the 
matter resolved in court.
Increasing the rent
Landlords cannot increase rent at will. There are various state laws which govern rent increases.  
The rules surrounding rent increases state that:
•  The landlord must first give notice (generally 60 days written notice) of a rent increase.
•  The tenant may appeal against any rent increase which they believe to be excessive.
•  If the tenant cannot successfully negotiate the changes with the landlord, he or she may approach 
the Residential Tenancies Tribunal (NSW) or the Victorian Civil and Administration Tribunal (Victoria) 
to have the dispute settled. Other states have similar bodies. 
Disputes
Disputes between landlords and tenants can occur for various reasons. Problems often arise when the 
tenant requests that certain repairs are carried out and the landlord or agent either does not act or 
disputes the need for the repairs. These disputes can escalate and sometimes need to be resolved by the 
relevant Tribunal for that state.

9 The condition report 
A condition report is a document that describes the general condition of the premises being let, 
including fittings and fixtures. It is necessary in situations where a bond has been paid. It is the duty 
of the landlord or his or her agent to prepare a condition report on the premises. They must give two 
copies of the signed condition report to the tenant before the tenant can occupy the premises. A fine 
can be imposed if this is not done. The tenant must fill out and promptly return the condition report 
to the landlord or agent. 
The condition report is an extremely important document. It may be used as evidence if there is a future 
dispute about who is responsible for any cleaning, damage, or missing items. It is important that tenants 
keep their copy of the condition report until the end of the tenancy. 
The landlord or agent has the right to claim some, or all of the bond money if there has been damage, 
if items are missing or if the premises are left dirty and untidy at the end of the tenancy. The condition 
report is therefore crucial as it is an agreement of the state of the premises prior to the tenancy. This 
protects the tenant from having to pay for any damage that they are not responsible for.

10 Connecting services 
When moving into a new home you will need to have services such as gas, electricity, water and 
telephone connected. These services are known as ‘utilities’. Having these services connected involves 
setting up an account with one of the providers of these services.
If you are renting, some of these services, such as water, may be included in the rent, and others, such 
as gas, may not be available in the property you are renting.
Energy costs 
Gas and electricity are both forms of energy. There are various energy providers and it can be worth 
shopping around for the best deals. Some energy providers offer green energy. This is usually more 
expensive, but it means that some or all of your electricity usage is matched with energy from 
renewable sources, such as wind or solar power. This offsets the environmental impacts of using 
electricity that is produced from burning fossil fuels, such as coal. 
Many homes are also connected to a gas supply. Gas is mainly used for heating, and sometimes also for 
cooking. Check whether gas is available in the property, and whether there are any appliances in the 
home that run on gas. 
Choosing a provider
You may be able to choose which energy provider you want to open an account with. When making 
this decision, it can be helpful to compare energy costs, off-peak rates, connection and disconnection 
fees and green energy options. There are several energy providers to choose from, including: 
Energy bills
Energy bills usually contain a lot of information. They can sometimes be difficult to read, but they can 
tell you a lot about your energy use. Your energy bill will list your electricity use, which is calculated in 
kilowatt hours (kWh) as well as showing the pattern of your energy consumption, usually on a graph 
(see below).

 10 Connecting services
Renewable energy
Most electricity is produced from burning 
fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas. These 
resources are limited and will one day run 
out. Burning fossil fuels to produce energy 
also harms the environment. Renewable 
energy is energy that is produced from 
sustainable sources – sources that will 
not run out. Forms of renewable energy 
include solar power, wind power, 
geothermal power, hydro-electric power 
and tidal power. At this point, renewable 
energy is more expensive to produce 
in Australia than coal-based energy. 
However this may change over time as 
new technology could develop, if a carbon 
tax or an emissions trading scheme is 
introduced or if more people switch to 
renewable energy.
Telephone costs
Telephone costs include both landlines and mobile 
phones. Telephone costs are rarely included in the rent. 
If you need a landline, you will need to open an account 
and get the phone connected. This usually involves  
a connection fee and then ongoing monthly fees and  
call charges. 
Paying bills
There are several ways you can pay your bills.  
These include:
•  by phone (Bpay, debit or credit card) 
•  in person at Australia Post (cash, cheque, debit or 
credit card)
•  by mail (cheque).
Overdue accounts often result in late payment fees being 
charged, so it is a good idea to note the due date on all 
bills received.

Useful terms
Broadband
A range of high-speed internet services, including ADSL, cable and satellite.
Dial-up
 A basic internet connection that runs through the telephone line. When connected  
to the Internet the telephone cannot be used
ADSL
 Stands for Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line. ADSL is an internet connection that  
runs through the telephone line but allows use of the telephone and internet at the 
same time. 
Upload
 If you send any material via the internet you are said to be uploading it. For 
example, sending emails or entering a web address into your browser.
Download
 When you receive material from the internet you are downloading it. This includes 
any web pages that you view as well as emails you receive and file attachments that 
you open.
File sharing
 This happens when you allow other users to upload a file, such as music or videos, 
from your computer. 
Megabytes  
and 
gigabytes
 How units of information on computers are measured. A megabyte is equal to 1000 
kilobytes or 1 000 000 bytes. A gigabyte is 1000 megabytes. A typical three-minute 
song will be about 30 megabytes. Text files use fewer megabytes than pictures or 
audio files.
ISP
 Stands for Internet Service Provider – a company that provides an Internet 
connection to customers. ISPs include Bigpond, iinet, Optus and Dodo.
11 Communication 
Communication is an essential part of day-to-day life. It takes many forms. There are two major forms 
of communication technology which have become a significant part of how we communicate every day. 
They are the telephone and the computer. 
The telephone
If you are sharing a house that has a landline it may be necessary to work out a 
system for paying the bills. This can be either an even split of each bill, including 
line rental and all call charges, or each person can be responsible for their calls 
and the line rental is shared equally. This can be time-consuming to calculate,  
but most phone companies itemise each phone call made, especially long 
distance calls or calls to premium-rate numbers.
The computer
Most people own either a desktop computer or a laptop. When moving into a 
new house you may also want to arrange to have internet access. If two or more 
people in a household are sharing a computer there needs to be an agreement 
about what kind of plan is needed and who pays the monthly charges to the ISP 
(Internet Service Provider).

 11 Communication
Hints for internet use
•  Research the options. There are lots of different 
plans and prices on offer. Consider your usage 
requirements. Most internet plans offer a certain 
amount of usage for a monthly fee. Exceeding 
the limit can result in excess usage charges. It 
may be better to select a plan with a higher 
limit, even if you don’t use it all, rather than 
selecting a plan with a lower limit and incurring 
charges if you exceed it.
•  Find out how flexible your plan is – can you 
change it? After a while you may want to 
change your plan to a higher or lower limit. 
Most providers allow this, but it is good to be 
aware of what the alternatives are and how easy 
it is to change.
•  Protect yourself against computer viruses with virus protection software. Also guard against 
unauthorised use by keeping your password private. It is best to memorise your password rather 
than writing it down, and change it regularly. Be wary of emails received from unknown sources 
and delete them without opening them. Never open an attachment from someone you don’t  
know and trust. If you have a complaint with your ISP, try to resolve it with them in the first 
instance. If that is unsuccessful, contact the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. They  
can be contacted by phone on 1800 062 058, or by email at tio@tio.com.au.

12 Moving day 
Moving to a new home can be a daunting task and requires some planning. You need to consider how 
you are going to move all your belongings to your new home. This will depend on:
•  the amount and size of your belongings
•  your transport options – you could:
 –  get help from family and friends who have vehicles to help transport your things 
 –  hire a van and organise people to help you 
 –  use a removalist. Note that some companies charge based on an hourly rate while others use  
a combination of time and distance travelled.
•  your budget. For example, if your budget allows for this, you may opt to have a removalist 
company do all the packing as well as the moving. 
Try to have a system.  
For example, pack  
one room at a time.
 
Label all boxes clearly, 
including contents, whether  
it is fragile or not, and  
which room it is for. 
Bubble wrap, towels, 
blankets and clothing 
all make good packing 
materials.
Use small boxes  
for heavy objects, 
such as books.
Tie electric cords 
in neat bundles so 
they don’t tangle. 
Leave your clothes on their 
hangers so you can rehang 
them as soon as you get to 
the new place.
Carry your valuables with 
you when you move, 
rather than packing  
them in a box.

up having to throw it all in boxes at the last 
minute! Bill borrowed his friend’s ute, and asked 
a few mates to help him with the move. Once he 
was all moved in, he bought everyone pizza as a 
thank you.
Ally
Ally was moving from a house into a unit. She 
had a busy, demanding job and didn’t have 
time to pack. She also knew it would be a tight

13 What do I need to buy? 
  
Some premises come fully furnished but if you don’t have any furniture and you are moving into an 
unfurnished place, there will be some items you need. If you haven’t lived out of home before there 
may also be other basics that you will need. What do you need immediately? What can wait? How do 
you proceed from here? You can divide your requirements into two categories:
•  essentials – things you need to have as soon as possible
•  options – things you can live without for a while. 
Essentials
Basic furniture
You will need some items of furniture for your new home. A bed is important, to ensure you have 
somewhere to sleep. A table and chairs will provide you with somewhere to eat, and could also serve as 
a desk if you are studying. You may also need a couch to provide a place to relax or to entertain friends. 
Basic appliances
Essential kitchen appliances are likely to include a refrigerator, a stove and an oven. Most properties will 
have a stove and an oven installed. Other appliances that you may consider to be essential include a 
washing machine and a vacuum cleaner. 
Other basics
Other items that you will need include cutlery and crockery, such as plates, bowls, cups, pots and pans. 
You may also need to buy sheets, towels and pillows.
Options
Expensive furniture is not necessary. Some people make do with milk crates to put things on, such 
as the television or stereo, until they can afford something else. Small kitchen appliances, such as 
rice cookers and sandwich toasters can be handy but are options, rather than essentials. Although a 
television, computer and mobile phone may be seen as essential by many people, others may be able  
to live without them. 
Making some choices
Here are some of the choices you may need to make:
•  Do you want a landline or a mobile phone – or both?
•  Will you use a laundromat or buy a washing machine?
•  Do you need to buy more furniture, or get rid of some,  
if you are moving into a smaller place?
•  Should you consider contents insurance, if you don’t 
already have a policy?
•  Would you prefer to buy new or second hand? Websites 
such as eBay and the Trading Post can be a good source 
of second-hand goods. Will you buy furniture and 
appliances or hire them? Hiring appliances means you 
need less money up-front, but this can work out to be 
more expensive in the long run.
•  When buying new items for a shared house, will you 
have joint ownership or make individual purchases? Joint 
ownership costs each person less money, but problems 
could arise if you later move to different places.

15 Share houses 
Housemates
We are all different, so when choosing a housemate we need to be 
aware of the sort of person, or people we can live with. Differences 
in cultural, religious, social or political backgrounds can sometimes 
cause conflict. Differences can also exist between smokers and non- 
smokers, people who like their space tidy and people who don’t mind 
a bit of mess, meat eaters and vegetarians, morning people and night 
people, outgoing and shy people and pet lovers and pet haters. 
It may be a good idea to try and get to know the people you are 
sharing with before committing yourself. It is also important that 
everyone tries to be understanding and considerate of other people’s beliefs and cultures. 
Housemates and conflict
Read the following case studies to discover the kinds of problems people can have in share 
accommodation situations.
Mia 
I am currently living with a female housemate who pretty much does what she likes. 
She works at the local pub and comes home around 7 or 8 in the morning. When she 
gets home she’s incredibly noisy. This wouldn’t be a problem normally, but I’m doing 
shift work and I can’t sleep with all the noise she makes. Things have gone missing 
from my room, too – I think she might be stealing from me.
Daniel
I moved into a house with two 
other students and at first, all was 
well. After about three months 
a new girl moved in. As soon as 
she arrived she started cleaning 
and rearranging everything. She 
would clean practically every day. 
At first we didn’t mind too much 
– at least the house was clean – but then things 
started getting worse. She told us we shouldn’t 
use our dishwasher because it was dirty, so we 
had to wash everything by hand. She would 
leave a mess and then criticise others. It got to 
the point where she was constantly complaining 
and we were basically ignoring her. We are 
relatively clean, but I don’t see the need to clean 
every single day.
Nick
I had a really bad experience 
once. I moved into a house 
with two girls under a joint 
tenancy. They were an 
absolute nightmare to live 
with and wouldn’t pay any 
bills so I gave up after two 
months and moved out. However, the tenant 
who replaced me cleared out before signing the 
contract that the landlord had sent him. It turned 
out that both girls hadn’t paid any rent since 
we moved in. It had been four months, but I 
wasn’t aware until the landlord decided to throw 
them out. Because my name was left on the joint 
tenancy I’ve been dragged into the whole mess 
and am now being pursued for the rent they 
didn’t pay. 
Serap
I moved into a share house early last year with a few other people. Everything was 
fine until we realised one housemate didn’t know how to use a bar of soap or a 
washing machine. He smelt terrible! We tried to explain why it was a good idea  
to shower daily, and why you had to actually clean the kitchen, not just wave a  
damp cloth over it. We went to the landlord, but he didn’t want to get involved  
in personal disputes between tenants.

 15 Share houses
Natalie
I moved into a share house near my university that was occupied by a really shy guy. 
He seemed fine and helped me carry everything when I first moved in. Things seemed 
very normal – until my boyfriend came over one night. After he left, my flatmate 
said he wanted to have a ‘chat’. He told me he had wanted a flatmate who was single. 
He thought that once we had spent some time together, we could have a romantic 
relationship. It was very awkward – I had to move out.
Household organisation
Moving in with other people can be a great experience, but living with people can be tricky. To avoid 
conflict, it can help to make decisions about how you want to run things. Agreeing on the details up 
front can keep them from becoming big issues down the track. 
•  cleaning the house (How will you divide up the jobs? How often do they need to be done?)
•  washing the dishes (Will everyone wash their own dishes, or will you take it in turns?)
•  preparing the meals (Will you each cook separate meals or will you take it in turns to cook  
for everyone? Will you share food or buy your own?)
•  paying the bills (Who is in charge of the bills? How will they be split?) 
•  use of communal spaces/things, such as living areas, TV etc. (Will you have a timetable, or just 
consult one another?)

16 The household budget 
Managing the household’s finances is an important aspect of 
living in shared premises. Making a budget is an effective way 
to keep things under control. 
 The key to managing a household budget is working out:
•  household income – money coming in 
•  household expenses – money going out 
•  priorities – which expenses do you have to pay, and which can you avoid. 
Establishing priorities
There are some things you have to pay for on a regular basis. These include food, rent, electricity and 
telephone bills. There are other items which may also need to be allowed for. These can include medical 
expenses, train fares and car or bicycle repairs. Then there are luxury items such as new electronic 
gadgets, overseas holidays or weekends away. If you can manage the essential items and allow for 
occasional added expenses it may also be possible to indulge in some luxuries from time to time. If you 
are having problems paying for the essentials, however, it is the luxury items that need to be cut first.
Sharing expenses
Some expenses, such as rent and electricity, may be shared with your housemates, while others, such as 
mobile phones, will be separate. How landline costs are shared will depend on whether one housemate 
makes more calls to mobile or long distance numbers. You may need to devise a system of either 
recording telephone calls or monitoring the bill when it comes in to ensure costs are split fairly. 
Some share houses set up a combined fund or ‘kitty’ to manage shared expenses. Each housemate 
puts in an agreed amount of money each week to cover expenses. The kitty might be used to pay for 
rent and electricity, and sometimes also covers food and other household items such as dishcloths, tea 
towels and toilet paper. In other share houses people prefer to buy their own food, particularly if some 
housemates eat out a lot while others prefer to stay at home. However, this can lead to difficulties when 
it comes to keeping food separate, and remembering what belongs to each person. 
Managing bills 
Managing bills sometimes requires a bit of planning. Most bills arrive regularly – they are usually issued 
either monthly or quarterly. It is a good idea to make a note of when you expect bills to arrive, and 
when they will need to be paid. This will help you to ensure that you have enough money set aside to 
pay bills when they arrive.
It is important to stay on top of your expenses. Failure to pay the rent on time can lead to disputes with 
the landlord or agent and can have serious consequences. If you do run into trouble with any of your 
accounts, it is a good idea to contact the company first to see what arrangements you can make. Many 
companies will be willing to let you pay in instalments to help you get on top of your debts. 
Creating a budget 
A good way to plan for your expenses is to draw up a simple budget. Using two columns, write down 
how much you earn each week (or fortnight or month) in the left-hand column, and how much you 
spend on essentials on the right-hand column. The money that is left over after you subtract your 
expenses from your income represents your savings. This money can be set aside for unforeseen 
expenses, or perhaps spent on luxuries.
Definition: A budget is a plan 
outlining your expected income, 
spending and savings patterns 
over a period of time.

17 Repairs and  
maintenance issues   
There can sometimes be conflict between tenants and their landlords or agents over repairs and 
maintenance. The following conversations demonstrate the kinds of conflict that can take place 
regarding this issue.
Melissa  
Mr Johnson, I’m not happy. 
(tenant): 
 Those repairs I requested three 
weeks ago still have not been 
done. This is the third time I  
have had to ring you – I’d like  
to know what’s going on.
Mr Johnson I have been in contact with the 
(agent):  
 landlord and he says that the 
repairs you’ve requested are  
not urgent.
Melissa:  
 I disagree. The leaking tap in the 
kitchen is wasting a huge amount 
of water, and the broken light 
fittings in the lounge room are 
inconvenient,  
not to mention dangerous. 
Mr Johnson:   I think you are being a bit fussy, 
Melissa. 
Melissa:  
 As a tenant I have 
rights, and that 
includes the right 
to have repairs 
done when I ask. 
I want these 
things fixed 
immediately 
or I will 
take further 
action.
Mr Johnson:   Making threats 
won’t help the situation, Melissa.
Melissa decides to ring her state consumer affairs 
department to seek some clarification. She talks 
to Jo, a consumer affairs public relations officer.
Melissa:  
 Hi Jo, my name is Melissa. I’ve just 
had an argument with my agent 
about some repairs to my apartment. 
I believe the repairs are urgent but 
my landlord doesn’t agree, and won’t 
fix them. 
Jo:  
 Okay Melissa, what kind of repairs 
are we talking about?
Melissa:  
 There are broken light fittings in the 
lounge room, and a leaking tap in the 
kitchen. Surely these things qualify as 
urgent repairs? 
Jo:  
 Urgent repairs usually involve safety 
issues, things like dangerous electrical 
faults, gas leaks, and blocked or 
broken toilets. Appliances or fittings 
that are not working properly would 
definitely be classed as urgent. 
Leaking taps where a substantial 
amount of water is being wasted can 
also be classed as urgent.
 Melissa:   Thanks for that. I will contact the 
agent again to tell them what you 
have said. If that doesn’t work, what 
should I do?
 Jo:  
 If they still won’t agree to the repairs 
there is an administrative tribunal 
you can apply to. See how you go.
Urgent repairs
It is important to distinguish between urgent and non-urgent repairs. Repairs are generally the landlord’s 
responsibility. If the tenant or resident caused the damage, however, the landlord can ask them to 
arrange or pay for repairs. Landlords or their agents also have a responsibility to respond to repair 
requests promptly. Tenants must continue paying rent when they are waiting for repairs to be done. 
Requests for urgent repairs
As a tenant there are a number of steps you should take if you need an urgent repair:
•  Contact the landlord or agent about the problem, and clearly state that the repair is urgent. It’s 
best to keep all your communication in writing, so you have a record of the discussions that have 
taken place. In most states, if the landlord or agent doesn’t arrange for the repair to be done, 
you can arrange this yourself, so long as it doesn’t cost more than $1000. 
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
37
•  You would then need to contact the landlord asking to be 
reimbursed for the repair. The landlord usually has to pay  
you within 14 days. 
•  If the landlord refuses to pay you, or if the repairs will  
cost more than $1000, you can apply to the administrative 
tribunal in your state, which will grant you a hearing.  
The tribunal can order the landlord to arrange the repairs. 
Non-urgent repairs 
If the repairs are not urgent, you still need to contact the landlord 
or agent in writing to request the repair. If the repairs aren’t 
carried out within a reasonable time (this depends on the nature 
of the repairs), you can contact the administrative tribunal in your 
state. In most cases you have 60 days to make your application. In 
the meantime, you must continue paying rent until the matter is 
sorted out. 
Tribunals
There are various state tribunals whose task is to resolve disputes 
between tenants and landlords, each with different names.

18 The neighbourhood 
Every neighbourhood is different. Whenever you move into a new area, there will be things you need to 
know and things you need to consider in order to ensure you get along with your neighbours and are a 
respectful member of the community. 
Know your neighbourhood
The following information can help you to settle into your new neighbourhood. Find out about:
•  rubbish collection – which day of the week the rubbish is collected, whether there are special bins for 
recycling and garden waste 
•  public transport – where is the nearest bus stop and train station? When do the buses and trains arrive?
•  shops and facilities – where is the nearest supermarket, petrol station, shopping centre, post office, 
bank, park, library, swimming pool, gym, etc. 
•  neighbours – get to know the people living nearby. Be considerate of any needs or concerns they may have. 
Being a considerate neighbour
There are many things you can do to ensure that you are a good neighbour. It is important to treat your 
neighbours with respect and consider their needs as well as your own when going about your day-to-day lives.
Privacy 
Many homes are built very close together, and in these circumstances it is particularly important to 
remember that you are entitled to privacy in your home, and so are your neighbours. It is not considerate 
to look over fences or in windows, or to eavesdrop on your neighbours’ conversations. Also consider your 
own conversations – it is best to discuss private matters indoors, where the neighbours can’t hear you. 
Noise
There is a federal government organisation which aims to control unwanted noise and the impact it has 
on the community. The website is at www.noisewatch.org.au. You may wish to make a complaint about 
unnecessary noise in your neighbourhood, or you could be the subject of a complaint about noise. Many 
people can be affected by noise in a neighbourhood. It is important to be considerate of your neighbours, 
particularly if making a lot of noise late at night. It is considerate to warn your neighbours if you are 
planning a loud party or event. 
Pets
It is important to be aware of any council laws regarding keeping pets in your area. Some councils have 
restrictions such as which breeds of animals can be kept as pets, and curfews for cats. It is also important 
to be aware of how your pet affects your neighbours – issues such as noise, smell and damage to 
property can all be concerns. 
Garden maintenance
As a member of the community, it can be considerate to ensure that your property is maintained to a 
certain standard. Keeping gardens tidy, trees trimmed and lawns mown are all ways of ensuring that your 
property looks good and is making a positive contribution to the neighbourhood.
Resolving disputes
If you have an issue with your neighbour, the best place to start is to talk to them about it. Find a time 
to discuss the matter with them calmly. Clearly outline the reasons for your concern, and try to sound 
objective, rather than critical. If each person considers the other person’s viewpoint calmly, it will usually 
be possible to reach an understanding. If you are unable to resolve your dispute in this way, most states 
have a dispute resolution service, such as the Dispute Settlement Centre of Victoria, or the Dispute 
Resolution Centre in Queensland.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
39
Getting involved in the community 
Getting involved in your local community has many benefits. It can be healthy and enjoyable to interact 
with other people in your local area, and the sense of satisfaction of contributing to your community 
should not be underestimated. By participating in community activities you also learn skills which you 
can apply in later years. 
Two common ways that people engage with their local community are:
•  doing volunteer work, such as working with a local charity or council organisation 
•  joining a club, such as a sporting club, music or craft club.
Community support
Local councils provide various forms of support for members of the community. This support can include:
•  help for disabled or elderly residents  
• neighbourhood watch
•  childcare 
 
 
 
 
• clubs and sporting groups
•  housing and emergency accommodation.
If you are in need of any help, whether it is emotional, physical or financial, your local council could be 
a good place to start. Similarly, if you would like to offer help to others in your community, volunteering 
for one of these organisations could be a great way to make a contribution.

the services available in your area.
