19  Health issues 
Moving out isn’t just about finding a new place to live. There will be other issues that you may not have 
had to consider until now. Taking care of your health is a big part of life.
Finding a GP
When you move into a new neighbourhood it may be necessary to register as a patient with a local 
doctor or GP (General Practitioner). Some medical practices have several doctors based in one medical 
centre. This means that you will generally have access to one of the doctors at all times, which can 
make it easier to get an appointment when you need one. If changing doctors, you may need to 
arrange to have your medical records transferred from your previous doctor. Some doctors will charge a 
small administration fee for doing this. 
Medicare
Medicare is Australia’s universal health care system. It provides all Australians with access to free or 
low-cost medical and hospital care. All Australian citizens can register with Medicare by filling in 
an enrolment form and being issued with a Medicare card. This card can then be presented at any 
Medicare branch to receive a refund on medical expenses. All you need is the doctor’s bill and your 
Medicare card. Alternatively, you can also claim your refund electronically, so the money is paid directly 
into your bank account. If your doctor bulk-bills, then you can simply sign a form acknowledging 
treatment and no payment is required. 
Health insurance
There are some medical services that Medicare does 
not cover. These include things like dental treatment, 
optical services and private hospital visits. Many people 
choose to take out private health insurance to help cover 
additional medical costs. There are several companies 
which offer private health cover (which gives you your 
own choice of doctor and access to a private hospital). 
Examples include Medibank Private, HCF and NIB. Some 
companies also offer extra levels of cover, for things like 
dental and optical care, for an additional fee. 
Ambulance
You may also choose to join an ambulance fund. 
This means that if you ever need an ambulance in an 
emergency, you don’t have to pay. Ambulance rides 
can cost hundreds of dollars, whereas the yearly fee to 
join an ambulance fund is usually only around $70 per 
year. Ambulance costs are not covered by Medicare.
Dental services
Regular dental check-ups can help prevent major 
dental issues from occurring. It’s a good idea to find a 
dentist in your area. Dental services are not covered by 
Medicare, but if you have a health care or concession 
card you may be eligible for public dental treatment, 
which is a lot more affordable. Some private health 
insurance funds also offer coverage for dental care.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 205 7	
Living & Work Literacy Book  7

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 7 
41
Mental health
If you are struggling to cope and need some support, there are many options available. Your GP will be 
able to refer you to a counsellor. Alternatively, organisations such as Beyond Blue, headspace and Lifeline 
can provide help. 
Sexual health
As well as your GP, there are several other places you can go for sexual health services. Your local Family 
Planning Centre or Sexual Health Centre will offer confidential advice and treatment, and many places 
will allow you to remain anonymous.
University health services
Most universities will offer information and treatment to students, including general health services, 
counselling, sexual health advice, travel advice and vaccinations. Most of these services are bulk billed.
Health and fitness
Although it is important to be covered for any medical problems that might occur, it is also important 
to look after your health, as this can prevent problems from occurring in the first place. Exercising 
regularly and eating a balanced diet will help you to stay fit and healthy. People who don’t exercise 
and who don’t eat a healthy diet run the risk of becoming unwell, overweight or even obese. Obesity 
is most commonly measured using the Body Mass Index (BMI), which measures a person’s weight-to-
height ratio.

Research two different private health insurance providers and the 
costs of basic hospital cover. Compare the cost of basic cover with

20 Voting 
The right to vote is an important aspect of living in a 
democracy. In Australia, voting is compulsory and all people 
over the age of 18 are required to vote in all elections, 
whether for federal, state or local government. Failure to vote 
may result in a fine.
In order to take part in elections, you must be enrolled in 
your current electorate. This is determined by where you 
live. To enrol to vote, you must complete an enrolment 
application form, which you can obtain from any post office 
or from the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) website 
at www.aec.gov.au. 
To be eligible to be listed on the electoral roll, you must: 
•  be 18 years of age or older
•  have lived at your current address for  
at least a month
•  be an Australian citizen (either born in Australia or granted Australian citizenship).
After you have been placed on the electoral roll you will receive a card indicating which electorate you 
are enrolled in. If you move after you have enrolled, you must notify the AEC of your change of address.
Getting involved in politics
While elections are held only every three or four 
years, there are other ways of participating in a 
democracy. They can include:
•  forming pressure groups to lobby the 
government about a particular issue
•  attending public meetings, demonstrations  
or protests
•  joining a club
•  writing letters to the editors of newspapers
•  writing letters to local members of 
parliament
•  making an appointment for a personal 
interview with a member of parliament
•  approaching radio or television journalists  
or ringing a radio station on talkback radio
•  expressing our opinions in public places
•  joining a political party.
Political parties
Australia’s main political parties are:
Australian Greens Party   
www.greens.org.au 
Australian Labor Party    
www.alp.org.au 
Liberal Party of Australia 
www.liberal.org.au 
National Party 
 
www.nationals.org.au
You can find out more about their policies 
and goals from their websites, which are 
constantly being updated. Information about 
the political parties is also regularly broadcast 
on radio and television and reported in 
national newspapers.

Glossary of important terms
Electoral roll 
A document that lists all enrolled voters 
Electorate 
A district consisting of people entitled to vote for a member of parliament
General election 
An election held to decide the government of the whole country or state
By election 
 An election held just for one particular electorate, for example after the 
death or retirement of that electorate’s member of parliament
Referendum 
A vote by the people on a particular question
Polling place 
A place where people go to record their vote in an election
Informal vote 
A vote which is not counted because the ballot paper is incorrectly filled in
Scrutineers 
People who oversee the counting of votes after an election
MP 
Member of Parliament, either federal or state
House of Representatives The lower house of federal parliament
Senate 
The upper house of federal parliament
Legislative Assembly 
The lower house of state parliament
Legislative Council 
The upper house of state parliament
Governor-General 
The Queen’s representative in Australia
Prime Minister 
The leader of the federal government 
Premier 
The leader of the state government
Mayor 
The leader or spokesperson of a local council
Constitution 
A list of basic rules and principles used to govern the country.

1 WHAT ARE YOUR SPENDING HABITS?
1 Needs are things we need to survive while wants are things 
we can do without.
2 No. Clothing is a need because it keeps you warm, but some 
items of clothing, such as expensive brands or fashion items, 
are not necessary to survival.
3 Luxury items are things that you don’t need. They are

1 What are your spending habits? 
Needs and wants
Managing your money is a juggle between spending and saving. When it comes to spending, we  
all have needs and wants. Needs are basic to our survival. They are the things we can’t do without.  
For example, we need food to survive, and we need basic clothing and shelter for protection against  
the cold. Wants, on the other hand, are the things that we would like to have but that are not basic  
to our survival.  
Some items can fit into either category. For example, a loaf of bread may qualify as a need, while a 
meal at an expensive restaurant could be seen as a want. They are both kinds of food, but the fancy 
restaurant meal is not essential to survival. Many items of clothing could also fall into both categories 
– some are necessary for survival, but others are luxury items. 
Your spending habits
It is good idea to analyse your spending habits. Remember that although we all have a limited income, 
there is no limit to the things we want. We need to decide which wants we satisfy and which ones we 
do without. This is not always easy – sometimes other factors are involved, such as emotion, and we can 
find ways to justify purchases that we may not really need to make. Consider the following comments:
Needs
•  food
•  clothing
•  shelter
Wants
•  television
•  movie ticket
•  mobile phone

2 Top tips for saving money 
There are two things you can do with your income – spend it or save it. Although it can be tempting to 
spend all your money, it’s a good idea to try and save some money whenever you can. 
Why save?
There are several reasons why it is a good idea to save some of your income, including: 
• saving for a rainy day – this means saving money in case you need a little extra in the future
•  saving for a major purchase
•  saving to guard against loss of job
•  saving money so you can invest it and make more money.
There are lots of tips for saving money. Different tips work for different people depending on their 
lifestyle, income and personal preference. Here are some suggestions for you to consider.
Saving tips
•  Be aware of when you make extra purchases – such as when you are tired, stressed or hungry – 
and try to avoid shopping at those times.
•  Leave your credit card at home if you are going somewhere where you think you will be tempted 
to spend.
•  Make your lunch every day instead of buying it.
•  Buy fresh foods to cook, rather than takeaway or pre-packaged foods.
•  Make a shopping list each week and stick to it. 
•  Try to buy clothes that are second-hand or on sale, rather than buying new or expensive clothes.
•  Don’t buy every gadget that comes onto the market.
•  Watch television or DVDs rather than go to movies.
•  Try to cut back on alcohol and cigarettes – the costs add up very quickly! 
•  Think about selling some of the things in your house that you don’t need.
•  Take cheap locally based holidays, and try to stay in places where you can cook your own meals 
rather than eating out all the time.
The story of Charles 
Charles had a good job and earned a good income. His only problem was that 
he couldn’t stop himself from spending it. As soon as he got paid he went 
shopping and spent all his money. One day Charles’ best friend Jake asked him 
if he would like to go on a holiday to Europe. Charles would have loved to go 
but had no money saved, so couldn’t afford it. 
Tina’s story 
Tina also had a job that paid well. She was careful with her spending patterns  
and only bought what she felt was necessary. She saved a percentage of her 
income every week. When her best friend, Leah, suggested that they should both 
go to Europe at the end of the year, Tina jumped at the chance. She had already 
saved enough for the airfare and by the end of the year would have enough 
money for a really good holiday.

3 The burden of personal debt 
The following two stories are fictitious, but they 
illustrate how easily personal debt can get out  
of control, and the burdens it creates. 
  
Dylan’s story
At 19 years of age Dylan had left school and was 
working in an office as a junior clerk. He was 
excited about earning money and decided to enjoy 
it. He applied for a credit card and was amazed 
at how easy it was to buy whatever he wanted by 
charging it to the card. When the account came, 
Dylan found that it was much higher than he 
had expected. As well as buying up big on clothes 
and DVDs, he had also been using his card to 
withdraw cash advances. He had been enjoying 
life without realising how much he was spending. 
Dylan couldn’t afford to pay off his account, so he 
just paid the minimum amount due. At the end 
of the following month Dylan was astonished to 
see the interest charges that had accumulated on 
the unpaid portion of his previous account. The 
interest was calculated from the original date of 
purchase. Dylan realised that every time he was 
unable to pay the full amount owing, he would 
have to pay interest, which would add up very 
quickly. He needed help.
Muna’s story
Muna was a single parent bringing 
up two children. Since moving to 
Australia she had supported her family 
with her savings and from casual work 
as a waitress at a city restaurant. The 
family had shifted between friends’ 
homes, as well as various motels and 
caravan parks while trying to find a 
rental property that they could afford 
in a safe neighbourhood. When Muna 
finally found a small house in the inner 
city, she felt that she could finally get 
on top of things. Then her youngest 
daughter fell ill and Muna was faced 
with mounting medical costs. With 
all these extra expenses on top of food 
and clothing, Muna found that she was 
falling behind in the rent. Muna found 
herself faced with the prospect of being 
homeless again. She became anxious and 
unwell, and was unable to meet her work 
obligations at the restaurant. She was in 
need of help.

4 Personal budgets  
A budget is a plan of anticipated income, expenditure and savings over a period of time. Governments 
produce budgets, as do businesses, as they need to plan for the future. Individual people also need a 
budget. Whether it is for the short term or long term, a budget can help you to plan your spending and 
ensure that you will have enough money to cover your expenses. 
A budget can also help you to plan ways to achieve personal spending goals. You could have a weekly 
budget, a monthly budget or a yearly budget.  
All personal budgets are different depending on individual circumstances. Here are some examples:
Susan Baker
Susan Baker is a millionaire.  
She has made her money 
investing in real estate. Susan 
owns the apartment she lives  
in on the Gold Coast. Her goal  
is to save as much money as 
possible in a short time so that 
she can retire early. 
John Duncan
John Duncan is a single 
parent. He works part-time at 
a supermarket. John has three 
young children and his goal  
is to save a little each week  
for emergency expenses, such  
as possible medical bills for  
any of his children should  
they become ill. 
James Wilson
James is a student in his first year 
at university. He lives at home 
with his parents. James’ long 
term goal is to establish a career 
in law and start his own legal 
practice. 
How do you prepare a personal budget?
To prepare a personal budget, you need to estimate normal income and expense items and subtract  
the total expenses from total income. The difference between the two is the expected savings (or debt, 
if the figure is negative).
Programs such as Microsoft Excel, Moneydance and Quicken can do all the calculations for you.  
They can also analyse trends and patterns in income and expenses and help you to calculate expected 
savings.

5 Buying goods 
What are goods?  
Goods are things that have been produced for us to buy that we can see or touch. Goods include 
things like a loaf of bread, a pair of jeans, a DVD or a car. Services are different from goods – they are 
tasks that are performed for us, such as a haircut, a holiday booking or a bus trip (see unit 6 for more 
information on services). The diagram below shows how producers provide both goods and services for 
us to buy.
How can we buy goods? 
Goods are produced in places such as in a factory  
or on a farm. They then need to be transported  
to a place where consumers can buy them.  
There are several different ways that 
consumers can buy goods.
Retail stores
Retail stores, or shops, vary in size  
and location, from small corner 
stores to large department stores in 
shopping centres. Retail stores try 
to create a pleasant environment to 
encourage the shopper to buy. This 
might involve colourful displays, car 
parking facilities, background music 
and friendly service.  
Factory outlets
Some stores advertise themselves as 
‘factory outlets’. Factory outlets often 
sell end-of-season products, samples 
and seconds at a reduced price.  
Factory outlets are often located in 
industrial areas or on the outskirts of a city or suburb because the cost of renting the space is cheaper. 
They may not have the comforts and extra facilities of a retail shopping centre but this can mean that 
the prices are often cheaper.
Local markets
Local markets are held regularly in many communities. They may be held on a specific day, such as 
the first Sunday in the month, or on a weekly basis. Shoppers can often pick up bargains at markets 
because the traders do not have the same overhead costs that a retail store has. 
Direct selling
Not everyone has the time to visit shops, and others may live in remote locations where there are fewer 
shops to visit. Direct selling is a way of shopping without having to visit the shops. It can take several forms:
•  door-to door selling, where a representative of a company knocks on doors and tries to sell their goods
•  ‘party‘ selling, where a host throws a party and invites a company representative to show 
their products. This is common with cosmetics, women’s clothing and kitchen goods (such as 
Tupperware). The host often receives a free gifts if a certain sales target is reached.
•  mail order selling, where goods are advertised in a catalogue that is sent to potential customers. 
Shoppers are not able to see the goods they are buying, but most mail order companies will allow 
the products to be returned if the purchaser is unhappy with them.

Consumers

6 What are services? 
What are services?
Unlike goods, services are those things you want to buy that you can’t see or touch directly. There are 
many different types of services.  
Where do services fit in the economy?
Economic activity refers to all the goods and services that are being bought and sold in the country. We 
often classify economic activity into three broad groups: primary, secondary and tertiary (see diagram below).
Type of industry
Characteristics
Examples 
Primary
Obtaining raw 
materials from  
the Earth
    coal mining            wheat farming          fishing
Secondary
Manufacturing  
or processing raw 
materials into 
finished products
  steel making    car manufacturing     soft drink bottling
Tertiary
Providing services 
for people
  banking              retailing              medical services
  
 
Banking and financial services
Banks and other financial institutions provide a variety of financial services. They store money, invest 
money over long periods of time and lend money to people who need it. For example: 
Claire earns a good income and finds that she has saved quite a lot of money over the past year. She 
decides to open an investment account with a bank. The bank will pay her interest on the money she 
has invested. The rate of interest varies depending on the health of the economy at the time.
Claire’s friend Mia just got married. Mia and her husband want to buy a house. They apply to the bank 
for a loan. The bank is able to take the money that people like Claire have invested, and lend it to Mia 
and her husband. Mia and her husband will have to repay the money they have borrowed plus interest, 
which is what the bank charges for the use of their money.
Medical services 
Doctors and other medical staff, such as dentists, nurses and hospital workers, provide a variety of 
medical services.
Mia’s husband Tony has an accident at work and needs to see his local doctor or GP (general 
practitioner). The GP examines Tony’s injured leg and recommends that he go to hospital for an X-ray. 
The leg is broken, so Tony is referred to a surgeon to set his leg in a cast so that it will heal. For this 
accident, Tony required the services of a GP, a radiologist (for the X-ray), a surgeon to set his leg as well 
as a number of nurses and hospital staff.

 6 What are services?
Educational services
Schools, universities and TAFE colleges are all educational institutions. Teachers, teachers’ aides, lecturers 
and other staff at these institutions provide educational services.
Mia and Tony have three children. Tina, the eldest, has enrolled in a law degree at a university. Jeff is 
doing his final year at high school and Jemma, the youngest, is in year 5 at primary school. There are 
many people providing educational services to this family.
Retail services
Retail services cover a wide variety of services performed by people such as store managers, shop 
assistants, delivery workers, advertising executives, door-to door salespeople and warehouse staff.
Rachel needed a pair of new shoes. She went to a large shopping centre and visited three different 
stores before she eventually bought a pair. Then she bought an ice cream before heading into the 
supermarket to buy the groceries for the week.
Tourist services
The tourism industry is one of the largest industries in Australia. Tourism encompasses a wide variety of 
travel, transport and hospitality services. 
Mia and Tony decide to go on a holiday with their three children. Mia visits a travel agent, who books 
the family on a package holiday to the Gold Coast. The people providing services in this package 
include the travel agent, the check-in staff at the airport, the pilot and crew of the aircraft, hotel staff, 
restaurant staff and the taxi drivers who take them to and from the airport at both ends. The staff at 
the theme parks they visited also provided services. You can see that there are lots of people involved in 
providing tourist services.

7 What is a contract? 
A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more people or organisations. It has two  
basic elements:
•  offer and acceptance
•  consideration
To explain these two elements using a simple example, imagine that you go into a shop to buy a 
television. You check out all the options and finally, after discussions with the salesperson, you decide 
which one you want to buy. The marked price is $850 and you offer $800. The salesperson checks  
with the manager and tells you that your offer has been accepted. You have made the offer and the 
shop has accepted it, so an agreement has been reached.  
Consideration means that something of value must be exchanged. In this case the $800 is the 
consideration that you have both agreed to. This is a very simple contract which has two basic  
elements that lead to an agreement. Contracts don’t always have to be in writing, although some are 
required to be by law. Examples include loan contracts and contracts for the sale of a house or land. 
Entering a contract
A contract is a legal document that is enforceable in law,  
so it is important that you understand what you are 
agreeing to. Never rush into an agreement that you are 
unsure about. The law provides some protection against 
being forced into a contract unfairly. In some contracts 
where a purchase is made, a cooling-off period applies, 
which means you have time to reconsider in case you 
rushed into a purchase. 
•  Entering into a contract doesn’t just mean signing  
a legal document. You can also enter into a contract 
by agreeing to a purchase and paying for it, or when 
you click on the ‘submit’ button on a website. 
Terms and conditions
Contracts often contain many terms and conditions.  
They outline the rights and responsibilities covered by the contract. Sometimes the terms and conditions 
are written in very small print but they are still legally binding, so it is important that you read and 
understand them. If you have any concerns about the terms and conditions, seek advice before signing.  
By signing a contract you are agreeing to the terms and conditions. Ticking the ‘I Agree’ box  
on certain websites also means you have entered into a contract. 
Note: If you have been forced into a contract by unfair or unreasonable behaviour, you 
have the right to seek help. Contact your state consumer affairs organisation, such as 
your state Department of Fair Trading. The ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer 
Commission) is a federal government department that also regulates unfair behaviour with 
regard to contracts.

8 Mobile phone plans 
When shopping for a new mobile phone plan, there are a lot of things to consider. The key things to be 
aware of are:
•  what kind of phone you want  
•  the mobile phone plan options available
•  how (and how much) you use your phone (see diagram below).  
Selecting a mobile phone plan – the three stages
1 Select a phone
2 Mobile phone plan
3 Mobile phone usage
Facts about phone plans
•  Monthly plans or contracts can be economical, particularly if you use your phone a lot. Some 
contracts actually give you a new phone up front, and lock you in for a fixed period of time. Your 
monthly fees over that time period will cover the cost of the phone, as well as your usage. There 
are many plans available and you need to look carefully at the details.
•  Prepaid phones are handy if you don’t want to be locked into a long-term contract. You buy a 
certain amount of credit up front and when your prepaid credit runs out you can easily buy more. 
Although the price per call may be more expensive than in a monthly plan, prepaid plans mean 
you can control what you spend and don’t get any nasty surprises when the bill comes. You can 
also change service providers more easily.
•  Coverage – mobile phone coverage varies greatly in some parts of Australia, and some providers 
provide better coverage than others. Some handsets are also better at picking up mobile phone 
signals than others.
Price per month:

 8 Mobile phone plans 
•  Cap plans – these are contracts where you pay a minimum amount each month which covers 
you for a set value of calls, downloads and SMS messages. For instance, a $49 cap plan may give 
you $300 of ‘included value’. Cap plans do not limit your actual phone bill. When you use up 
your allowance you will be charged additional costs, and these are charged at varying rates. For 
example, call charges vary according to time of call, so calls after 8 pm may be cheaper than calls 
during the day.
•  Included value – every plan offers a different amount of included value, which is calculated at 
different rates and includes different types of calls and services. This means that ‘included value’ 
amounts cannot always be easily compared.
•  Bundling – many service providers offer special deals or discounts if you ‘bundle’ your landline, 
mobile phone and internet connection with the one company. It’s important to check whether you 
are actually saving money by doing this, as packages can be difficult to compare. 
Responsibilities
It is important to remember that a phone plan is a contract (see previous unit). When you sign up you 
are entering into a legal agreement to pay a certain amount of money for a set period of time, such as 
24 months. Even if you don’t make any calls, or if you lose your phone, you will still have to pay up each 
month. Be aware of any penalties for breaking a contract before it has expired. Owning a phone outright 
can be expensive initially, but protects you from having to enter into a contract with the provider.

9 Paying your mobile phone bill 
Mobile phone technology has come a long way in a very short space of time. The first generation mobile 
phones were analogue but digital technology quickly paved the way for a new generation of phones that 
could send data at high speeds and provided extra features such as text messaging, or SMS.
New phone technology
Third generation technology, known as 3G, allows phones to send and receive information up to ten 
times faster than second generation phones. Handsets come with built-in cameras and microphones. 
Colour screens mean that messages can now include pictures, video and music, not just text. Mobile 
phone technology now allows people with 3G mobile phones to take photos, send and receive emails, 
watch movies, access public transport timetables and restaurant menus, open garage doors, activate 
security systems and turn on home heating or air conditioning. 
Mobile phone bills
The new range of features available on 3G mobiles mean that mobile phone bills have become 
much more complicated. Instead of just including call charges, they now include data charges, SMS, 
multimedia messages and voice and video calls. All of these things are charged at different rates, which 
can make it hard to keep track of the costs. 
Hannah 
Hannah was so excited when she got her 
first mobile phone. It was a present from her 
parents, who wanted her to be able to contact 
them in case of emergencies. Unfortunately, 
Hannah’s parents didn’t explain the different 
costs associated with using her new phone. 
The first thing Hannah did was to organise her 
contacts, entering the names and numbers of 
all her friends. She made a few calls while she 
was doing so, and ended up chatting to some 
friends for over an hour. Hannah didn’t realise 
how much the calls would cost.
She was also thrilled by how easy it was to 
send text messages (SMS), and she messaged 
all of her friends. She was sure they didn’t cost 
very much. Hannah’s friend showed her how 
to download ring tones for her phone, and she 
changed them regularly. She found that she 
could download video clips of her favourite 
songs. Unfortunately, she didn’t realise that 
these were ‘premium services’ that are charged 
at a higher rate.  
When Hannah received her first bill, she was 
horrified to find that it came to $1200. There 
was no way she could afford to pay the bill. 
Hannah’s parents helped her out this time, but 
they explained that she would not be bailed 
out again.

10 The online shopping experience 
Online shopping has become extremely popular in recent years.  
There are many advantages to online shopping, such as:
•  it is convenient
•  it saves time
•  it is often cheaper than buying from retail stores
•  you can shop interstate or even overseas
•  more and more companies are offering online shopping facilities.
Tips for smart online shopping
•  Find out as much as you can about the product that you want to buy. Ask the seller questions, 
and see if you can find photos of the same item on other sites, so you know exactly what you’re 
getting.
•  Make sure you know all the details of the sale, including shipping costs, delivery times, and 
whether you can return the product if it’s faulty or not as described.
•  Take steps to ensure that the seller is trustworthy. Do they have a registered business? Can you 
check customer feedback to show that they have a good record?
•  Check the payment options and make sure they are secure. Look for a padlock symbol at the top  
or bottom of the screen – this usually means that your information is safe.
•  Know what to do if something goes wrong. Do you have contact details for the seller? Does the 
website offer a mediation service to resolve disputes?
•  Check online auction sites. Learn how they work, what your rights are and what you can do if 
anything goes wrong.
•  Keep records. You should keep copies of any documents such as forms, emails or web pages as 
they are a record of the sale. Terms and conditions, warranties, receipts and payment forms and 
even advertising brochures could all provide proof of the sale that took place.
Problems may arise
• If something goes wrong with an online purchase there are some things you can do:
•  Start by contacting the seller. There might have been a simple misunderstanding that could easily 
be resolved.
•  If that doesn’t work, contact the people who run the website to see if they can help. Keep copies  
of all your correspondence.
•  Contact your bank to see if you’re able to stop the payment from going through.
•  Contact your local office of fair trading, or the ACCC. They may be able to help, or at least  
offer advice.
Problems with an overseas seller
If things go wrong when buying goods online from an overseas seller, you may have more difficulty 
in resolving the dispute. Start by trying the steps outlined above. If that doesn’t work, contact ICPEN 
(the International Consumer Protection and Enforcement Network. This worldwide organisation aims 
to protect consumers around the world by sharing information and encouraging global cooperation 
among law enforcement agencies.

11 Scams: A case study 
A scam is a trick aimed at gaining a person’s trust in order to defraud them. Many scammers use email 
and SMS to contact people in the hope that someone will read their message and believe it to be true.
The following is the type of email that is often circulated by scammers trying to defraud innocent 
people. The email tries to gain people’s confidence by offering them money. The extract below is 
based on real emails, but names and some of the wording have been slightly altered. The spelling and 
grammatical errors contained within are typical.
From: BARRISTER RICHARD JONES
Subject: HELLO SIR/MADAM
Dear Sir
With all due respect,
My name is Richard Jones an attorney by profession. In my quest to find a reliable trustee to  
manage the assets/estate of my late client valued at only $15,000,000.00 (fifteen million US dollars) 
this is the reason why you are receiving this email from me. She was a great woman doing good 
especially in the area of charity, in the last five years of her life.
I shall be willing to supply you with more detailed information concerning this business project upon 
hearing from you. I have no intention whatsoever to delve into your private life considering the fact 
you have never had any communication with me in the past, but due to the nature of this business 
project based on the fact that I lack the power to assume the role of a trustee or appoint any of my 
relation to become the trustee. By virtue of the facts and circumstances surrounding this project,  
I am left with no other choice but to carry out a discreet search for a reputable person outside the 
shores of my country in the United Kingdom and consequently seek your stewardship to stand as  
the Deceased’s Next of Kin.
You will be entitle to 40% of the total sum as your share, 10% will be mapped out to offset any 
expenses both parties might make during the course of this transaction while 50% will be for me.
If you wish to render your selfless service, but very rewarding, do provide me with the following 
information.
1. Your full names
2. Tel and fax numbers
3. Complete address
4. Your occupation and your age
I shall provide you with more detailed information upon hearing from you. If this transaction interests 
you kindly send your reply on this my personal email address.
Kind regards 
Richard Jones, Esq.
Why people get tricked by scams
Most scams work by convincing people to give out either money or their personal details to a complete 
stranger. There are many ways they can go about this. It is easy to be tricked by something that seems 
legitimate because it has a website, or a legitimate-sounding business name. But anyone can set up a 
website, and there is no way of being sure that it really is ‘official’. 
A lot of scams are ‘get rich quick’ schemes, which work by convincing people to part with large 
amounts of money by promising a much bigger return down the track. However, scams can also involve 
very small amounts of money – scammers can make just as much money convincing a large number of 
people to part with a small amount of money as they can by getting one person to put up a large sum.
Kinds of scams
There are many different kinds of scams. They may include:
•  Job opportunities, which target people looking for a new job. Promises of big incomes for little 
work are often part of the scam. They tend to be ‘work from home’ schemes. You may be tricked 
into signing a contract and/or paying an up-front fee.

 11 Scams: A case study
•  Business opportunity schemes such as pyramid schemes. These can be dangerous because, 
although you are promised big earnings, the scheme requires you to buy up supplies of a product 
up front before trying to sell it.    
•  Lottery scams, in which you are notified that you have a won a big prize in a lottery and you need 
to send some money to cover expenses so that the prize money can be sent to you. Remember 
that you cannot win money in a lottery unless you have entered it yourself or someone else has 
entered on your behalf.
•  Gambling software packages which promise to accurately predict the results of sporting events, 
such as horse races and major sporting contests.
How to avoid being scammed
•  Do not agree to an offer or deal without spending some time considering it or getting 
independent advice.
•  Do not hand over money or sign anything until you have thoroughly checked out the company, 
organisation or person you are dealing with.
•  Never give out your personal information or bank account details to anyone you do not trust.
•  Don’t believe everything you read. Do some research to verify the information that has been sent to 
you. If you suspect an email is a scam, it is best not to even open it, and definitely don’t reply to it. 
SCAMwatch is a website designed to help people become aware of scams and how they work. 
SCAMwatch is run by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. The site is at  
www.scamwatch.gov.au.

12 Credit card fraud and  
identity theft 
What is identity theft?
Identity theft is accessing someone else’s personal details and pretending to be that person. This is 
usually done for some kind of financial gain. The most common forms of identity theft are:
•  someone buys items using your credit card or credit card details 
•  someone assumes your identity and: 
 –  withdraws money from your accounts 
 –  borrows money in your name  
 
 
 
 –  sets up a business under your name
 –  conducts illegal activities in your name.
Identity theft is a serious crime and it can have devastating effects.
How is it done?
Stealing 
The most obvious and direct method of identity theft is to steal your credit card or your wallet or 
purse, which may contain vital personal information.  
Card skimming 
Card skimming uses a device inserted into an ATM that records information from the magnetic strip 
of the credit card or ATM card. The PIN number is also recorded using cameras or other methods. 
The scammer can then use the information to create a fake card with your details on it. 
Searching 
Scammers can also gain access to your personal records by rummaging through your garbage or 
through council rubbish tips looking for personal information. Scammers can also get information about 
you from social networking sites such as Facebook and Twitter, so it is important to be careful about 
the information you post on those sites. 
Phishing 
Many scammers send emails pretending they are from a bank and are checking their records or security 
systems. They then ask you for your account number. This process is known as phishing. Some of these 
emails can look quite authentic and often contain the bank’s logo. 
Another method used is to send you money and then ask you to transfer that money to someone you 
don’t know. This is known as ‘money laundering’, and is a way of transferring funds earned illegally in 
order to hide their origin.
It is important to remember that banks will never send you an email asking you for your account 
number or other personal details. If you are in doubt, contact the bank and talk with them directly.
ISBN 978 1 76020 206 4

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 8 
27
Spyware
Spyware is software that spies on what you do on your computer. It may be sent to you in an email 
attachment which then sits in your computer somewhere and collects your personal information 
(especially banking and credit card details) without your knowledge. 
Key logging is a variation of this, whereby someone at another computer is able to record and copy the 
key strokes you make, especially when entering personal information such as your bank account details. 
How to protect yourself
•  Protect your computer by installing reputable antivirus and/or anti spyware software programs  
and keep them up to date.
•  Never send money or give your bank account details to anyone you don’t know.
•  Remember that a proper bank or financial institution will never email you asking for your  
personal details. 
• Contact your bank immediately if you notice any suspicious or unexplained transactions from any  
of your accounts.

13 Buying second-hand goods 
  
‘Someone’s trash is another one’s treasure’.
Buying second-hand, rather than new, goods is a great way to save money. Some people love buying 
second-hand goods, while others will only buy new. There are advantages and disadvantages for each, 
as this scenario illustrates.
 A lunchtime discussion
Jessica: 
 Hey, I went down to the Sunday markets yesterday and bought  
a whole lot of clothes, really cheap.
Sophie: 
 I bet you bought rubbish. Yuck – imagine wearing clothes that 
someone else has worn.
Jessica: 
They’re all right when they’re washed.
Sophie: 
 I never buy second-hand stuff. If I want clothes, I go out and  
buy new stuff.
Jessica: 
Yeah, and you pay a fortune for them.
Noah: 
 What’s wrong with second-hand stuff? My brother rides a motor 
bike and he is always off to swap meets, where other riders swap 
bike parts. It’s a good way of getting stuff for your bike without 
spending too much.
Sophie: 
 But how do you know that what  
you buy is going to work? What if  
the parts break down? 
Noah: 
 Well, for starters, you can usually  
tell if what you are buying is OK.  
And anyway, you know the regulars at 
the meets. They won’t try to dud you.
Sophie: 
 But you get a warranty with stuff you buy new – you don’t get 
that if you buy second-hand.
Jessica: 
 But what about the environment? If we all bought new stuff 
and threw it away when we got sick of it imagine the waste. 
Buying second-hand is a type of recycling, really.
Sophie: 
Well, I guess it depends on the individual.
Where do you buy second-hand goods? 
There are many different places you can go to buy second-hand goods. They include:
•  local markets – there are many local markets operating throughout the country, often on a regular 
day of the week (Sunday is a very common day for local markets). 
•  garage sales – often someone within your neighbourhood will hold a garage sale. This is a way of 
getting rid of books, clothes and household goods quickly and cheaply. Garage sales can be a great 
place to pick up bargains. Sometimes keen buyers queue up in the early hours of the morning just 
to get the best things. 
•  charity stores – charity stores, or op shops, take goods donated by people and then sell them to

•  private sales – many people sell used goods by advertising them in their local newspapers. The ads

14 The influence of marketing 
Marketing is more than just selling. It includes the strategies used to promote, advertise and sell goods 
and services to consumers, including packaging, market research and sales promotion.  
The four Ps of marketing
Product 
Place
Price
Promotion
Product refers to the actual goods and/or 
services you are buying. This can include the 
item itself, the packaging, and also other aspects 
such as warranties, customer support etc.
Place is where you actually buy the product and 
how it gets there from the manufacturer
Price is the agreed financial value of the goods 
and/or services being purchased
Promotion is the way the product is advertised 
to bring it to the buyer’s attention.
Promotion and advertising
Advertising and promotion are the ways a company tries to get the attention of buyers and convince 
them to buy the product. Advertising takes many forms, from catalogues in your letterbox to 
major television and newspaper ads. The kind of advertisement used, and even the style of the 
advertisement, the newspaper it is placed in or the time it is shown on television are all carefully 
chosen depending on who the advertisement is aimed at.
Advertising is a highly specialised business and many companies hire an advertising agency to 
produce an ad or sometimes even a complete advertising and marketing strategy. Advertising costs  
a lot of money, and the cost of this is usually built into the price of the product.
Brand loyalty
Advertising may be informative, persuasive, or both. Informing potential customers of a new product 
and its features is only part of the purpose of an ad. Advertisements also try to ensure a product is 
recognisable, and to differentiate that product from its competitors. This is part of a strategy called 
‘brand loyalty’. Companies want customers to be familiar with, and drawn to, their brand. Apple, 
Nike and Coke are examples of companies that have established a strong brand.
Market research
Before a manufacturer spends money creating a product, they will conduct extensive research into 
their target market. This is so they can be sure that people will buy what they produce. Companies 
go to a lot of trouble to find out what you like. 
Market research is carried out in order to answer the following questions:
•  do customers like the product?
•  how much should we sell the product for?
•  what is the likely size of the market?
•  are there similar products already on the market?
ISBN 978 1 76020 206 4

© Brian Parker and Blake Education 2011
Living and Work Literacy 8 
31
Market research is carried out by a variety of methods, such as surveys, shopping centre interviews  
or taste tests.
There are different types of markets that products might be aimed at:
•  Target market – the customers you are targeting, or aiming to attract. 
•  Niche market – a small select market for a limited number of customers.
•  Mass market – a large number of potential customers.

6

drink to, and how you might get their attention.

Apple 
Apple is one of the largest companies in the world. It started off developing computer technology 
but has since been successful in marketing a variety of innovative products. When Apple released the 
iPod in 2001 they revolutionised the way we listen to music. Apple has now sold 275 million iPods 
worldwide. The iPhone and iPad have also been marketing triumphs. Apple is an example of a strong 
brand with a clear marketing strategy, meaning its products are highly sought after and instantly 
recognisable.

15 Responsible consumer behaviour
‘The customer is always right.’
This is a phrase often used to train sales staff in good customer relations. But is it true? Is the customer 
always right? Or are some customer behaviours unethical or even illegal? Being a consumer comes with 
both rights and responsibilities.
Returning goods
As a consumer you have the right to return goods if they are faulty or damaged. You may have your 
money refunded or you may be provided with a replacement item that is not faulty or damaged. 
However, you cannot return goods simply because you have changed your mind. Some stores may 
allow you to do this in order to maintain a good relationship with you, but it may not always be fair  
on the retailer. Consider the two scenarios below:
Ryan buys some new CDs from a music 
store. He takes them home and copies 
them onto his computer. He then takes 
the CDs back to the store and says he has 
decided he doesn’t want them anymore 
and wants his money back.
Samantha loves shopping for dresses. She often buys 
a few dresses, takes them home and wears them for 
several weeks, then takes them back to the stores, 
claiming that they don’t suit her and asking her 
money back. She loves telling her friends about how 
she always has a new outfit, and never has to pay.
Paying bills on time
Paying your bills on time is fair to the retailer or 
service provider, who might need money coming 
in to keep the business running. Although it is 
not illegal to pay bills late, it can result in late 
charges. If you find that you regularly have 
trouble paying your bills you may need to look 
at ways to reduce your spending. If you are not 
careful, bills and late charges can escalate very 
quickly. Consider the case below:
Sally had three credit cards. She boasted to her 
friends that she could use one credit card to  
pay off the others, so she could keep shopping 
as much as she wanted. The bills kept adding  
up until they were more than Sally could pay. 
Sally realised that the interest charges on her 
unpaid bills had accumulated. Sally was being 
charged interest on the total amount owed, 
including the interest she had already been 
charged, so the debt just kept on growing. 
Bag checks
In large, busy department stores and supermarkets, it is possible for people to walk out with goods that 
they have not paid for. To keep this from happening, many stores have a sales assistant at the front 
door to inspect people’s bags as they leave. Most people accept this procedure without any objections. 
All bag checks are voluntary, and a store cannot detain you, or touch you or your bag without your 
consent. However, a store has the right to set conditions of entry and can ask you to leave if you refuse 
to comply. If they suspect shoplifting they can call the police to deal with the matter. Consider the two 
scenarios on the next page.

 15 Responsible consumer behaviour
Lindsay goes into a large department store but decides not to buy anything. As she walks out of the 
store she is asked to display the contents of the bag she is carrying. Lindsay strongly objects to this 
and angrily shouts that this is an infringement of her rights. She refuses to open her bag.
Ethan also strongly objects to bag searches. Ethan, however, objects to bag searches because he often 
shoplifts and doesn’t want to get caught. Although he has been caught numerous times shoplifting 
from stores, he has also got away with it on some occasions.
Abusive behaviour
As a consumer you do have rights, but this doesn’t mean that you should be aggressive or abusive 
when trying to resolve a dispute with a company or store. Even if you are angry about the situation, 
being aggressive towards the salesperson makes them less likely to see your point of view. You can 
still be assertive in maintaining your rights, but there are other ways of doing this. Some consumer 
advocates recommend the ‘broken record technique’ in which you quietly and reasonably explain your 
concern and what you want done about it. Keep stating this until you feel you have been heard. Most 
stores want to maintain good customer relations and will respond to your request if it is reasonable. If 
you are not satisfied with the store’s response, you have the right to contact the office of fair trading in 
your state and take the matter further.

16 Understanding credit cards 
What is a credit card?
There are lots of plastic cards you can acquire, such as loyalty cards, club membership cards and ATM 
cards (debit cards). A credit card, on the other hand, is a card that you can use instead of cash or debit 
to purchase goods and services. When your credit card is swiped you can either sign a sales docket or 
enter your PIN (Personal Identification Number) and you can take the goods home. This means you 
don’t have to pay for them immediately. When you receive your statement you need to pay for the 
goods you have purchased over the past month. Your statement will list a minimum amount that needs 
to be paid. However, if you only pay the minimum amount due, you will still be charged interest on 
the outstanding amount. When taking out a credit card, check the terms and conditions of the contract 
and, in particular, the interest charged on overdue accounts. Some people have several credit cards – 
this can be dangerous, as it makes it hard to keep track of all your purchases.

Co-branded credit cards
Sometimes several companies join together to offer special credit card deals. These cards are

Westpac–QANTAS–Mastercard or ANZ–Frequent Flyer–Visa card. Nearly all of these cards charge an

17 Warranties 
A warranty is a written promise, given by the seller or the manufacturer, that the product they are 
selling is free from faults. A warranty also means that if a fault is found, the seller or manufacturer  
agrees to repair or replace the faulty product. As well as the warranty offered by the seller or 
manufacturer, almost all goods that you purchase are covered by an implied warranty. This means  
that the manufacturer is required by law to ensure that their product meets certain standards.
Manufacturer’s warranties
The manufacturer’s warranty guarantees that the goods will work for a certain period of time (this is 
known as the warranty period). If any faults occur within the warranty period, the manufacturer agrees 
to replace or repair the product. 
Express warranties
Express warranties are the normal warranties given by the manufacturer or retailer, including the details 
of what is covered and what is not. The express warranty may state that some parts are excluded, or 
whether both parts and labour are included. An express warranty may also state that a product will not 
be covered by faults caused by misuse, accident or carelessness.
Extended warranties
Some manufacturers or retailers offer what is called an 
extended warranty, at an additional cost. This is designed 
to cover you if the product stops working outside of the 
manufacturer’s warranty period. Extended warranties 
often offer cover for an extra 1, 3 or 5 years. Some 
extended warranties actually offer protection that you  
are already entitled to under the consumer guarantee,  
so it is important to find out what the extended warranty 
provides before purchasing one.
Implied warranties
When it comes to warranties, many people are unaware 
of their rights. If a product comes with a 12-month 
warranty, many people assume that after 12 months 
they have no more protection. However, there is also 
an implied warranty on all goods. This means that any 
product you buy must do what it says it will do for 
a reasonable period of time. For example, if you buy 
a lawnmower, you would expect it to be able to cut 
grass. This expectation should continue well beyond the 
12-month warranty that the manufacturer may provide. 
Implied warranties are also called statutory warranties. 
Knowing your rights
It is important to know your rights when it comes to warranties. If you have a problem with a product 
you have purchased, you should stop using it immediately and contact the seller or service provider. 
You might be able to negotiate whether the product should be repaired or replaced, or your money 
refunded, depending on the nature of the problem.

18 Gambling 
Gambling can take many forms, but it is generally accepted to mean placing a bet or wager on an 
event or playing a game of chance for money. It may be putting a bet on a horse race or playing a 
poker machine – there are lots of examples.  
Why do people take the risk?
Many people find gambling fun. Some people only gamble occasionally (such as a once a year bet on 
the Melbourne Cup) while others gamble more regularly. Some people never gamble at all. Although 
gambling can be fun, there is a lot of risk involved, and some people take big risks that don’t always 
pay off. In Australia, people under the age of 18 are not allowed to take part in any form of gambling. 
This includes buying lottery tickets or scratchies, which are also kinds of gambling.
What are your chances?
Gambling is all about taking a risk in the hope that you will win some money. Generally, the greater the 
risk, the more money you could win. You may be familiar with the laws of probability – this means that 
there is a formula for predicting the likely outcome in each case. Many people keep gambling because 
they ‘feel lucky’ or think their number is bound to come up soon, but the laws of probability often show 
that the chances of this happening are actually very small.
For example, take the discussion between Daniel and Ellie.
Daniel: When I toss this coin Ellie, what are the chances of tossing a head?
Ellie: 
Well, I would say 50/50.
Daniel:  Correct, as there are two possibilities. But what if I told you that I have just tossed ten heads in  
a row? What are the chances of a head on this next toss?
Ellie: 
Oh, that would be a lot less than 50/50.
Daniel:  Wrong. Each individual toss still has a 50/50 chance of coming up heads. But if I asked what are 
the chances of tossing 11 consecutive heads, that is different. Do you follow?
Ellie:  
 I think so. You really need to understand the laws of probability if you are going to gamble,  
don’t you?  
Commercial gambling such as poker machines and horse racing is usually organised to make money  
for the organisation running it. This means that the more a person gambles, the more likely he or she  
is to return a certain percentage of their winnings to the organisation. Winning can be exciting, but  
the temptation to keep gambling in the hope of winning more can be a trap. In the long term, you  
are most likely to lose. The only way to avoid getting into trouble is to only gamble what you can  
afford to lose.
Compulsive gambling
Some people find that gambling becomes a habit that they are unable to control. This is known as 
compulsive gambling. Compulsive gamblers are characterised by:
•  a continual need to gamble, whether they are winning or losing
•  an inability to stop gambling
•  a tendency to gamble much more than they can afford.
Many compulsive gamblers don’t believe they have a problem. Compulsive gamblers may avoid telling 
people how much they gamble and how much they lost, or they may gamble until they run out of 
money. Some will sell or steal things to raise more money to gamble.
Compulsive gambling can lead to family relationship breakdown, an inability to work efficiently, financial 
problems and even criminal activity. Problem gambling is recognised as a mental health issue.

Lee started gambling when he was 14, playing card games at home on the internet. ‘Internet poker is 
great, because you don’t have to be over 18 to play’, he boasted to his mates. By 19, Lee was a regular

19  Consumers and the environment 
As consumers we can help to preserve the environment. Everything we buy can affect the environment 
in many ways, from how it was made to how it was packaged and what happens when we dispose of it. 
Manufacturing and use
The way a product is manufactured can affect the environment in a number of ways. The manufacturing 
process can result in chemical by-products or pollution and can sometimes use large amounts of water, 
which is a limited resource. Some companies are taking steps to reduce or offset the environmental 
impact of manufacturing their products. Although we can’t always avoid buying certain products,  
we can become aware of how the item was produced and try to choose the option that has the least 
environmental impact. 
Using some products can also harm the environment. Some appliances, for example, use a lot of 
electricity. Most electricity is generated by burning fossil fuels, which is unsustainable and harms the 
environment. By choosing energy-efficient products, we can minimise our energy use, reducing our 
impact on the environment.
Packaging
In recent years there has been a dramatic increase in the packaging of goods. Even some fruits and 
vegetables are packed in plastic these days. Packaging is often designed to make a product more 
attractive to consumers. It is also used to communicate information to the consumer. Some packaging  
is necessary in order to keep the item in good condition. However, a lot of products come with a lot 
more packaging than necessary. 
After an item is purchased, the packaging is almost always thrown away, creating a huge amount of 
waste that needs to be disposed of. Not all of this waste is recyclable, and a lot of it goes to landfill, 
where it can take hundreds of years to break down.
Some companies ensure that their packaging is made from recyclable material. Others try to minimise 
the amount of packaging they use. Purchasing products that use environmentally friendly packaging  
can help to minimise the amount of waste your purchase creates. 
Disposal and waste
As well as the packaging, it is also important to consider how the product itself can be disposed of at 
the end of its life. Some kinds of glass and plastic can take thousands of years to break down – and 
others may never fully break down. When purchasing a product, it’s important to be aware of whether  
it is recyclable or biodegradable, which means that it will be able to be re-used or will break down 
quickly when it is disposed of.
Electronic items, such as computers and mobile phones, can release toxic chemicals when they are 
thrown into landfill. The increase in the use of electronic goods, combined with the fact that they are 
usually replaced fairly regularly, means that electronic waste is a big issue today. Some companies have 
found ways to recycle electronic goods, often by taking them apart and re-using the components.  
This is known as ‘e-cycling’.
Being ethical consumers
Being an ethical consumer means making informed choices. As consumers become more aware 
of environmental issues, many manufacturers try to capitalise on this issue by claiming that their 
products are ‘green’, or environmentally friendly. The term ‘greenwashing’ describes the deceptive 
use of advertising or marketing in order to falsely claim that a company’s policies or products are 
environmentally friendly. Companies use tricks such as packaging their products in a green colour,  
to suggest that they are environmentally friendly. Recently, the Australian Competition and Consumer 
Commission (ACCC) has reported an alarming rise in complaints about misleading ‘green’ advertising, 
particularly by energy retailers.  The ACCC has made it very clear they won’t tolerate excessive claims 
being made in an attempt to fool consumers and are taking steps to stamp this out.

Fairtrade
It is also important to consider the conditions of the workers who produced the product. Not all 
workplaces provide safe working conditions, and some countries use child and slave labour to produce 
high volume at low cost. The Fairtrade movement aims to help producers in developing countries obtain 
better trading conditions and promote sustainability. 
Fairtrade ensures that products from developing countries are purchased at a fair price from individual 
producers and sold with a ‘fairtrade’ label to tell consumers in developed countries that the item was 
produced under fair conditions. 
What can we do?
There are many things we can do to ensure that as consumers we are environmentally aware. A green 
consumer will:
• buy goods that are environmentally friendly, such as recycled paper 
•  take cloth bags to the supermarket rather than accept plastic bags, which can contribute to landfill
•  refuse to buy any goods which have excessive packaging
•  buy energy-efficient light globes
•  buy appliances that have a high energy-efficiency rating
•  buy products that can be refilled (such as cleaning products), to minimise packaging
•  pressure the government to regulate packaging and greenwashing
•  recycle and reduce your waste.

 20 Tax returns 
Almost everyone who earns money has to pay tax on the money they earn. If you have been in paid 
employment, at the end of the financial year you will need to fill in a tax return. If you earn more than 
$6000 in a financial year (1 July to 30 June) you must pay income tax.  The first $6000 you earn is 
called the ‘tax-free threshhold’. The amount of tax you will pay on the rest of the money you earn will 
be calculated according to your income. 
Tax file number
When you start work for the first time you will need a tax file number. This is a nine digit number 
that identifies you to the Australian Tax Office. To change jobs, apply for government benefits from 
Centrelink or to file a tax return, you will need this number. There are two ways of applying for a tax  
file number (TFN).
1.  If you are a secondary school student, the quickest and easiest way for you to get your tax file 
number is via the secondary schools TFN program. Applying this way is easy because your school 
verifies your identity, so you don’t need to provide any documents proving your identity.  You will 
still need to provide some information from your Australian birth certificate, Australian citizenship 
certificate or overseas passport.
2.  If you have left school you will need to complete a Tax File Number application. You can get an 
application form online from the Australian Tax Office at www.ato.gov.au or by phoning the tax 
office. You will need original documents to prove your identity.  
How income tax works
You pay income tax during the year as you earn it. If you are an employee, your employer will take it 
from your wages. The amount of tax you pay depends on how much you earn and whether you can 
claim any deductions, such as work-related expenses. When you start a new job, you have 28 days to 
give your tax file number to your employer before they must start deducting tax from your pay.  
Completing a tax return
At the end of the financial year, you need to work out whether you have paid too much tax or not 
enough. To do this you complete a tax return.  
A simple calculation: 
Gross income – work-related expenses (or deductions) = taxable income
Tax already paid – tax payable on your taxable income = tax refund.
Note that if you owe more tax than you have paid you will owe the tax office the difference.
Some people do their own tax return, either using e-Tax online or using the Australian Tax Office 
booklet (TaxPack) as a guide. Tax laws can be very complex so many people use the services of a tax 
agent or qualified tax accountant.    
To complete your return you will need your tax file number and a yearly payment summary, or group 
certificate, from your employer, as well as any other financial documents or records you’ve received 
during the income year. The income year ends on 30 June each year. You have until 31 October to 
lodge your tax return. If you use a registered tax agent you can lodge later than 31 October, but you 
need to see your agent before 31 October to qualify for their lodgement dates.
The tax office will process your return and issue you with a Notice of Assessment and refund, usually 
within a few weeks. If you owe tax, the earliest you will have to pay it is 21 November, regardless of 
when you lodge your return. If you have any problems or queries you can contact the tax office or your 
tax agent.

 20 Tax returns
What can you claim?
Work related expenses – You can claim many expenses that relate to your work. To claim an expense, 
you must have spent the money and not been reimbursed by your employer. Expenses may include 
tools you need to do your job or work-related books. You may also claim expenses if there is a specific 
uniform that you must wear for your job.
Car expenses – You cannot claim travel between your home and your workplace but you can claim 
car expenses if you have to use a car as part of your work. In this case you need receipts and your car 
logbook as proof that the expenses were part of your job.
Travel expenses – You may be required to travel by aeroplane or by some form of public transport as 
part of your job. You can claim the cost of this travel so long as it is essential to your job.
Self-education expenses – You can claim your self-education expenses if you can show that the study 
has a sufficient connection to your current employment.
The Medicare levy
Medicare is the scheme that gives Australian residents access to health care. To help fund Medicare, 
taxpayers pay a Medicare levy. The amount you pay is based on your taxable income and is in addition 
to your income tax.
John started work as an apprentice carpenter with Acme Constructions. His employer deducted $5000 
tax from his wages. He claimed $3000 of work-related expenses, including tools and self-education at 
TAFE. John’s gross income was $25 000. The tax payable on his taxable income was $4500.

1 What is money?
© Blake Education, 2006
4
Living and Work Literacy 1
Money is very useful to us as it is a means by which we can buy things. It also enables us to compare
values and to measure our relative wealth. Money acts as a:
• medium of exchange
• measure of value
• measure of stored wealth
• means of recording and paying debts.
All modern forms of money should be:
• acceptable – everyone must be able to recognise it and accept it for payment
• divisible – it is needed to make both small and large purchases 
• portable – it must be easy to carry
• durable – it must last for a long time without being easily damaged or wearing out
• scarce – it must be limited in supply so its value is retained.
 Stones are used as money on the Pacific
island of Yap.
 Cowrie shells were accepted as money on
the west coast of Africa. They were used in
some parts of Africa until the middle of
the 20th century.
 Cigarettes were used as a medium of
exchange in prisoner-of-war camps during
the Second World War.
 Gold and silver have been used as money
throughout history.
 Precious stones such as diamonds have
been used as money.
 Rum was used as a currency in the early
colonial period of New South Wales.
 The first coins were struck in Lydia in
Turkey in the 7th century BC. They were
made from gold and silver.
 The original gold and silver coins were
known as standard coins.
 Early coins were not perfectly round. This
meant that people could clip or shave off
some of the precious metal before passing
them on again as coins. Coins were then
made with a milled edge to prevent this
practice.
 Coins today are made of a combination of
copper and nickel. They are worth more
than the value of the metal in them and
are therefore known as token coins.
 Most gold today is held as bullion (gold
bars) by the world’s largest banks.
 Paper money was first issued by the
Chinese in about 650 AD. Bank notes
became more widely accepted in Europe 
in the 17th century AD when ‘goldsmiths
notes’ were issued as receipts for the gold
they held for safekeeping.
 Cheques were first introduced in about
1650. Bank messengers were used to 
collect and distribute the cheques from
bank to bank.

5
Forms of money
We think of money in general terms as consisting of coins and bank notes (or paper money). Coins
and notes collectively make up what is termed currency, but there are other forms of money.
Cheques, for example, can be viewed as money in that they are used as a medium of exchange. 
A cheque is really a request from a person to his or her bank for the bank to pay a sum of money
to a person or organisation. Cheques are not as easily used or universally accepted as currency because
they are subject to certain rules and regulations. Sellers do not have to accept cheques as payment,
but they are legally obliged to accept currency. 
Debit cards and credit cards can also be classed as money in that they too are used in the commercial
exchange of goods and services, but they are also subject to rules and regulations.
Value of money
Goods and services have a money value that is measured by their price. Also, the money income we
receive is a reflection of the value of our labour.
We like to know what our money is really worth in terms of what we can buy with it. This is a measure
of its purchasing power. If prices increase, we can buy less with the money we have, while if our
income increases, we can buy more goods and services (assuming prices remain unchanged).
In fact, both income levels and prices change constantly. When prices and income levels rise rapidly
together there is inflation. This can be unfair to people on fixed incomes. In Australia, both the
government and the Reserve Bank of Australia attempt to control the rate of inflation.

2 Australian currency
Currency is the system of money that is used in a
particular country. Coins and bank notes make up
the Australian currency.
Australian coins are made at the Royal Australian
Mint in Canberra and consist of ‘silver’ coins
(5, 10, 20 and 50 cents) and ‘gold’ coins ($1 and
$2). Bank notes are printed by the Note Processing
Centre of the Reserve Bank of Australia at
Craigieburn, near Melbourne. All of Australia’s
currency is issued by the Reserve Bank and
distributed through banks. 
Prior to 1988, Australia’s bank notes were printed
on paper. Since then they are printed on plastic
(polymer), which is more durable and lasts about
four times as long. Furthermore, the polymer notes
are recyclable. They are also more difficult to
reproduce (by counterfeiters).
© Blake Education, 2006
6
Living and Work Literacy 1
Legal tender
Legal tender is currency that cannot be legally refused in payment of a debt. However, someone
who offers to pay a debt of $10 000 in 5 cent coins would not be popular. This is why the Reserve
Bank sets limits in relation to what people are obliged to accept when someone tenders (or offers
to pay) for an item. These limits are:
• $5 limit on 5, 10, 20 and 50 cent coins
• $10 limit on $1 and $2 coins.
There is no limit for bank notes – so you can pay a $10 000 debt in $5 notes and the person is
legally obliged to accept it.
Counterfeit money
Counterfeiting is copying money to make your own coins or bank notes. It is illegal and there are
heavy penalties for counterfeiters who are caught.
To guard against counterfeiting, the Reserve Bank publishes a detection guide to highlight the
differences between a counterfeit note and a genuine note. There are hidden patterns and specific
symbols in the clear window of legal notes. You can find out more about counterfeit money on the
Reserve Bank’s website.
 Australia was the first country in the
world to print all of its banknotes on
polymer rather than traditional paper.
 Australia’s first polymer bank note was
the commemorative Bicentennial $10
note, issued in January 1988.

2 Australian currency
Unfit and mutilated notes
Unfit and mutilated notes are those that are no
longer suitable for further circulation. An unfit note
is one that is stained, defaced or torn.
A mutilated note is one where 20 per cent or more
of the note is missing; it has been subject to
significant heat damage; or it has been contaminated
so as to prevent direct handling. 
Banks are authorised to assess these notes and
compensate people who discover them. The banks
then forward these notes to the Reserve Bank to be
destroyed under supervision.

3 Foreign currency
When you travel to foreign countries you will find that they have different money systems or
currencies. For example, in the United Kingdom they use pounds, in Thailand they have Baht, while
in China the yuan is the currency used.
Exchange rates
Many countries use dollars, such as the United States, New Zealand, Singapore and Canada, however
they are still considered foreign currencies in Australia. If you are in Canada and want to buy a
hamburger you will need Canadian dollars. So you have to convert your Australian dollars into the
local currency. You can do this at a bank, financial institution or foreign exchange dealer. The conversion
is done by means of the exchange rate. This is simply the rate at which one currency exchanges for
another. For example, on 15 March 2005, the official exchange rate for Australian to Canadian dollars
was: A$1 = C$0.85. Below is a list in Australian dollars of the exchange rates on 11 March 2005. 
© Blake Education, 2006
8
Living and Work Literacy 1
Exchange rates fluctuate on a daily basis according to forces acting in the market place. Australia’s
exchange rate tells us how much other countries are prepared to pay for our goods and services.
For example, an increase in the demand for Australian coal would be likely to lead to an increase in
the demand for Australian dollars to pay for it. This puts upward pressure on the price of Australian
dollars (in relation to other currencies). Similarly, an increase in the demand for Japanese cars will
mean an increase in the demand for Japanese yen to pay for them. The value of the yen would then
be likely to increase. A fall in the exchange rate for Australian dollars will make it more expensive
for us to buy overseas goods and services.

3 Foreign currency
The euro
On 1 January 2002 several European currencies, such as the German mark, the Italian lira and the
French franc, were replaced by a single currency, known as the euro. This single currency, now used
in 12 European countries, has made it much easier to conduct business across Europe.
The currencies of Finland, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom have been retained.
(Norway and Switzerland are not members of the European Union.)

4 Cheques
A cheque is simply an instruction from a person to his or her bank to pay a certain amount of money
to a person or organisation. The person writing the cheque is called the drawer, as they are drawing
on their bank account. The person or organisation who is to receive the cheque is the payee.
Below is an example of a typical cheque.
© Blake Education, 2006
10
Living and Work Literacy 1
Advantages of cheques include:
• they are easy to use
• they are relatively safe
• they can be sent through the mail
• they are easy to keep track of
• they have a record (the cheque book butt and bank
statement).
Disadvantages of cheques include:
• they use paper (in an age of electronic communication)
• signatures can be forged
• they are time-consuming to process
• some organisations or people may not accept cheques
without some form of identification
• they can go astray in the mail.
How cheques work
Linda Roberts hires an electrician to do some electrical work. As payment for the work, she writes
the electrician, Ron Sparks, a cheque for $250. Ron takes the cheque to his bank (Apex Bank) and
deposits it in his account. His bank account is then credited $250 (increased by $250). This is
subject to the cheque clearing. Linda has to have enough money in her account to cover the
cheque amount. Apex Bank then makes contact electronically with Linda’s bank (Vectra Bank) and
Linda’s bank account is debited $250 (reduced by $250, leaving a balance of $500). This may take a
few days. Once the cheque is cleared, Ron may draw on that $250 from his Apex bank account.
Linda meanwhile has a record of the transaction on her cheque butt and on her next statement.

Stopping cheques
If a cheque is lost in the mail or stolen, you can stop payment on the cheque. This involves contacting
the bank (either in person, via the Internet or telephone banking system) and instructing the bank
to stop payment. A small fee is charged for this service.
Dishonoured cheques

dishonour (or refuse to pay) the cheque. The payee is informed and then must pursue the drawer
for the amount.
