5 Credit cards and debit cards
People often get confused with credit cards and debit cards, especially as they are both made of
plastic and appear about the same size.
The term ’credit’ involves purchasing goods or services and paying for them later or over time. In
other words, you can purchase something without having the actual money in your bank account.
You are then given time to pay this amount to a credit card company. When you purchase something
using a credit card you will sign a sales docket.
At the end of each month, the credit card company sends you a statement, which lists all the credit
purchases that you made in that month, the minimum amount that must be paid and the total
amount owing (this could include credit purchases from previous months). This statement also requests
payment by a certain date. If you only pay the minimum amount and not the full credit amount
you will be charged interest.
Credit cards are not necessarily linked to bank accounts. Examples of credit cards are Bankcard,
Mastercard, Visa, American Express and Diners Club.
A debit card, on the other hand, is linked to a bank account. When you use a debit card, the funds
are immediately deducted from (debited to) your bank account. You may use a debit card at an ATM
(Automatic Teller Machine) or at a retail outlet that has an EFTPOS facility (Electronic Funds Transfer
at Point of Sale). In this case, money is immediately transferred from your bank account to the store’s
bank account. You can pay for goods using a debit card and also draw out additional cash. Either
way, the funds come out of (are debited to) your bank account.

6 Telephone and online payments
There are now many ways available to consumers to pay for
goods and services. The most common one, especially for
purchases of small value, is to pay cash in person. If you buy
an ice-cream, for example, it is appropriate to pay for it in cash. 
When you pay for something, you can:
• pay in cash
• write a cheque and deliver it in person or send it via the post
• pay in cash or with a cheque at a bank or post office
• use a debit card
• use a credit card
• use telephone banking
• use Internet banking
• use a direct debit order.

Telephone banking
By using the keypad on your telephone you can not only make payments, but also do most of your
banking. Using telephone banking, you can:
• check your account balances, including loan accounts
• check your transaction history
• stop payment on a cheque
• transfer funds from one account to another
• pay bills with BPay
• order a bank statement
• check interest earned on your investment accounts.
Telephone banking allows you to get information or carry out a transaction by ringing your bank
and following the prompts to press particular numbers on your telephone keypad. For example, if
you want account information you may be prompted to press 1, or to transfer funds to press 2.
Internet banking 
Internet banking is now very popular. The great advantage with this method is that you don’t have
to leave your home to do most of your banking.
Once you have organised to have access to Internet banking (this normally involves the bank issuing
you an account number and you choosing a password, see the Internet banking diagram on the
next page), you can do everything that you do using telephone banking, plus more, including ordering
a new cheque book; transferring money from your bank account to another person’s bank account;
and analysing your financial transactions on a monthly basis. 
Banks use special coding devices or encryption technology to ensure that no one else has access to
your banking details.
BPay
BPay is another way of paying bills or accounts using the Internet or telephone. You need to have
an organisation’s biller code (four or five numbers) and your customer reference number (usually
eight or more numbers). These are found on the bill or account that you are paying. You then use
your bank’s website or telephone service, entering both of these numbers with your computer keyboard
or telephone keypad, together with the amount you wish to pay (see the BPay system diagram on
the next page).
If you make regular BPay payments to an organisation you can save the details for future transactions
(such as Fern Hill City Council in the diagram on the next page).

8 Buying wisely
Have you ever bought something and later regretted it? Did you forget to check out the alternatives?
Did you spend too much money? Did you later find out that you could have bought it at a much
cheaper price? Everyone has probably done one or more of these, so it is important to analyse just
what is involved in buying wisely. 
Consumers operate in a commercial economy by earning (or receiving) a money income and using
it to satisfy needs and wants. With a limited amount of money and unlimited needs and wants,
consumers must therefore choose wisely in order to gain the maximum satisfaction for their money.
So what is involved in buying wisely? Here are some useful tips:
• Clarify the purpose of your intended purchase. Ask yourself: Why do I want it? 
• Are you buying on impulse, or have you really thought about the purchase? If it is a hamburger
you want because you are hungry, this may not require much thought, but if you want to buy
a car or some expensive clothes you may need to think about it more. 
• Check the price. Does it truly reflect the likely level of satisfaction you will derive from the
purchase?
• Check the quality. Is it better to purchase a more expensive brand or is a cheaper brand better
value for money?
• Check other brands and visit other stores. This is called comparison shopping. Obviously this is
more important for relatively expensive items than it is for buying, for example, a milkshake.
There are many places where you can purchase goods, such as discount stores, factory outlets
and local markets. You can also check newspapers, magazines and the Internet. 
• Can you afford to buy this item? Is it within your budget? The consequences of poor budgeting
can be quite dramatic.
• Should you consider what alternative uses you could put your money towards? This is a good
check to see if you really do want something.
There are several key factors that affect what we buy. Price is an obvious one and so too is the state
of our finances – how much money we have and how much we are going to allocate to spending.
Other factors that influence what we buy include:
• Our age: older people usually have different wants and needs from younger people.
• Our gender: women and girls sometimes want to buy items that are different from men and
boys, however many of the same items are bought regardless of gender.
• Advertising and marketing: we are all influenced in some ways by advertisements and by
marketing schemes such as sales and special offers.
© Blake Education, 2006
18
Living and Work Literacy 1
• Convenience: we may decide to buy
something at a local shop because it is
closer, even though the item may be
more expensive than in a supermarket
located farther away.
• Service: because some items that we buy
may be faulty or may break down, we
may choose to buy from a retailer that
provides after-sales service. We may also
want to know whether an item has a
guarantee or a warranty. 
• The environment: more people today are
becoming conscious of the environment
and are purchasing goods that are
environmentally friendly. Some of these
products have ‘green labels’, which
indicate that a product has not and will
not harm the environment.

9 Protection for consumers
Consumer shopping rights
Refunds: consumers are entitled to cash refunds or an
exchange if the goods they buy are defective or faulty. If you
change your mind about a product and want your money
back, the store is not legally obliged to give you a refund.
However, many stores do give refunds as an act of goodwill
(in the hope you will visit their store again).
Cooling-off period: consumers are protected against door-
to-door salespeople who visit uninvited. If you buy a product
and later change your mind, you are entitled to cancel the
deal. The cooling off period varies from state to state, but is
generally between five and ten days. The cooling-off period
only applies to contracts of $50 or more in all states (except
New South Wales where there is no minimum). It also does
not operate if you invite a salesperson to visit your home.
Guarantees: all goods for sale must meet a basic level of
quality and must ‘do what they are supposed to do’. For
example, if you bought a watch you would expect it to tell
the time, regardless of how nice it looks on your wrist.
Guarantees also contain specific conditions, for example, a
12-month guarantee to repair the product if a fault develops
during that period. Whatever the specific guarantees, there
is still the implied guarantee of basic quality (as mentioned
above). A warranty is basically the same as a guarantee.
Buying goods online: the rights of the consumer shopping
online are also protected. There are, however, additional risks.
For example, you may be dealing with an overseas company
whose reputation and honesty you cannot check. Therefore,
it is important to check an online seller’s contact details and
terms and conditions of sale. Security and privacy are also
important to avoid your personal details being made available
to others. Details about refunds, returns and guarantees
should also be checked. Dealing with an overseas company
has additional risks as some goods, for example, electrical
goods, have different systems that may not work in Australia.

How to complain
If you are unhappy with a product you have purchased, here are some steps that you can take:
• Go to the store where you purchased the product. Explain your case clearly and politely and ask
for a replacement or repair. If you are unsuccessful, you can ask to speak to the manager or
person in charge.
• Write a letter to the store outlining your complaint.
• Lodge an official complaint to the consumer affairs or fair trading organisation in your state. 
• Take your complaint to the Small Claims Tribunal. Your case may be heard with a representative
of the store and a referee who acts as a judge. The aim of the hearing is for the two parties to
reach a mutual agreement.
• Contact the ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission), a federal government
body, or the ombudsman in your state.
• Approach the media (radio, television or newspapers).

10 Borrowing money
If you have insufficient money to cover a purchase, then you can borrow the money. It is important to
be aware that this money must be repaid over time and that you will be charged interest. The interest
is a percentage of the loan amount and is paid to the lending authority for the use of their money. 
When you borrow money you enter into a legal contract with the financial institution. The institution
may be a bank, a credit union, an insurance company or any organisation licensed to lend money.
By law, loan contracts must be easy to read and understand; outline the rights and responsibilities
of the borrower; and set out all the costs involved and details of the loan calculation.

Applying for a loan 
Financial institutions risk their money when they lend to customers and they want their money repaid
according to the conditions of the loan. Therefore, financial institutions have to be certain of a
customer’s ability to repay a loan.
To do this, when a person applies for a loan, he or she is asked many questions about his or her
financial situation. This includes a person’s monthly or yearly income, his or her credit card details
and details of any other loans that he or she may have with other financial institutions.
Each financial institution has a different policy regarding the level of risk and their assessment of the
applicant’s ability to pay. For example, some loan application forms ask for full details of an applicant’s
assets (the things owned) and liabilities (money that is owed), and some even require an estimate
of an applicant’s monthly budget, including the average amounts spent on electricity and telephone,
clothes and food, entertainment and so on.
Most financial institutions will now allow customers to apply for a loan online. An example of a
simple online loan application form is on the previous page.

11 Budgeting
Budgeting is an important aspect of your life. A budget is simply a plan of your regular income and
expenses over a period of time. You may have a weekly budget, a monthly budget or a yearly one.
Businesses and governments also prepare budgets as they need to plan their financial dealings ahead
of time. Budgets help people and organisations to achieve goals, especially long-term goals.
Preparing a budget
To prepare a budget you need to follow a few simple steps:
• Define your goals: for example, you may want to buy a new bicycle or a second-hand car, go
on an overseas holiday, or you may want to buy some new clothes or a new stereo. 
• List all your regular sources of income: these might include pocket money or your weekly wages
if you have a job. You may also expect to receive occasional gifts, perhaps from relatives on
your birthday. You may also earn money doing odd jobs.
• List all your expenses: for a personal budget, these can be ordered into categories, such as
food, clothing, fares, entertainment, sports expenses and credit card repayments. If you are
preparing a household budget you would need to add things like electricity and telephone
charges, car expenses, rent or house repayments, rates and insurance.
• Set aside an amount of money for unexpected expenses or emergencies.
A budget will help you work out how much you are likely to save over a certain period of time. This
may involve making adjustments to how much you spend. You can also build the amount you want
to save into your budget.
When you analyse your income and regular expenses over time, you will start to see if you are over-
committed or if you are able to save some of your income to achieve your goal.
Spreadsheets
Spreadsheets are a useful way of recording financial transactions and making useful calculations,
especially for a budget. A spreadsheet is computer software that allows you to enter information in
columns and then make calculations using a formula.
A spreadsheet looks like an alphanumeric grid, with letters of the alphabet across the top and numbers
in sequence down the left-hand side, creating a series of cells that can be identified as A1, H4 or M25.
At the top of the spreadsheet is a space for entering a formula so that you can make calculations.
For example: M25 = M24+M23+M22 or M25 = J25+K25+L25
In the example below the formula is A5=SUM(A1:A4) There are more complex formulas than simple
additions, such as calculating interest rates and loan repayments.
There are also many more functions to a spreadsheet, including sorting words alphabetically in
ascending or descending order. The help menu of the software will help you learn more about using
spreadsheets.

12 Changing prices
Have you ever noticed that the prices of goods and services often go up and down? For example,
prices can be reduced in the short-term when stores have a sale, a special promotion or offer a discount.
As a consumer, you should know whether these reductions are genuine. For example, when you see
a sale sign with ‘50% OFF’, you should be asking: ‘50% off what?’ What was the price before the
offer? Is the discount genuine? Wise consumers need to be well educated and aware of the marketplace
before buying.
Long-term changes in prices are also worth studying. A loaf of bread was much cheaper 30 years ago
than 10 years ago and cheaper than the price today. This is an indication that the general level of prices
is gradually rising. But are we necessarily worse off? To work this out it is important to look at what is
happening to average wages and general income levels. History has shown that they too are rising.
To measure price levels in relation to wage levels you can use a statistical tool called the Consumer
Price Index or CPI. This helps you to see if goods at ‘real’ or ‘constant’ prices have actually risen or
fallen relative to wage levels. For example, some goods have increased, such as petrol and some
food items, while others have actually fallen in price in real terms. For example, cars, airfares and
stationery items such as pens and paper have been consistently falling in price in real terms.
You can also measure whether real prices are rising or falling by calculating how many days the
average worker must work before he or she can buy a new car. That figure has dropped significantly
over the past 10 or 20 years.
What is the CPI?
The Consumer Price Index or CPI is an official measure of the change in the level of prices. It measures
the change in prices of a variety of goods and services over a three-month period. These items
include the goods and services typically bought by Australian households, including food, clothing,
household furniture and appliances as well as education, transport and health.
The index is calculated by assigning a value of 100 as a base, so that an index of 105 would indicate
that prices rose by 5%. The CPI is published every quarter, in March, June, September and December.
The CPI is also used as a measure of inflation (see below).

What is inflation?
Inflation is a rapid rise in the level of prices over a period of time. The rate of inflation is normally
an annual measure and takes the CPIs of four successive quarters. For example, if the CPI for March
was 1.5%, for June 1.0%, for September 1.2% and for December 1.3% the rate of inflation would
be 5%. It is possible that prices in one quarter could actually drop but this would most likely be
offset by rises in the other three quarters.

14 Buying a car
Imagine that you have decided to buy a car. It would be very unwise to go out and buy the first car
you see without doing some important research. New cars are naturally likely to be more reliable
than used cars, but they are also very expensive. Here are some generally agreed tips on buying a
second-hand car. 
• Decide how much money you want to spend.
• Research car insurance: there are two types of car insurance. The first is comprehensive
insurance. This insures your car against damage. This means that if you smash your car and it is
insured for $10 000, the insurance company will assess the damage and pay some or the entire
amount depending on the damage. The second is called third party property insurance. This
covers you for any damage you do to another person’s car. It is cheaper than comprehensive
insurance as your own car is not covered. This should not be confused with compulsory third
party insurance (sometimes known as a ‘Green Slip’). This insurance is paid for as part of your
car registration and is designed to compensate people injured in car accidents, regardless of
fault.
• Research finance if you need to borrow money to buy the car you want. This involves checking
interest rates and general borrowing terms. It is also important to budget for the loan
repayments.
• Be aware of additional costs of motoring. These include costs of petrol, registration and
insurance, servicing and repairs, spare parts and the depreciation of your car’s value. When you
want to sell the car you will find its value has dropped and you need to factor this into your
calculations. 
• Check the details of the car, such as the year and make. This can be found on the compliance
plate, a small metal plate inside the car bonnet. It records the make and model of car and the
month and year the car was manufactured. 
• Check if a warranty is being offered and what the details are.
• Remember that there are other costs. For example, a new car will have a delivery fee, and a
used car will have to be transferred into your name, which involves a transfer fee and a 3%
stamp duty fee.
• If you are buying a second-hand car a vehicle check is a good idea. The NRMA, the RACV and
other motoring organisations conduct inspections for a fee. Licensed dealers must guarantee
that the cars they sell are roadworthy, registered and that no money is owed on them.
© Blake Education, 2006
30
Living and Work Literacy 1
Where to buy? 
The options available include:
• A licensed dealer: this method may be more reliable,
especially if a warranty is offered, but the
disadvantage is that prices are generally higher.
• Private sale via newspaper advertisements: you may
get a bargain in a private sale, especially if the seller
is in a hurry to sell and you can negotiate a price,
however you take a risk on the quality of the car. 
• Sale via the Internet: there are numerous websites
that list cars for sale. This method is increasing in
popularity as more people use the Internet for many
different types of transactions. Some of the websites
will have useful hints to assist you, however the same
risks apply as with a private sale.
• A car buying service: some companies and credit
unions offer a service (sometimes free) to search for a
car for you. This is especially useful if you are busy
and don’t have time to look.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 199 9

14 Buying a car
Selling your car
If you want to sell your car the first thing you need to do is find out how much it is worth. You can
research this by checking the cars for sale advertisements in the newspapers and/or the Internet.
You can choose to sell your car privately and hope you get someone to buy or you can approach a
dealer. A third option is to trade-in your car on a newer model. If you are selling privately you need
to make sure you are paid in cash or with a bank cheque in case the buyer’s cheque is dishonoured
(bounces). 
Whichever method you decide it is always useful to wash and clean your car to make it presentable.

15 Renting a place to live
Many people at some time in their lives face the prospect of finding a place to rent. There are legal
requirements when renting – for both those who are renting and those who are offering a place for
rent.  
Some important terms that you may come across when renting a place to live:
• Tenant: the person who occupies a property and pays rent.
• Landlord: the person who owns a property and leases it to a tenant.
• Lease: the legal document that is an agreement between a landlord and a tenant. It states the
terms under which the agreement is made.

16 Buying and selling real estate
Whether you are buying a house, an apartment or a block of land, there are procedures that must
be followed, including research. This involves looking at advertisements for houses for sale or auction,
which can be found in newspapers, on the Internet and at the offices of real estate agents.
It is also important to calculate how much money you have for a deposit, how much you may need
to borrow and what would be the likely repayments.
When you have found the property you want, it is advisable to contact a solicitor. The purchase of
a house or unit involves:
• paying a holding deposit (this is not legally binding, but it gets things moving) 
• exchanging contracts (a legal document that binds the sale and involves the payment of an
agreed sum, usually 10% of the purchase price)
• arranging settlement (paying the balance of the money owing to the vendor or seller) – when
this happens, the property is legally owned by the purchaser.
Below is a typical newspaper advertisement for a unit.
© Blake Education, 2006
34
Living and Work Literacy 1
Westwood
$520 000
SUNNY WITH VIEWS
Inspect Sat.11.30am–12.30pm
2 bedrm unit at rear of building. Int. laundry, LUG & north balcony
with fabulous views. Stroll shops & transport
LMN Property. 8740 5555
Conveyancing
Conveyancing is the term given to the legal procedures required to arrange the purchase of a property.
These procedures are usually carried out by a solicitor, but they can also be done by a conveyancing
company with expertise in the process.
Conveyancing usually involves:
• a search on the title of the property to see that the current owner is legally entitled to sell it
• a survey check to see that the land or property described is in accordance with official maps of
the area (from the land titles office)
• obtaining council certificates of compliance that indicate that the plans comply with all council
regulations and that all rates and charges have been paid
• obtaining permission from other government departments in case the land is subject to future
development or resumption plans (such as a new freeway)
• obtaining a building certificate that describes
the condition of the building in case there are
faults (this is not compulsory but advisable) 
• arranging finance – a solicitor will usually help
with the document used as security for a loan,
called a mortgage (most buyers don’t have
enough money to buy a property outright and
have to borrow)
• checking the  contract for the sale of the
property – the contract can sometimes be a
complex legal document with many provisions
and clauses. It must be signed by both buyer
and seller when agreement is reached.

17 Insurance
How it works
Insurance is all about spreading risk. For example, if a group of 20 softball players all decide to put
$50 into a fund to cover any medical costs in case one of them is injured, then they have $1000 in
the fund. So if a player is injured, then there is $1000 to spend on medical treatment for that person.
The fund means that all the players are covered in case of injury and everyone agrees it is worth
$50 to ensure that there is money to go towards any possible costs. Insurance companies operate
in much the same way.
There are three main principles upon which insurance is based:
• Utmost good faith: this means that the person taking out an insurance policy must answer the
questions asked by the insurance company truthfully and disclose all relevant information. This
relates to both application forms and when making an insurance claim.
• Insurable interest: this means that the person who takes out an insurance policy must have an
interest in the property being insured. For example, you must own the car, boat, house or
whatever item that you are insuring.
• Indemnity: this means that when a person makes an insurance claim, he or she should be
compensated for the loss and no more. In other words, you are not meant to make a profit out
of insurance.
When you make an insurance claim, a person from the insurance company calculates the risk and
determines the premium for a policy (the actuary), while another person calculates the value of the
loss sustained (the assessor).
© Blake Education, 2006
36
Living and Work Literacy 1
Types of insurance
• Life insurance (assurance): protection against loss of income.
• Property insurance: insurance for damage or loss of items such as a house, boat or caravan.
• Accident insurance: workers’ compensation and public risk policies.
• Motor vehicle insurance: a type of property insurance.
• Health insurance: protection against the high costs of health care.
• Travel insurance: insuring yourself against loss of luggage, cancellation of travel or accidents
overseas.
© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 76020 199 9	
Living & Work Literacy Book  1

18 Looking after the environment
As consumers, we are confronted with a wide variety
of products and it is important that we ask questions
such as: Are the manufacture, distribution and
consumption of these products harming the
environment? Are there alternatives to plastic bags?
Can more materials be recycled? Are there products
that are made in an environmentally friendly way? 
Green labels
You will notice that there are products marketed
as ‘environmentally friendly’, often with their labels
coloured green. This could mean that they have
received a ‘Good Environmental Choice’ label from
the Australian Environmental Labelling Association,
or it could be simply a marketing ploy by the company.
The issue of labelling also applies to food that has
been genetically modified (GM). GM foods are
those that have been engineered by genetics to
make them grow faster or become more disease
resistant. Genetic modification is a controversial new
technology and therefore there is a demand for
modified products to be labelled accordingly.
Another trend is the increasing popularity of organic
food. These foods are produced without the use of
fertilisers, pesticides or other chemical additives.
© Blake Education, 2006
38
Living and Work Literacy 1
The Australian Environmental
Labelling Association 
The Australian Environmental Labelling
Association was created to provide consumers
with a clear guide to the environmental
factors involved when they purchase a
product.
It encourages consumers to purchase products
with less environmental impact so that the
quality of the environment is improved in
the long term. It also encourages producers to
consider the effects on the environment in
the manufacture of their products. This is
part of the move towards sustainable
management of resources. 
There are now a growing number of
‘ecolabelled’ products, from laundry
detergents and cosmetics to timber products
and organic foods. Energy rating labels on
electrical appliances are another example. 
To find out more about The Australian
Environmental Labelling Association you can
look at their website.
Recycling 
In order to keep up with the demand for paper, forests of trees are being cut down in Australia and
in the rest of the world. However, paper can be recycled and many local councils in Australia now
have recycling policies to assist with this process. 
Plastic bags
Non-biodegradable plastic bags are very harmful to the environment; they don’t break down over
time, they clog the waterways and are a danger to fish and bird life. Currently there is a big push to
ban, or at least limit, the number of plastic bags.
In some countries, for example Ireland, consumers pay for plastic bags. This has dramatically reduced
the number of bags being used.
Saving energy
As a society we have become reliant on
fossil fuels to generate energy. Each year
a typical house pumps approximately 11
tonnes of carbon dioxide into the
atmosphere.
The benefits of reducing energy
consumption are immediate. Not only
does it save money, it will result in a
healthier world for future generations.

19 Planning an overseas holiday
Congratulations! You have saved enough money for an overseas holiday. How do you plan for it?
Where do you begin?
Documents
The most important document you will need is a passport. This shows proof of your identity and
your country of citizenship. You cannot travel overseas without it. In fact, you would not be allowed
out of Australia, let alone allowed into another country. A passport is checked when you leave a
country and when you enter another country. You can obtain an application form for a passport
from any post office. You will need your birth certificate and two recent photographs to complete
the application.
Other documents you may need, depending on the destination, are:
• A visa: some countries require you to obtain ‘permission’ to enter. This is in the form of a stamp
in your passport that allows you to enter the country. Visas are obtained from the country’s
consulate in Australia and usually involve a fee.
• A health certificate: indicates required vaccinations that may be necessary to enter some
countries. 
• A work permit: may be needed if you want to work overseas. If you don’t have one and the
immigration officer at the point of entry suspects you are going to work in the country, you
may be refused entry. 
It may also be advisable to buy some foreign currency as Australian dollars are not generally accepted
for payment. You can buy foreign currency in cash at a bank or at the airport before you leave, or
you can purchase travellers’ cheques, which you can cash when you are overseas.  Most major travel
destinations today have ATMs and your debit or credit cards can generally be used to withdraw cash.
Your PIN is the same wherever you are in the world.
Organising the trip
Some of the decisions you will need to make before you go on your trip include:
• Destination: where do you want to go? Often people try to fit too many places on their
itinerary and end up with a rushed trip. Making a priority list of your most favoured
destinations is a good way to start.
• Method of travel: will you fly, go by ship, overland or a combination?
• Type of travel: you could choose a package tour, where everything is organised and you pay
upfront, or you can travel independently and do your own thing.  You can book
accommodation in advance or find it when you get there (or a combination of both).
• Costings: you need to research how much it is all going to cost and decide if you can afford it.
It is important to work out a budget. 
• Booking method: you can use a travel agent or book over the Internet. The advantage of using
a travel agent is that they have expert knowledge about airfare structures as well as special
deals, shortcuts for planning and other advice. Booking via the Internet is becoming very
popular and it may save you money, but you may not have the same safeguards that a
reputable travel agent can provide. Also, not all Internet fares and accommodation listings are
necessarily cheaper than booking through a travel agent.  
• Travel itinerary: it is a good idea to prepare an itinerary even if you don’t follow it exactly when
you are away. You can build in some flexibility in an itinerary.
• Travel insurance: for an overseas holiday this is a very good idea and in some countries it is
compulsory. Insurance will cover you not only for lost luggage, but also for medical expenses if
you get sick overseas. 
• Research: the more information you have the better prepared you will be for your trip. It is
important to get travel brochures, read travel books, check travel websites and talk to friends
who have travelled. This will ensure a more enjoyable trip.

20 Joining a club
Most people have joined at least one club in their lives and many are members of several. Being a
member of a club, whatever it is, can provide great enjoyment and satisfaction for people, if only
because it provides a sense of belonging. Below is a list of some of the different types of clubs.   
Types of clubs
• Large licensed clubs
• Fan clubs
• Sporting clubs
• Music and drama clubs
• Craft clubs
• Friendship clubs
© Blake Education, 2006

Club documents
The following is a list of the typical documents of a club:
• Constitution: a set of rules by which the club is run.
• Register of members: a list of all members and their
contact details.
• Attendance book: a record of member attendance at
meetings.
• Minute book: a record of the proceedings from each meeting.
• Correspondence file: letters received and copies of letters sent.
• Annual report: a summary of the year’s activities.
• Financial statement: a summary of financial records.
• Club journal: a regular magazine or newsletter sent to members.
Club office-bearers
The following is a list of the typical office-bearers of a club:
• President: chairs meetings and acts as the club spokesperson.
• Vice president: assists president and acts on his or her behalf if absent.
• Secretary: records minutes of meetings and handles correspondence.
• Treasurer: handles all finances, including receiving subscriptions and making payments.
Meeting procedures
Accepted meeting procedures involve the right of members to present a motion (a proposal put
forward). For the motion to be considered, it needs to be seconded by another person. The members,
either by a show of hands or a written secret ballot, then vote on the motion. If a majority of members
vote in favour of the motion, it is said to be ‘carried’; if not, it is lost.

Map symbols and key

A map uses symbols to represent features or objects on the
ground. A map is not a drawing of how things really look.
Most maps use many symbols. So we can easily understand
the map, all the symbols used are grouped together in one
place. This is called the key. Another word used instead of
key is legend. A key on one map could be called a legend on
another map.

Max Quickdrawer and Paula Mapmaker help us learn
about maps. Last week Max and Paula went on a hot-air
balloon flight. The flight left from the park near their school.
They floated over their school and landed about five
kilometres away at Cape Beauty.

Paula drew the map of Cape Beauty (on a
separate sheet) as they floated by. Paula used
symbols on her map to show clearly some of
the features that she saw. The symbols help us
to get a good idea of what Cape Beauty looks
like.
A symbol is not a drawing of a feature. It is 5
a representation. It needs to be simple. It is
good if we know what the symbol represents

The four main directions are North, East, South and
West. One of the best ways of working out directions is to
use a compass. The needle on a compass always points to
the north. You can use directions to find your way from one
place to another. On a map you can use directions to find
out where one point is compared to another.

Max Quickdrawer and Paula Mapmaker will help us
learn about maps. Last week Max and Paula went on a hot-
air balloon flight. They took their compass with them. They
floated over their school and passed over Blair Town.

and West. These directions are also known as
the cardinal points of a compass. They are

directions. Paula shows Max how to find north

pointing magnetic needle. Then the E is

Using the linear scale

You can use the linear scale to work out the
real distance between two points on a map.
Use a straight edge of a piece of paper and lay
it on the map so the edge of the paper touches
both points. Mark the two points on the piece
of paper. Place the paper against the linear
scale with the first mark aligned with the zero
position on the linear scale and the second
mark along the scale. Use the second mark to
read the real distance off the scale. If the
second mark is between numbers on the scale,
estimate the reading from the numbers before
and after the mark.

You can use the scale of a map to calculate the distance
between any places or features on a map. You can work
out the straight-line distance between two places. That is
the distance ‘as the crow flies’ or as an aeroplane flies. It
is the shortest distance between two points.There are
different ways of calculating straight-line distance just
as there are different ways of stating the scale.

Approximating distance and

travel time

As maps are drawn to scale, they often have to
leave out much of the detail on curvy bits. We
all know that there are many more bends in a
river or stream than can ever be shown on a
map. We can only approximate the real length.

The length measured along a curve on a
map will depend on the scale of the map.
Large-scale maps show more objects and
features than small-scale maps, so they show
more curves.

When distances are very long, such as from.
the east to the west coast in Australia, they are
usually only an approximation when calculated
from a map. Again the scale of the map will
affect the approximation.

People use distance to help them make other
approximations, such as the time that it takes
to travel from one place to another. But
distance on maps, whether straight-line or
curved, does not take into account the flatness
or steepness of an area.

NOTE TO TEACHER

This worksheet uses the map
of Cape Beauty on page 42.
Students will need a copy of

Students will also need a
piece of tracing paper at least
10 cm square.

Creating a grid

Sometimes you might want to calculate the
area of a feature on a map. It could be the area
of a national park or the area of a lake. You
can do this by creating a grid over the area
and multiplying the number of grid squares
covering the feature by the area represented
under each grid square.

One way to do this is to use a piece of
tracing paper larger than the area on the map
that you want to calculate. On the tracing
paper, use your ruler to mark points one
centimetre apart along the top and bottom of
the paper. Join each pair of marks with a line.
Then mark points one centimetre apart along
each of the sides and join these. You will now
have a grid of one-centimetre squares.

Grid references

Grid references are used to more accurately
pinpoint a feature than an area reference. This
is done in your mind by subdividing each grid
square into tenths. These subdivisions do not
appear on the map.

This allows you to estimate in your mind a
three-figure reading for the eastings and
another three-figure reading for the northings
just as you did in question 4, but without
having the drawn subdivision lines.

By combining both three-figure readings you
get a six-figure reference, which is known as a
grid reference. Therefore the lookout is at grid
reference 847338.

Read the information about the laws regarding work that apply to young people.
There are laws to protect young people who work while they are still at school. Many 
students have casual jobs and some start working as soon as they are legally old enough. 
The legal age at which you can get a job depends on the state or territory of Australia you 
live in and the type of work you would be doing. For example, at 13 years old you may be 
old enough to get a job delivering newspapers but not old enough to work in a restaurant 
or fast food outlet. 
There are limits on the times of day and night you can start and finish work and on the 
number of hours you can work during a school week. There are also laws which restrict 
young people from working in places that serve alcohol or where there is gambling unless 
they have special certificates and are at least 18 years old.

There are many types of work arrangements and it is important to understand the 
differences between them.

1 
Fixed-term contract work is work that people do
a on a contract with a starting date but no finishing date.
b for one school term or semester while at school.
c on a contract that specifies the dates the work will start and finish.
2 
Voluntary work
a does not help you because you don’t get paid for your work.

2.5 Casual work
Read the information about casual work then answer the questions on the next page.
Most students are employed on a casual basis and, like most things in life,  
there are advantages and disadvantages.
Let’s start with the not-so-good news about  
casual work. 
•  There are no fixed hours or days of work, so your income is not regular.
•  The number of shifts you are rostered on for can vary from week to week. 
•  It can be difficult to plan your social life until you have your roster.
•  Your employment can be terminated 
without notice.
• There is no paid sick leave or holiday pay.
Now some good news about casual work.
•  Casual workers get paid an extra 
percentage per hour because they don’t 
get sick leave or holiday pay. This is 
called casual loading.
•  If you work in hospitality – for example, 
in a café or hotel – you might get tips as 
well as your wage.
•  After school hours, weekends, public 
holidays and school holidays are often 
the busiest times for retail, fast food 
outlets and cafés. These are all times 
during which students are often available 
for casual work. 
•  Students can usually negotiate with their 
employers to take time off during exams.
•  Casuals are often paid an extra amount 
per hour for working at different times 
such as late evenings, weekends or public 
holidays. These are called penalty rates. 
The extra amount you receive depends  
on the award or agreement you are  
covered by.
•  Casual workers learn new skills and gain 
life experience and work experience. 
Be aware!
•   You should be paid for all the hours 
you work. If you are asked to do a one-
week trial or given a probation period, 
you should be paid for this time. Casual 
workers are paid by the hour which 
means that if you are asked to come in 
before your shift to ‘open’ or ‘close’ the 
business, you should be paid for this 
time.
•   A young worker at, for example, a 
fast food outlet, can be employed on 
a casual basis or on a traineeship. 
Sometimes young workers sign a 
traineeship agreement without clearly 
understanding what they are signing up 
for. There is a big difference between 
casuals and trainees in terms of wages, 
training and conditions of employment.

2.7 Other types of work and wages
Read the information about fixed-term contract work, temporary work and labour 
hire, working for commission and piecework. Then answer the following questions.
Piecework employees are paid a fixed 
amount for each unit they produce. The unit 
could be a piece of clothing or furniture you 
make, or a bucket of fruit you pick. So the 
faster you work, the more money you make. 
Working for commission means you 
get a percentage of each sale you 
make. Working for ‘commission only’ 
is illegal unless you are self-employed 
or working in real estate or in car 
sales. You should always receive the 
minimum wage for work that you do 
so make sure you understand what is 
involved before you accept a job that 
involves commission. 
Temporary work and labour hire is short-
term work. Employers often hire full-time 
or part-time temporary staff in busy times 
or when a full-time staff member is on 
leave. The job can be for days, weeks or 
months. Many employers find it easier 
to pay an agency to supply experienced 
workers. In these situations, the agency 
pays the workers an hourly casual rate. 
This is often called labour hire when the 
job involves manual work; for example, in 
manufacturing, trades or construction. 
Fixed-term contract work is usually 
done by workers with particular skills 
and experience who are needed for 
a specific job or project. Generally 
these workers are needed for a 
certain time, such as two weeks or 
during the snow season.

Apprenticeships and traineeships in Australia
•  These systems combine paid work with 
training in a wide range of industries.
• They can be full-time or part-time.
•  You may be able to start one while you are 
still at school.
•  Training is on-the-job and/or off-the-job at

•  The qualifications earned can be used to  
get a full-time job, continue studying or start 
a business.
•  Training is competency-based, which means 
you are assessed on your knowledge and the 
skills you can perform.
•  Rates of pay depend on the type of apprenticeship or traineeship you are doing,  
your age and sometimes your level of education.
•  Because you are being trained as you work, the pay rate is usually less than for casual, 
part-time or full-time jobs.
•  Make sure you understand all the details before you sign a contract or training 
agreement.

3.2 Tax forms
Read the information about tax file numbers then answer the following questions. 
Tax file number (TFN) 
The Australian Taxation Office issues tax file numbers 
to people who work in Australia. This allows the 
government to manage and keep track of tax records. 
If you don’t have a tax file number, your employer will 
have to take more tax from your wages. You only get 
one TFN in your lifetime, so keep it safe and private. 
Don’t share it with your friends, put it on the Internet 
or store it in your phone.
If your school is part of the Secondary Schools TFN 
Program, you could get a tax file number through 
school. If not, visit the website www.ato.gov.au for 
information about getting a tax file number. It is a 
good idea to organise this before you start looking for 
jobs as it can take 28 days to process your application. 
If you are under 16 years you will need a parent or 
guardian to sign the application. You will also need 
to provide proof of identify documents such as your 
birth certificate, passport or Medicare card.
Tax file number declaration
When you start a job you will be asked to fill out a tax file number declaration. 
This is a form on which you declare or state your tax file number, which allows 
your employer to take the correct amount of tax from your wages. Your gross 
wage is the total amount you earn before tax is taken out. Your net wage is the 
amount you have left after tax has been taken out. 
1 
Penny has filled out a tax file number declaration for her 
employer. Her gross wage is $400 per week. Her employer will 
deduct $9.00 each week from her wages. What will be Penny’s 
net wage (amount she gets after tax is taken out)?
2 
Sam doesn’t have a TFN so cannot fill out a tax file number 
declaration. His wages are $400 per week but his employer 
must deduct $92.00 from his wages each week. What will Sam’s 
net wage be?
3 
Sam gets a TFN and fills out a tax file number declaration for his 
employer. How much more will his net wage be?

4.2 All about awards
Read the information about awards then answer the following questions. 
It’s a great feeling when you get your first pay – whether its cash, cheque or an amount 
credited to your bank account. Your employer must also give you a payslip which shows 
how your wages have been calculated. This is where you need to understand awards and 
how they affect your pay. 
An award is a legal document that sets out the minimum pay and conditions for employees 
working in a particular industry or type of occupation. For example, casual staff working in 
fast food outlets or take-away businesses could be covered by the Fast Food Industry award, 
while a casual sales assistant could be covered by the General Retail Industry award. 
Your employer should provide details of your employment status (casual, part-time or  
full-time) and the award you are covered by. The state or territory you live in, your age  
(until you are 21), the tasks or duties you perform and your job title (occupation) also  
affect the amount you are paid. 
Pay rates for trainees are usually based on the level of schooling 
completed, the type of traineeship and how long you have been 
out of school. Apprenticeship pay rates generally depend on the 
type of apprenticeship and whether you are in the first, second, 
third or fourth year of your apprenticeship. 
As there are so many different conditions of employment and 
different pay rates, understanding your wages and checking your 
pay can be confusing. Luckily, there is a great deal of information,

4.3 Understanding base rates and extras
Read the information about base rates and extra amounts then answer the  
following questions. 
Penalty rates, loadings and allowances are all extra amounts that can be added to your 
base hourly rate. The extra amounts you should receive are set out in the award you are 
covered by. Base hourly rates are calculated by dividing the minimum weekly wage by 
the normal number of hours worked per week by a full-time worker. For example, if the 
minimum weekly wage for a full-time worker is $400.00 per week, divide this by 38 (the 
number of normal hours worked each week) to find the base hourly rate of $10.52: 
$400.00 (weekly wage) ÷ 38 (hours worked) = $10.52 (base hourly rate)
1 
What is the base hourly rate if the weekly wage is $494.00 and the  
number of hours worked is 38?
2 
What is the weekly wage if the hourly rate is $20.00 and the number  
of hours worked is 38?
Casual loadings are extra percentage amounts added to the base rate of casual workers 
because they don’t receive paid annual leave or paid personal leave. The actual percentage 
depends on the award you are covered by, but is usually 15–30%. Under his award, John’s 
base hourly rate is $11.00. However, John is a casual employee so he is entitled to an extra 
15% of this amount per hour. 
To work this out on a calculator, press these keys: 1  1  .  0  0  ×  1  5  %  
The answer is 1.65, which means that $1.65 is added to John’s base hourly rate to make 
$12.65 per hour: $11.00 (base rate) + $1.65 (15% casual loading) = $12.65 (hourly rate)
3 
If Alyson is a casual worker with a base hourly rate of $12.00 and a casual loading  
of 20%, what is her hourly rate? Circle the correct answer.
$15.00          $14.40          $13.50
4 
On her 17th birthday Alyson’s base hourly rate goes up to $14.00. She  
also gets a casual loading of $20%. What will her new hourly rate be?
Penalty rates are higher rates of pay for work done outside normal working hours, such 
as late at night, on weekends and on public holidays. Penalty rates are sometimes called 
‘getting time and a half’ for 150% or ‘double time’ for 200%. The rate is calculated  
as a percentage of your base hourly rate and depends on your 
award. For example, some awards state that you must be paid 
200% of your hourly rate for working on a public holiday. 
Let’s look at John whose casual hourly rate is $12.65. If he works  
on Australia Day and his award states that he should receive 200%  
of his usual rate for working on a public holiday, his hourly rate for 
that day would be: 
$12.65 (hourly rate) × 200% (penalty rate)  
= $25.30 (public holiday hourly rate)
5 
Ben receives a penalty rate of 150% for working on a Sunday.  
If his usual hourly rate is $12.00, what is his Sunday hourly rate?

if he works for 8 hours on a Sunday.
Allowances are extra amounts paid to employees for expenses such as cleaning your 
uniform, using your own car or tools, or for working in certain areas or in dirty or 
dangerous conditions. For example, when John has to work in a refrigerated coldroom, he 
receives an extra cold work allowance. He is also required to wear a uniform and receives 
an extra amount each shift for laundering (cleaning) it.

4.4 Superannuation
Read the information about base rates and extra  
amounts then answer the following questions.  
You may need a calculator or working paper.
Superannuation (super) is an extra amount an employer 
must pay to help fund their employees’ retirement. This 
means that when people retire from work and are not 
earning any wages, they can use their superannuation 
funds to pay for their living expenses. The rules about 
superannuation change from time to time. Currently, an 
employer pays 9.25% of their employees’ gross weekly 
wage for all employees:
•  aged 18 years or over and earning $450 or more 
each month
•  under 18 years, working more than 30 hours per 
week and earning $450 or more each month.
This amount must be paid directly into 
a superannuation fund. You can choose 
your own superannuation fund or your 
employer must pay into the MySuper fund. 
It makes sense to keep the same super fund 
throughout your working life – that way, you 
pay less in fees and it is easier to keep track 
of your superannuation savings. 
The percentage rate that employers 
have to contribute to their employees’ 
superannuation fund can change.  
In July 2013 the government proposed 
these rate changes in the future:
• 2012–13: 9% 
• 2013–14: 9.25% 
• 2014–15: 9.50% • 2015–16: 10%.

monthly earnings are $440.00. Does his employer have to pay Anthony superannuation?

superannuation fund after one year (52 weeks)?

4.5 Deductions and income tax
Read the information below about deductions and tax then answer the following 
questions.
Deductions are amounts that are taken out (deducted) from your wages. Your employer can 
deduct income tax from your wages but cannot deduct anything else that is not required by 
law without your written permission. If you are under 18, the employer must get permission 
from your parent or guardian. For example, if you work in a restaurant and you break 
something or a customer doesn’t pay their bill, this cannot be taken out of your wages. 
Employers use a ‘tax table’ from the Australian Tax Office (ATO) to work out how much tax 
to take out of their employees’ wages, and pays this money to the ATO. The ATO then has 
a record of how much tax you have paid and how much money you have earned. This tax 
is called PAYG, which stands for Pay As You Go. All employers must provide a payment 
summary at the end of each financial year (1 July to 30 June) which lists your earnings and 
tax paid for that financial year. You need this summary to fill out your tax return. 
If you filled out a tax file number declaration when you started your job and you earn 
under a certain amount, you may not have to pay any income tax at all. For example, in the 
2012–13 financial year, an Australian resident with an income of up to $18,200 each year 
($350.00 each week) usually did not have to pay income tax.

An expense is something you spend money on. Expenses are sometimes called 
outgoings because your money is ‘going out’. If your income is more than your 
expenses, you can save money. But if your expenses are more than your income you 
will owe money. 
An expense can be for goods or services. Goods are solid things you can touch, such 
as food, books, cars or clothing. A service is something a person or company does for 
you, usually for payment. Examples of services include hairdressing, medical advice 
and treatment, accountancy, banking and phone and internet provision.

5.4 Different types of expenses
Oh no! The Year 10 formal is on next Saturday night

appointment with my hairdresser and, if I can afford it, I’ll 
book the manicurist for my nails too. Dean is my date for 
the night and he said he would book the transport for our 
group but I must remember to book the photographer. I 
hope Dean has remembered to organise his suit and tie for 
the formal. I should also pay for my mobile phone service 
before Saturday night. Alice said she would get some 
flowers for Ali’s mother too because we’re all going to her 
place for the after-party. Can’t wait, should be so much fun!
Fixed or variable? 
Expenses that don’t vary much and have to be paid regularly each week or month are 
called fixed expenses. These include rent, car payments and loan repayments. Variable 
expenses are those that vary or change according to how much you choose to spend. For 
example, food, clothing and entertainment expenses can vary from week to week.

5.4 Different types of expenses (cont’d)
Tax-deductible or non-tax-deductible?
Expenses that are necessary for you to earn an income or run your business are usually  
tax-deductible expenses. This means that these expenses are deducted from your gross 
income so you pay less tax. For example, if you own a business, the wages you pay to your 
staff and the rent you pay for your shop are tax-deductible expenses. If you are an employee 
and your job requires you to wear protective clothing, that clothing is a tax-deductible 
expense. Anything that is not related to earning your income is a personal expense and is 
not tax-deductible.

Read the information below about needs and wants and answer the following 
questions.
Basic needs are the things we require to survive. They include water, food, clothing and 
shelter. We also have other needs that significantly improve our quality of life, such as 
transport, education and health care. 
Personal circumstances, such as the place you live and your age, can determine whether 
something is really a need. For example, for someone living in a rural area or a place with 
no public transport, a car could be a need. It may not be for a person living close to school 
or work in an area with good public transport.
Wants are things we would like to have but these things are not absolutely necessary for 
survival. We should pay for our needs first and then decide which wants we can afford. Let’s 
face it – life would be pretty boring if we have none of our wants! However, advertising, 
marketing and peer pressure can persuade us to buy things we don’t need and cannot 
afford. When you are trying to stick to a budget or to save money, always think twice before 
spending. Ask yourself: Do I really need this? Can I live without it? What will happen if I 
don’t have it? How much can I save if I don’t buy it? Is there a cheaper alternative? 
It is important to understand your own 
needs and wants so you can make wise 
spending choices and learn how to budget 
and save. When you earn your own money 
you are able to see how much you have to 
work to earn the money you spend. This 
is called learning the value of money 
and it is an important lesson. Perhaps 
you will be less likely to splurge 
on expensive items you don’t 
really need when you 
consider how hard you 
have to work to earn  
that money.
